Accuracy and availability of NPR transcripts may vary. Transcript text may be revised to correct errors or match updates to audio. Audio on npr.org may be edited after its original broadcast or publication. The authoritative record of NPR’s programming is the audio record.

World.title: Kennedy Center Board votes again to shut main building down — and add Trump's name back
World.content:
Kennedy Center Board votes again to shut main building down — and add Trump's name back

toggle caption Alex Wroblewski/AFP via Getty Images

On Thursday, the board of the Kennedy Center voted a second time to shut down most of the Washington, D.C., arts complex for what is being described as a two-year major renovation plan, according to a person briefed on the vote.

In March, the center's board approved a full shutdown of the complex for major renovations, but a federal judge later ruled to temporarily block the planned closure, saying that no board members had "sufficient information" to make such a decision.

In a test of both the same judge's previous ruling and a related appeals court ruling, the board also voted on Thursday to put President Trump's name back on the center's entry, calling the complex, "Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump."

Sponsor Message

In this most recent vote, the board elected to close the center's main building, while keeping The REACH, a 2019 addition, open for limited programming and as a memorial to the late President John F. Kennedy. According to the plan approved by the board, the $250 million project includes structural repairs, new marble floors, nearly $12 million in "acoustical improvements" and a plan to temporarily move the famed, eight-foot, bronze bust of Kennedy that sits in the center's main foyer. Under this plan, the main campus would reopen in the summer of 2028. The details of the proposal and the potential name change were first reported by The New York Times. The individual who was briefed on the vote spoke to NPR on the condition of anonymity, because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

The board's decisions will be subject to the federal judge's approval. Thursday's board meeting was held by Zoom, and was not public.

In the days leading up to Thursday's vote, Democratic legislators who serve as ex-officio Kennedy Center trustees told the Washington Post that they had still not been given access to any assessments of what such a closure would mean for the long-term wellbeing of the institution. The arts complex is chaired by President Trump, and the majority of its current board are Trump allies appointed by the president.

Sponsor Message

NPR has requested comment from the Kennedy Center, but did not receive an immediate reply. It is unclear whether or not the construction management firm named in the plans, JLL, has any experience with arts venues that feature unamplified performances, such as the orchestras, solo and chamber instrumentalists, opera companies and dance ensembles that have comprised much of the Kennedy Center's programming for decades. It is unclear how many companies bid on the contract, or how the firm was selected.

Last December, one of the center's ex-officio board members, Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, filed a federal lawsuit against Trump and the board to reverse the center's name change and halt the renovation plans. In March, a group of eight architecture and culture groups filed a separate suit to block the renovation. In May, the judge in the Beatty suit temporarily blocked the Trump closure plan. Judge Christopher Cooper wrote: "None of the board members had sufficient information in advance of the March 16 meeting to make a well-considered decision to close the center."

In February, Trump wrote on Truth Social that there had been "a one year review of The Trump Kennedy Center, that has taken place with Contractors, Musical Experts, Art Institutions, and other Advisors and Consultants" to decide between a complete or partial closure for his intended renovations. In his May ruling, Judge Cooper wrote: "The evidence of any such review is nil."

In a statement emailed to NPR Thursday afternoon, Rep. Beatty said: "This morning's decision to close the center and the surprise agenda item to put Donald Trump's name back on the building was more of the same. This latest development is a transparent effort to circumvent the court's ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed. I will continue to fight for this treasured national monument."

Sponsor Message

The center, once a bustling arts complex that offered free public performances 365 days a year along with its ticketed concerts and educational offerings, now sits largely empty. In January, one of the center's primary resident organizations, Washington National Opera, left, and many marquee artists canceled their planned performances after Trump's name was added to the center in December 2025. Ticket sales plummeted, and scores of Kennedy Center staffers and administrators have also departed.

On Tuesday, the Washington Post reported that another resident artistic organization, the National Symphony Orchestra — whose budget is tethered to the complex — has been pushed to "the deepest financial crisis in its recent history," an assessment that multiple internal sources who were not authorized to speak with the media shared with NPR.

Last month, a federal appeals court denied President Trump's request to stop the removal of his name from the arts complex, saying that the president had failed to prove that the Kennedy Center would be "irreparably injured" without Trump's name attached to it.

On Monday, a Washington, D.C., superior court judge ordered the Kennedy Center to pay Chuck Redd, a jazz musician, more than $252,000 to cover his legal fees after the center sued him. Redd had canceled a December 2025 performance

after Trump's name was added to the complex

— it was a Christmas Eve show that Redd had hosted there for nearly 20 years . The Kennedy Center told NPR that it intends to appeal the decision.

A large tarp has covered the building's entrance since June, when the center complied with the court's order to remove Trump's name from the complex. As of Thursday, the tarp remains in place.



This digital story was edited by Jennifer Vanasco.

World.title: Mangione could plead guilty in federal case ahead of N.Y. murder trial
World.content:
Mangione could plead guilty in federal case ahead of N.Y. murder trial

toggle caption Steven Hirsch/Pool New York Post

Federal prosecutors and Luigi Mangione's defense team will hold a special court conference Friday morning in Manhattan federal court, raising intense speculation that the two sides may have reached a plea agreement.

The two sides requested the surprise hearing before Judge Margaret Garnett less than a month before Mangione's state trial is set to begin. Asked about the purpose of the session at a press conference Wednesday, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, James McDonald, declined to comment.

"There's a conference scheduled for 11 a.m. on Friday — that's all we can say at this time," McDonald said.

Sponsor Message

Mangione faces criminal charges in both state and federal court following the murder of Brian Thompson, the UnitedHealthcare CEO who was gunned down on a Manhattan street in December 2024.

"Why would they be going to federal court tomorrow when they should be preparing for the state trial?" said Gary Galperin, a professor of law at Cardozo School of Law and former prosecutor in the New York County district attorney's office. "It would be reasonable to speculate that they may be trying to enter a guilty plea."

After a nationwide manhunt, Mangione was later arrested in Altoona, Penn. Police officers seized a pistol and a notebook that included writings critical of the U.S. healthcare and insurance industries.

The case has drawn intense media scrutiny. Mangione, despite facing state and federal charges in what some are characterizing as a vigilante-style action against soaring medical costs, has attracted surprising levels of public support.

Federal charges against Mangione that threatened him with a possible death penalty were tossed by a judge in January 2026. Remaining charges, including a count of "interstate stalking resulting in death" could bring a sentence of life behind bars.

NPR sent a request for comment on the scope of any possible plea deal to federal prosecutors and to Mangione's attorneys, but received no immediate response.

Sponsor Message

Legal experts say a federal plea deal could limit or even derail efforts to try Mangione in state court on separate murder charges. That's because New York state has especially strict rules limiting "double-jeopardy" prosecutions, where a defendant is tried more than once on related charges.

The same rules prevented state prosecutors from bringing fraud charges against former Trump campaign manager Paul Manafort in 2019. A panel of state judges ruled that Manafort had already been convicted on similar counts in federal court. Manafort was later pardoned by President Trump.

To avoid that kind of legal bottleneck, the Manhattan district attorney's office maneuvered to hold Mangione's state trial first, with jury selection scheduled to begin on Sept. 8. The federal trial is expected to start in January.

In a letter sent last month to state Judge Gregory Carro, assistant Manhattan district attorney Joel Seidemann warned of possible complications if a federal plea deal is reached before a jury can hear the case.

"If a proposed federal guilty plea would operate to defeat a just outcome in the state prosecution, the people [the Manhattan DA's office] could advise the federal district court of that consequence, and the court should consider that fact in deciding whether to accept the plea, as well as any opposition by the victim's family to such a resolution," Seidemann wrote.

NPR asked the Manhattan DA's office whether it expects to play any role in Friday's hearing. A spokesperson directed all questions to the U.S. attorney's office.

World.title: Vladimir Putin's first visit to disputed Pacific islands draws Tokyo protest
World.content:
Vladimir Putin's first visit to disputed Pacific islands draws Tokyo protest

toggle caption Gavriil Grigorov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin

MOSCOW — Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday made his first visit to the Kuril Islands, a Moscow-controlled Pacific archipelago that also is claimed by Japan, which voiced a diplomatic protest over the trip.

Putin visited a fish plant, a hospital and a school on Iturup, one of the volcanic chain's southern islands. He also briefly spoke to local residents and met with the governor of Russia's Sakhalin region, Valery Limarenko.

Japan asserts territorial rights to the four southernmost islands of the chain, which it calls the Northern Territories. The Soviet Union took them from Japan in the final days of World War II, and the dispute kept the countries from signing a peace treaty formally ending their hostilities.

Sponsor Message

Decades of diplomatic efforts to negotiate a settlement haven't produced any visible results. Moscow over the years has also bolstered its military presence on the Kurils in moves that appeared to underscore its firm stance in the dispute.

Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said his country "strongly protests" Putin's visit to Iturup, which Japan calls Etorofu.

"The Northern Territories, including Etorofu (Iturup) Island, are Japan's inherent territory both historically and from the perspective of international law," Motegi said in a statement.

He summoned Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to the ministry in Tokyo and lodged a strong protest over the visit, requesting that he "promptly report the message back to Moscow," the minister told reporters afterward.

Later Thursday, the Russian Embassy in Japan called Tokyo's protest "unfounded" and said Nozdrev had explained that "the southern Kuril Islands are an integral part of the Russian Federation and became part of it following World War II on legitimate international grounds."

toggle caption Gavriil Grigorov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin via AP

Putin's travels are "sovereign decisions of the Russian leadership and can't be subject to discussion with foreign states," the statement added.

Japan also protested in 2021 when Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin visited Iturup.

Putin in recent days has visited several regions in Siberia and the Far East. Before coming to Iturup, he stopped on Sakhalin Island to attend the final part of drills by Russia's Pacific Fleet.

Sponsor Message

Speaking aboard a warship that was participating in the naval exercises, Putin said Wednesday that the current status of the Kuril Islands "is enshrined in international documents as a reality that arose following the outcome of World War II."

"But even here, Russia was prepared to seek a solution with the goal of concluding a peace treaty with Japan," he said.

Putin said that in the past, Moscow "had developed constructive relations with a number of Japanese leaders, including the tragically deceased former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, who did much to bring Japan and Russia closer together, to align our positions."

Japan imposed sanctions on Russia after it sent troops into Ukraine in February 2022 and "listed Russia as a source of primary threats," a change in that constructive relationship, he added.

Russia remains ready "to cooperate with all its neighbors, including Japan and other states in the region," Putin said.

toggle caption Kenzaburo Fukuhara/Kyodo News via AP

Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Putin's visit is "incompatible with the Japanese position on the Northern Territories" and is "absolutely unacceptable."

She said the visit was a further blow to the already-strained ties between the two countries over Ukraine, and that Moscow should understand the consequences.

"We must say this visit has further hardened Japanese public sentiment toward Russia and has made it more difficult to restore bilateral relations in the medium to long term," she said. "We hope the Russian side fully understands the seriousness of this."

One of the reasons Japan has made the effort to maintain ties with Russia is to allow former Japanese residents to return to the islands and pay tribute at their graves as a humanitarian consideration.

Dmitry Medvedev, Russia's former president and prime minister who now serves as deputy chair of the country's Security Council, responded to Takaichi's remarks on X by saying, "This chatter won't change a thing."

Sponsor Message

The Kuril Islands "were, are, and will remain Russian land," Medvedev, who himself visited the Kuril Islands four times as president and prime minister, wrote. "Anyone who fails to understand this will face the monstrous consequences of their delusion."

World.title: Carney, Trump to be given 'options' following latest trade talks, says U.S. rep
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said both U.S. President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Mark Carney will now be given "options" following trade talks between Canadian and U.S. trade officials on Thursday.

"The president, the prime minister, obviously they'll be given options and discussions," Greer said, in what is the clearest indication yet about how the negotiations are going from the Trump administration's perspective.

Greer, who spoke to CBC News exclusively following the talks, called the meetings "good" and "cordial."

"We are going to speak with the president. I believe Canadian officials will speak with the prime minister," Greer added in French.

Following the meeting, Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc told reporters he would "continue to do the work Canadians expect us to do."

LeBlanc didn't give a timeline as to how many more meetings there would be with Greer, adding "we'll have as many meetings as it takes."

CBC News has also learned that LeBlanc will brief the federal government's Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations on Friday afternoon to update them on how the negotiations are going, according to two sources with knowledge of tomorrow's meeting.

The committee serves as a forum where members can develop strategy for how Canada should approach its economic relationship with the U.S.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc, right, and chief trade negotiator Janice Charette take part in a news conference during the G7 summit in June. The two met again on Thursday with U.S. trade officials. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

LeBlanc will also brief provinces on Friday, according to Louise Blais, Quebec's envoy for the review of the CUSMA, who shared the details during an interview with Radio-Canada.

Both LeBlanc and chief trade negotiator Janice Charette met with Greer this afternoon. It was the second meeting this week between the Canadian and American trade officials, and the fourth in just three weeks.

The two sides have ramped up discussions since Trump threatened to impose 50 per cent duties on hundreds of Canadian goods, on top of sectoral tariffs already in place. Those tariffs are slated to come into effect Aug. 19.

Following this afternoon's meeting, Charette returned to the U.S. Trade Representative office to continue discussions with her counterpart late into the evening, a source told CBC News.

WATCH | New pitch for Trump in the works: Canada-U.S. trade reps working on new pitch for Trump | Duration 2:22 CBC News has learned Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer are working on a proposal to pitch to U.S. President Donald Trump before a tariff deadline that could see hundreds of Canadian goods hit with a 50 per cent levy.

As previously reported, sources on both sides of the border say the Americans offered a new proposal on Tuesday which would lower some of the sectoral tariffs but not to the degree that the Canadian side would like to see.

The Americans are also seeking a deal that would see preferential access to Canadian critical minerals and which covers security and energy, the sources said.

CBC News previously reported LeBlanc and Greer are aiming to present Trump with a path to a potential trade deal as early as Monday.

However, sources also told CBC News last week that the Canadian side has aggressively argued to the Americans that there would be no political appetite among Canadians to keep talks going if the Aug. 19 tariffs come into place.

Those tariffs, according to the U.S. government, are due to a number of trade irritants, including Canada's retaliation against U.S. trade policy with the removal of U.S. alcohol from provincial store shelves and alleged discrimination against U.S. motor vehicles and dairy.

The Canadian side is willing to offer movement on some of those concerns, according to industry sources with knowledge of the situation. In addition to ending the booze bans, Canada is also considering lifting retaliatory tariffs on U.S. autos and making some changes on dairy.

Ford open to putting U.S. booze back on shelves

Also Thursday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford — a frequent critic of Trump — said he'd be "more than happy" to bring U.S. booze back onto his province's shelves if a fair deal is reached that protects Ontario's steel, auto, forestry, agriculture and manufacturing sectors.

Ford also said his message to Americans is "a tariff on Canada is a tax on the American people."

"Remember when it comes to the [U.S.] midterms, you have to get that bully and send him a message," Ford said.

The Ontario premier's comments on U.S. alcohol bans echo those from Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette's office, who said in a statement last week the removal of U.S. alcohol from Société des alcools du Québec (SAQ) outlets will remain in effect "until an agreement that we deem fair has been negotiated."

"The sale of alcohol falls exclusively under the jurisdiction of the Quebec government. Quebec, and Quebec alone, will make that decision," the statement says.

World.title: WestJet agrees to pay settlement in sexual harassment suit
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WestJet has agreed to pay $4.5 million to settle a sexual harassment class-action lawsuit launched a decade ago involving more than 3,000 flight attendants, according to the lead plaintiff and her lawyer.

They say a B.C. judge on Monday approved the terms of the settlement, which were finalized in June. WestJet said in a statement it is "pleased" to have reached a settlement.

Former flight attendant Mandalena Lewis alleged that a pilot sexually assaulted her on a layover in Hawaii in 2010. After launching a lawsuit in 2016, other women who worked for the airline came forward and the case was certified as a class action by the B.C. Court of Appeal in 2022.

The flight attendants allege WestJet failed to provide a safe workplace with adequate anti-harassment measures.

Lewis told CBC News on Wednesday she is relieved the case is done with, but doesn't feel like the plaintiffs got "full justice." She said she is feeling deflated by the "symbolic" dollar amount and the fact that WestJet did not admit wrongdoing under the terms of the agreement.

"It's the best we could get given the circumstances. I had to fight tooth and nail for these slivers," Lewis said.

The $4.5 million will be distributed among 3,452 flight attendants after expenses are deducted, including legal fees.

She said that works out to about $400 for each flight attendant involved in the suit.

Lewis says the judge also reduced her honorarium that was agreed to be paid out in the settlement, to $10,000 from $20,000.

"At the end of the day, I'm glad this is over, I am glad we set a legal precedent. I'm not glad with the number, I don't think it's enough."

Mandalena Lewis in a video interview with CBC News Wednesday. Lewis says she is relieved the legal process is over, but doesn't feel the plaintiffs got 'full justice.' (CBC News)

WestJet said in an email to CBC News it is "committed to strengthening our operations and training, focused on the safety and well-being of all WestJetters" and "focused on advancing a culture of empowerment."

Under the terms of the settlement, WestJet is to retain a third-party consultant to conduct a workplace assessment to determine the prevalence of harassment in the workplace, the extent of underreporting and how to make reporting and response systems more effective.

Legal process a 'nightmare': Lewis

In an affidavit, Lewis said speaking with and supporting more than 100 former flight attendants regarding their experiences with sexual harassment — conversations she had in her role as lead plaintiff — took an extreme physical and emotional toll throughout the legal process.

She told CBC News on Wednesday that the experience has been a "nightmare."

Lewis said the sexual assault and harassment of female flight attendants is a "deep-seated, historical, systemic issue" that continues in the airline industry today.

"I took it on because I knew what a huge problem it was," she said. "I did it for myself and I did for other flight attendants who I know went through what I went through. And many are still going through it."

WATCH | WestJet agrees to pay $4.5 million to settle class-action lawsuit: WestJet to settle flight attendants' sexual harassment suit for $4.5M | Duration 2:07 WestJet has agreed to a $4.5 million settlement in a decade-long class action lawsuit launched by female flight attendants alleging the company failed to maintain a safe workplace after the alleged sexual assault of two female flight attendants by a pilot.

Lewis has said she reported the alleged 2010 assault to her managers and to the RCMP, who contacted police in Maui at the time. The U.S. federal prosecutor in Maui laid charges, but Lewis said she was told the pilot could only be arrested if he returned to the island.

Later, another flight attendant reached out to Lewis and alleged that she had been sexually assaulted by the same pilot in 2008.

In 2016, the airline fired Lewis for insubordination after she had demanded for months to see her employment record to determine whether WestJet took any action on her complaint.

The class-action suit settled Monday alleged that WestJet “breached contracts of employment with female flight attendants by failing to implement and maintain an adequate anti-harassment program, including adequate systems and practices for reporting, investigating, and responding to workplace harassment” between April 4, 2016 and Feb. 28, 2021.

WestJet denied those allegations.

The basis for compensation was costs that WestJet allegedly avoided through its failure to implement an adequate anti-harassment program, rather than compensation for harms suffered by the flight attendants.

Good deal for WestJet: lawyer

Joshua Coratti, associate lawyer with the Toronto employment law firm Ball Professional Corporation, says the settlement looks like a "pretty good deal" for WestJet, as it absolves them of liability for individual claims from plaintiffs, which could have been more costly.

"Doing a class-action lawsuit, you often end up with a lot less in terms of the monetary value for each individual plaintiff. As it turns out, typically lawyers are the ones who win the class action lawsuits. They're the ones collecting very large legal fees," Coratti told CBC News.

"What it can do, is it can show that certain behaviour is not permitted. It can get companies to be a little bit more hesitant to engage in large-scale violations to that effect."

World.title: 'Stuff happens': Doug Ford says he was unaware party allegedly followed former Liberal leader to Jamaica
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said he was unaware until Wednesday of his Progressive Conservative Party spending money to allegedly surveil former Liberal leader Bonnie Crombie in Jamaica in 2023.

The Trillium and POLICORNER reported on Thursday that the provincial party allegedly spent nearly $3,000 in donor and taxpayer dollars on two five-star resorts in Jamaica "to spy on" Bonnie Crombie as part of opposition research work. The story cited the claims to anonymous sources familiar with the plan.

The alleged surveillance took place six days after Crombie won the Liberal leadership in December 2023, when she was on a three-day vacation in Jamaica, The Trillium and POLICORNER reported.

CBC News has not independently confirmed The Trillium and POLICORNER's reporting.

However, in a statement on Thursday, the Ontario PC Party said: "The Ontario PC Party, like other political parties, conducts opposition research. In this instance, that work included travel to Jamaica in December 2023."

Ford said at an unrelated news conference Thursday that he does not approve of the alleged spying and he spoke to the party after hearing the claims Wednesday.

Ford said it was party money spent on the expense. Political parties in Ontario receive a per-vote subsidy, so party budgets are partly made up of taxpayer money.

"Things happen" in politics, Ford said, adding the trip was "no different" than when members of the media follow him on trips to the U.S.

Former Liberal leader Bonnie Crombie did not comment on the allegations, but did confirm that she vacationed in Jamaica in December 2023 and that she stayed at one of the hotels listed in the PC party's 2023 financial statement. (Patrick Morrell/CBC News)

When asked if being unaware of the incident absolves him of any blame, Ford said he relies on his team to make sure money is being spent appropriately.

"I don't watch every single dollar when I'm in the middle of a campaign," he said.

Ford was also asked if these tactics would continue, to which he replied, "I hope not."

"Let's just have fair and balanced elections," he said. "Stuff happens during elections."

Crombie said she is not commenting at this time, but confirmed to CBC News that she did take a vacation in Jamaica after the leadership race in 2023 and stayed at the Ocean Eden Bay resort.

CBC News obtained a copy of the PC Party's 2023 annual financial statement from the NDP. It showed office and administration expenses of $1,000.05 at the Ocean Eden Bay and $1,971.67 at the Royalton Negril Hotel, another resort in Jamaica.

The statement did not have information on when these expenses were incurred, for how long, or who claimed them. There are also no details on what the spending at the Royalton Negril Hotel was for.

'Heads need to roll': opposition party leaders

In a post on social media platform X, NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the alleged spying is "disgusting" and that Ford should not be allowed to "shrug it off."

"Spying on a woman who is one of your political opponents on her private vacation is creepy Trump-style politics that has no place here," she said.

Stiles said someone within the party had to sign off on the expense and that Ford will know exactly who it is.

"Heads need to roll," she said.

John Fraser, interim Leader of the Ontario Liberals, called on Ford to explain why someone was allegedly sent to follow Crombie to Jamaica and who exactly was involved.

"This isn't politics. This is creepy, disturbing behaviour and a complete abuse of power," said Fraser.

He said it was "extraordinary abuse of public money" to use donor and taxpayer funds to follow an opponent.

"It raises serious questions about how far Doug Ford is willing to go to target his political opponents, and whether this has happened before."

World.title: Summer McIntosh shatters Pan Pacs record in 400m medley, beating Aussie Jenna Forrester
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

World record holder Summer McIntosh won gold in the women’s 400m individual medley in 4:28.01 at the 2026 Pan Pacific Swimming Championships in Irvine, Calif.

Summer McIntosh earned a gold medal Thursday night, her first-ever victory at the Pan Pacific swimming competition, defeating Jenna Forrester of Australia in championship record time in the women’s 400-metre individual medley in Irvine, Calif.

The Toronto athlete, who was on pace early on to lower her world record from last year, finished the butterfly, backstroke, breaststroke and freestyle in four minutes, 28.01 seconds. Forrester was nearly three seconds behind in 4:31.50 for silver, while Agostina Hein of Argentina took bronze (4:32.54).

American Elizabeth Beisel held the previous Pan Pacs record time of 4:31.99 since 2014.

"I wanted to attack the race coming off yesterday," McIntosh, referring to a silver medal in the 200 free on Wednesday, told USA Swimming. "I was really pumped up. It's good to get the win."

In the 200 free, McIntosh touched the wall in one minute 53.86 seconds, nearly 2-10ths behind Australia's Lani Pallister, who clocked a championship record 1:53.67.

" I don't think I was out fast enough. My turns were still not right and I think I was just over-thinking it, rather than just racing," McIntosh told Devin Heroux of CBC Sports post-race.

WATCH | McIntosh 'happy to get my hand on the wall first for Canada': Summer McIntosh believes she was 'capable of more tonight' | Duration 1:33 Summer McIntosh spoke with CBC Sports’ Devin Heroux after winning gold in the women’s 400m individual medley at the 2026 Pan Pacific Swimming Championships.

"You have to forget about it and focus on the next day and take it one race at a time, which is what I always try to do, good or bad," the Canadian added Thursday.

McIntosh believed she was "capable of more" in the medley but happy she touched the wall first.

After the race, the Canadian national anthem drew a roar and much excitement from a throng of youths in the crowd.

"That group of kids up there [in the stands] is cute to see," McIntosh said. "Even giving them a small wave, they went crazy. It's an honour to give people a show every time [I race] and be part of that. I know all the swimmers here, that's their goal."

WATCH | McIntosh says relay bronze 'big moment' for Canadian team: Summer McIntosh admits she ‘forgot how fun relays are’ after Canada's bronze-medal performance in 4x200m | Duration 1:48 Canada’s relay team of Mary-Sophie Harvey, Summer McIntosh, Emma O’Croinin and Brooklyn Douthwright spoke with CBC Sports’ Devin Heroux after winning bronze in the women’s 4x200-metre freestyle relay at the 2026 Pan Pacific Swimming Championships.

Later in the evening, McIntosh pulled Canada into third spot after two legs of the women's 4x200 freestyle relay, and Emma O'Croinin and anchor Brooklyn Douthwright were able to help keep Canada there for a bronze medal.

The Canadians, who had Mary-Sophie Harvey swim the opening leg, posted a time of 7:52.74, well back of victorious Australia (7:42.40 championship record) and the United States (7:43.10).

Harvey admitted to being nervous and not in peak form in the team's post-race interview with Heroux.

Australia led for all but 150 metres

"I knew I had to get [the job] done for the girls and I'm very happy we came away with the bronze," she said. "We want to stay on that [medal] podium until L.A. [and the 2028 Olympics]."

Australia led for all but 150 metres, with Inez Miller, Lani Pallister, Hannah Casey and Milla Jansen lowering the country's championship mark of 7:44.12 set at the 2018 Pan Pacs.

Katie Ledecky swam the anchor leg for the U.S., but couldn't overhaul Jansen although she got within a body length in the closing metres. Erin Gemmell, Anna Peplowski, Rylee Erisman and Ledecky also went under the old championship mark.

"I've kind of struggled with the 200 individually from a flat start over the last couple years, but I always know I'll have something in me for the relay and I'll pull out a good split," Ledecky said. "I love swimming that anchor leg."

WATCH | McIntosh helps Canadian women to 200m freestyle relay bronze: Summer McIntosh snags 3rd medal of Pan Pacs as Canada’s women’s 4x200m freestyle relay hold on for bronze | Duration 12:04 Canada’s relay team of Mary-Sophie Harvey, Summer McIntosh, Emma O’Croinin and Brooklyn Douthwright finished just ahead of China to win bronze in the women’s 4x200-metre freestyle relay, clocking 7:52.74 at the 2026 Pan Pacific Swimming Championships in Irvine, Calif.

McIntosh said she forgot how much fun she has competing in a relay race.

In the men's 400 IM, Tristan Jankovics of Puslinch, Ont., and Calgary's Lorne Wigginton were 7-8 in a field of eight. Jankovics clocked 4:14.14, with Wigginton 80-100ths behind him. Japan's Tomoyuki Matsushita won in 4:06.75, a championship record.

His time erased American Ryan Lochte's championship mark of 4:07.59 set at the 2010 Pan Pacs, also in Irvine.

"Next time I come back to the U.S. I'm going to get gold again," a smiling Matsushita said through a translator.

Taylor Ruck of Kelowna, B.C., delivered a fifth-place finish in the women's 100 free.

The 26-year-old recorded a time of 53.16 seconds after going 53.69 to qualify for the final at William Woollett Jr. Aquatics Center.

Meg Harris of Australia charged late, overcoming Gretchen Walsh in the final 25 metres to win in 52.60, 18-100ths of a second in front of the American sensation. Harris's teammate, Olivia Wunsch reached the finish in 52.98 for the bronze medal.

Ruck grabbed three bronze on the opening day of competition Wednesday in the women's 50 butterfly, 100 backstroke and was part of the 100 medley relay team with Ingrid Wilm, Oliver Dawson and Finlay Knox.

WATCH | Full replay coverage of Day 2 Pan Pacs finals in California: 2026 Pan Pacific Swimming Championships: Day 2 finals | Duration 3:11:11 Watch the second day of competition at the 2026 Pan Pacific Swimming Championships in Irvine, Calif.

University of Calgary swimmer Alexanne Lepage delivered a 1:05.94 personal best in the women's 100 breaststroke, 2-10ths off the Canadian record held by Annamay Pierse (1:05.74) since July 9 2009.

Teammate Sophie Angus was also in the race and was seventh (1:06.70) following a 1:06.38 PB in the qualifiers.

Recently, the 27-year-old captured her first individual Commonwealth Games medal, tying for third in the women's 50 breaststroke. Angus w as born in Connecticut, but her parents are Canadian.

McKenzie Siroky of the U.S. topped the field in 1:05.32, followed by China's Tang Qianting (1:05.46) and Japan's Satomi Suzuki (1:05.65).

World.title: Young grizzly bear with limp killed in Nelson, B.C., sparks rally
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A rally took place in Nelson, B.C., on Thursday to protest the B.C. Conservation Officer Service's decision to kill a young grizzly bear.

The bear belonged to one of two families of grizzlies whose images have been shared widely as they travel in and around Nelson.

"There were a lot of tears and a lot of hugs at the rally," said Katie Graves, founder of the non-profit Ursa Project Society.

The Ursa Project Society said community members gathered on Thursday after a young grizzly bear with a leg injury or deformity was killed by conservation officers. (Bix Burkhart/The Ursa Project Society)

Graves said the grizzly — a yearling with either a leg deformity or leg injury — shouldn't have been killed.

She said the wild animal was mobile, kept up with its family and was able to feed.

“Especially as it got older, you could see it running, and it would run so fast, but it would really hold up that leg, basically run on three legs.

"There are many, many bears in the wild that are what we call tripods and they live full lives."

In a statement issued Wednesday, the B.C. Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS) said the bear's age, injury and history of conflict made it unsuitable for rehabilitation or relocation. It did not provide details about any conflicts.

"It is always unfortunate if an injured, sick or conflict bear needs to be safely and humanely put down," the BCCOS said. "These decisions are not made lightly."

Graves said the mother bear brought cubs to the area in 2023, was relocated and returned shortly afterward.

The conservation service has not replied to requests about the status of the other grizzlies — a sow and two yearlings — but said any captured bear will be assessed to determine next steps.

The incident has sparked hundreds of comments in community Facebook groups, most of which have been critical of any decision to kill a grizzly.

A number of other people noted that conservation officers are trying to protect the public and don't want to have to shoot bears.

There was widespread agreement that people could do a better job of securing their garbage and keeping the bears at a distance.

WATCH | Ban on grizzly bear hunting should remain, said conservationist: Conservationist says B.C. ban on grizzly bear hunting should remain | Duration 6:50

Wildlife biologist Clayton Lamb said that to prevent more bear deaths, the province and municipalities need stronger policies to reduce attractants.

“At the heart of it, we as people that live in these mountain landscapes are at times attracting bears in the town … whether it's unmanaged garbage or not picking your apple tree or not putting an electric fence around your chickens,” he said.

“It's really trying to harden off the attractions of those communities and reduce those conflicts before they start.”

Lamb said once a bear becomes habituated or food conditioned, it’s very challenging to rehabilitate and relocate them, especially when they are comfortable being in town.

“At the end of the day, she still is a grizzly bear. Her cubs are still grizzly bears, that base instinct to protect your cubs and to ... defend your space and yourself is in that bear’s DNA.”

Managing attractants, he said, will prevent more grizzly bear families from entering towns in the future.

The City of Nelson said in a statement on Thursday that it’s working to prevent conflict and keep bears wild. That includes helping the community install bear-resistant garbage cans and providing public education programs.

It also said bylaw services are working to ensure waste and wildlife attractant rules are being followed and will address unsecured garbage and unmanaged compost when necessary.

World.title: 12 international students at Calgary protest referred to CBSA office after status check
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A dozen people who took part in a weeks-long international student protest in northeast Calgary have been flagged as "being possibly inadmissible" and, according to an immigration lawyer, could be forced to leave Canada.

Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) confirmed officers were called to attend the protest site on Wednesday to check attendees' immigration statuses.

According to a CBSA spokesperson, officers verified the statuses of 20 people, and 12 were identified as being possibly inadmissible under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

“The individuals were asked to attend the CBSA office later that day for a follow-up interview. Due to privacy legislation, no additional details on these cases will be provided,” said the spokesperson.

The agency says everyone who's subject to immigration enforcement action, including those ordered to be removed from Canada, "have access to due process before the law."

International graduates and others in support of their cause had been protesting issues with work permits at Saddletowne Circle, down the street from the Genesis Centre, for weeks.

Similar protests are happening in Edmonton, with some Alberta students participating in hunger strikes to draw attention to the issue.

Protesting work permit denials

Some graduates who studied at Portage College say they were under the impression they would be eligible for post-graduation work permits when they finished school.

But once they applied, many of their permits were denied.

Portage College says it’s seeking clarification from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC).

“Portage College's understanding was that students enrolled in non-credit public-private partnership programs prior to May 15, 2024 would be eligible to apply for a Post-Graduation Work Permit, if they were enrolled before the May 2024 changes, consistent with the information available at the time and the way these applications had historically been administered by IRCC,” said spokesperson Andre Delaire.

CBC News has reached out to IRCC for comment.

Calgary police requested status check

It was the Calgary Police Service that called the CBSA for help on Wednesday.

In a statement to CBC News, a police spokesperson said the demonstration began on July 24 and “has largely been peaceful in nature,” but police had received complaints about excessive noise, obstructing businesses, disturbances and public intoxication.

On Wednesday, police responded to a report of people blocking parts of the sidewalk and impeding pedestrians.

“During that interaction, officers requested identification from individuals who had set up tents or other structures without a permit on city property,” said a CPS spokesperson.

“As a result of concerns related to the identification provided, officers contacted the Canada Border Services Agency for verification.”

The CBSA said officers were initially called to check the status of four people, and after two of them were “not in compliance with their immigration status,” they did a broader check.

‘Like sheep waiting for the fox’

Jatin Shory, a Calgary immigration lawyer with Shory Law, is representing roughly a dozen students challenging their work permit denials in federal court. He advised them not to attend any public protests.

“This situation is unique in the immigration context because it is a large group of now officially undocumented individuals effectively advertising that they’re undocumented,” said Shory.

“It’s like sheep waiting for the fox to come into the den.”

Shory said CBSA has the right to investigate any tips it receives, and it’s likely the agency wanted to send a message “that immigration in Canada is fully transforming and you have to kind of get used to it.”

LISTEN | Canada's immigration 180: Front Burner 21:48 Canada's immigration 180: Part 1 It wasn't too long ago that much of Canada's political class was united in their embrace of immigration to help grow the population and with it, the economy. Now, many of those same politicians are singing a different tune as it's regularly stated as fact that Canada's immigration consensus is broken. Today, part one of a two-part documentary on the political 180 on immigration, how it happened so quickly, and what it means for Canada as the country shrinks its population for the first time in history. For transcripts of Front Burner, please visit: https://www.cbc.ca/radio/frontburner/transcripts [https://www.cbc.ca/radio/frontburner/transcripts]

While the CBSA wouldn’t say whether the 12 people attended their interviews or what the outcome of those meetings was, Shory said there’s a common next step.

“It’s very common that if you were without status inside of Canada, you’re called in for an interview with CBSA, that you will be issued an exclusion order,” said Shory.

An exclusion order “means an individual must leave Canada immediately, confirm departure with the CBSA and cannot return to Canada for one year,” according to the CBSA website .

Shory said there are legal avenues people can take to fight that order, but they’re tough to win. Removal could be enforced within weeks, he said.

World.title: Liberal MP's travel documents show claims he voted on bills while in China are false
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

After Liberal MP Shaun Chen announced on Monday his plans to resign his seat in the House of Commons, he was accused online of breaking House rules by voting on legislation while he was in China earlier this year.

The claims, which were amplified by right-wing influencers and a handful of current and former Conservative MPs, are based on the date stamps on videos shared to the popular Chinese social media platform WeChat showing Chen visiting China.

The claim

"Shaun Chen enjoys some ice cream in a video posted on March 25th in China. Voting records show Shaun Chen voted electronically six times in the House of Commons on March 25th," reads one of a series of posts from independent journalist Andy Lee this week.

"If Shaun Chen voted remotely while in China, this is potentially a serious breach of national security. Accessing CCP controlled networks to sign in to secure parliamentary systems does not seem very smart," reads a post from another account.

Conservative MP John Barlow reposted a thread about Chen's travel, saying, "This goes much deeper than a trip to China. There are serious questions that need answers."

In a now-deleted reply to that post on X, Barlow then cited the House of Commons standing orders, which prohibit members of Parliament from voting while outside of Canada.

Many of the posts claimed Chen voted on the government's controversial hate crime legislation, Bill C-9, on March 25 while he was in China.

Lee said in a later post that it's possible the WeChat videos were edited and posted after the trip, but added it was "more than fair to question if he voted in China."

The facts

Members of Parliament are forbidden from participating in House votes while they are outside of the country.

The House of Commons standing orders, the rules that govern House procedures, state that electronic votes can only be cast within Canada.

Standing order 45 (12) (a) also states that a member's identity will be visually confirmed. MPs must log into an app to record their vote. The app uses facial recognition technology to confirm they are who they say they are.

A spokesperson for the office of House Speaker Francis Scarpaleggia said there are technical controls and human validation processes in place to ensure MPs are inside the country when they vote.

"These measures are implemented in accordance with House of Commons security and technology policies and are intended to detect and address circumstances that may indicate voting activity originating from outside Canada," the Speaker's office said.

Chen's office said the MP was in China between March 14 and March 22, and returned to Canada for the House of Commons sitting on March 23 following its spring recess.

Chen's office shared a copy of his boarding pass for the trip, which shows he was on a flight that left Taipei for Toronto at 6:50 p.m. local time on March 22. That route typically takes around 14 hours and lands on the same day, due to the time change.

The Canadian Press also has viewed a photo of the visa stamps in Chen's passport, which show his arrival in China was dated March 14 and his departure was dated March 22. CP is not sharing the photo because it contains private, personal information.

"The member of Parliament did not vote from outside Canada. As shared in his recent message about his resignation, his ongoing significant health issues prevent him from travelling to Ottawa as frequently as the role requires, so he has decided to step down," Chen's office said in an email.

"This was his first and only trip to China since May 2019, a trip he took with the Canada-China Legislative Association on official parliamentary business with other MPs and senators."

Chen said in a statement issued when he resigned that he was in a vehicle accident last fall while commuting between Toronto and Ottawa. He plans to leave his post next month.

A number of critics, including Lee, questioned this week why Chen would be well enough to travel to China but not to travel to Ottawa.

The trip to China was sponsored by the Hakka Canadian Association, a group that states its aim is to "promote friendships" among members of the Hakka ethnic group in Canada. It is chaired by Markham Coun. Joe Li.

Chen's office also shared emails between Chen and House of Commons IT staff co-ordinating his use of a loaned tablet and a phone with a temporary SIM card during the trip. The emails note that his travel was evaluated as having a "potentially high cybersecurity risk."

The Office of Canada's Conflict of Interest and Ethics Commissioner posted to its website a public disclosure including details of Chen's trip. The invitation from the Hakka Canadian Association says the trip was from March 14 to 22 and included seven nights in hotels.

World.title: Guacamoles and salsas linked to U.S. jalapeño salmonella outbreak recalled in Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) has issued a recall of some Whole Foods Market brand products, saying they've been linked to a salmonella outbreak in the U.S.

Various guacamoles, pico de gallos, salsas and prepared foods it says were distributed in Ontario stores and online are part of the 22-item recall list issued Thursday.

CFIA says there have been no reported illnesses associated with the consumption of these products in Canada, but urges anyone who thinks they may have become sick from consuming a recalled product to contact their health-care provider.

More than 300 cases in U.S.

The agency says the recall is associated with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) investigation of salmonella illnesses related to jalapeños from Sinaloa, Mexico, distributed by Coast Citrus Distributors.

The FDA says at least 345 people have fallen ill across the U.S. Officials say 36 hospitalizations are linked to the outbreak, with no recorded deaths.

A Public Health Agency of Canada spokesperson told CBC News in an email that the agency continually monitors outbreaks of enteric illnesses such as salmonella, and it is not currently investigating any salmonella illnesses associated with the U.S. outbreak.

A CFIA spokesperson told CBC News in an email last Thursday that, "at this time, there is no evidence that products implicated in this outbreak were distributed in Canada."

Food may not look or smell spoiled: CFIA

Salmonella is a type of bacteria that makes people sick with salmonellosis, an intestinal tract infection.

People most frequently get salmonella infections by ingesting food or water contaminated with feces that contains salmonella bacteria.

CFIA says food contaminated with salmonella may not look or smell spoiled, but can still make you sick.

Healthy people may experience fever, headache, vomiting, nausea, abdominal cramps and diarrhea, while young children, pregnant women, the elderly and people with weakened immune systems may contract serious and potentially deadly infections, according to CFIA.

People usually begin to exhibit symptoms between six hours and six days after they are infected, and the symptoms can last between four to seven days, according to the CDC.
