World.title: The job Zelenskyy can’t fill: Ukraine’s envoy to Trump’s Washington
World.content:
Zelenskyy moved his reshuffle plans forward so he could offer the ambassadorship to Yulia Svyrydenko, the outgoing prime minister, according to a former senior Ukrainian official and a Republican foreign expert familiar with the background to the shake-up. But she declined, disrupting his plans.

“It is no secret that I counted on and offered Yulia Svyrydenko the post of ambassador to the United States,” Zelenskyy said at a press conference in late July. He added that he was looking for a candidate with the highest possible qualifications: “a person at the level of a deputy prime minister, minister, or prime minister.”

Since then, however, other prospective candidates have proved equally reluctant, spurning what would in any case be the difficult job of handling Donald Trump’s unpredictable White House.

Ukrainians with sufficient heft and skill for the ambassadorship are looking at it askance, “worrying that they would not enjoy the conditions they would need to do the job properly,” said Ivanna Klympush-Tsintsadze, a prominent Ukrainian opposition lawmaker and former deputy prime minister who is a regular critic of Zelenskyy.

“Certainly that would be the case without having the ear of the president or his trust,” she added. That narrows Zelenskyy’s options sharply. The person would likely have to come from his tight inner circle of trusted aides, Klympush-Tsintsadze said, but there is no one there who seriously fits the bill.

“Framing it as if nobody wants the job would be a kind of oversimplification,” said a former Ukrainian diplomat who was granted anonymity in order to speak freely. “Of course, there are people who want the job, but there’s no one who really measures up to it. Zelenskyy is having a hard time filling the position.”

World.title: EU leaders are on holiday. The crises affecting the bloc aren’t.
World.content:
“Physical presence can signal much more effectively that these emotions are taken seriously and are heard,” she added.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez was just hours away from kicking off his weeks-long summer break when 72,000 migrants surged into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta on July 30. The Socialist leader duly postponed his plans and traveled to the North African coastal city, where he delivered a televised address pushing back against criticism from other EU leaders.

But as soon as the emergency was deemed to be under control, Sánchez resumed his scheduled vacation at a state-owned villa on the island of Lanzarote.

His decision to take time off, even as the political aftershocks continued to roil the bloc, drew criticism from opposition politicians like Elías Bendodo, deputy secretary of the center-right People’s Party, who this week accused the prime minister of “unprecedented selfishness” for taking time off while the situation in Ceuta is “far from normal.”

“Sánchez insults the Spanish people by remaining on his beach vacation,” he added.

The Spanish government rejected the criticism, noting the prime minister is not only reachable but actively participating in remote meetings, and insisted the state remains fully operational even when its top leaders are away.

World.title: Magyar casts doubt on Hungary-Russia nuclear power deal
World.content:
Rosatom CEO Alexei Likhachev wrote that the Russian state nuclear company was still on schedule with two new reactors at Paks despite Hungary’s change of government in April, which saw Magyar oust Russia-friendly incumbent Viktor Orbán.

Concrete preparation for Unit 5 is more than 80 percent complete, he said, while work on Unit 6 is advancing and reactor components are already being manufactured.

“We are ready for dialogue,” Likhachev said, adding that Rosatom had received no questions from Hungary’s new government.

Magyar challenged that account hours later. Under the original contract, Paks II should have been operating by 2024, he told reporters in a press conference Thursday. Instead, Hungary has spent roughly 1,000 billion forints (€2.8 billion) on a site he described as little more than depots and “two large concrete pits.”

“I don’t really see that they have adhered to the contract,” Magyar said. His government is now carrying out a full review of the project, including its financing and cooling arrangements.

The review cuts at one of Orbán’s signature deals with Russia. Orbán struck the Paks II agreement in Moscow in 2014, handing Rosatom the two-reactor expansion backed by up to €10 billion in Russian state financing. Two years later, he called it the “deal of the century.”

Those ties survived Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. As recently as March this year, Orbán’s foreign minister Péter Szijjártó admitted to discussing EU sanctions with senior Russian officials after leaked calls showed him boasting that a bank linked to Paks had been kept off a sanctions list.

Downstream, Romania shut the second and last operating reactor at Cernavodă on Thursday after the Danube fell too low to supply its cooling pumps.

World.title: NATO’s plan for a drone-infested battlefield: Let AI fly while humans decide who dies
World.content:
For NATO, AI-assisted drones would be part of the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative — a digital battlespace network the alliance is building to track threats along its borders with Russia and Belarus, which stretch from northern Finland to the Black Sea.

The new concept includes thousands of drones, sensors and satellites linked with AI to detect potential breaches of allied territory and repel attacks as the first line of defense. Conventional military forces, such as tanks, fighter jets and artillery, will remain the backbone.

U.S. Army Maj. Ben Schiff, a software operations officer, told Bild — which, like Business Insider and POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network — that both Ukraine and Russia still rely on humans to control drones.

While some systems have AI or machine-learning capabilities that allow brief moments of autonomy in flight, piloting is primarily performed by operators on the ground. Schiff said that “the most boring parts of flying”— drones loitering above the battlefield looking for targets — should be automated. But when it comes to deciding what the drone should strike, that’s where a human comes into play.

“So the humans are deciding what the drone does, but they don’t necessarily need to take the action of flying it because we don’t have a million pilots. We can’t fly a million drones at the same time,” said Schiff at the U.S. Army Europe and Africa headquarters in Wiesbaden, Germany.

Schiff is a product manager for the EFDI Data Backbone, a developing framework designed to help NATO forces detect, classify, share and act on information at speed and scale. The backbone bridges incompatible computer and command systems across multiple allied nations, allowing real-time data to flow from forward-deployed sensors all the way back to headquarters.

World.title: 'Total Eclipse Of The Heart' - Data reveals most popular songs played during this week's solar eclipse
World.content:
This week, more than 90 per cent of the Sun was obscured by the Moon, and in some cases in mainland Europe, was completely obscured in the first total eclipse since 1999.

 

According to new listening data from Spotify, streams of eclipse and space-themed songs surged during the solar eclipse, with Bonnie Tyler leading the way.

The data comparing streams on eclipse day against the 1-11 August daily average shows that the Welsh singer's hit song 'Total Eclipse Of The Heart' experienced a 14 per cent boost worldwide, including a whopping 94 per cent rise in the UK on 12 August.

The 80s power ballad had already seen a rise in streams following 8 July, the day Bonnie Tyler died "unexpectedly" aged 75 at a Portugal hospital.

Other "celestial" tracks to gain global momentum during the eclipse were:

Evolfo - Moon Eclipsed the Sun (+1,251%)

Chris Staples - Dark Side of the Moon (+405%)

Pink Floyd - Eclipse (+144%)

Delta Goodrem - Eclipse (+40%)

Bill Withers - Ain't No Sunshine (+3%)

Not to brag or anything, but three out of those six spiking songs were in Euronews Culture's curated eclipse playlist. Just sayin'...

Shannon Carragher, senior editor at Spotify, said: “Cultural phenomena like the solar eclipse naturally bring people together, and we instinctively look for the perfect soundtrack to share that moment."

She added: “Whether it’s collectively returning to iconic anthems like Total Eclipse of the Heart or seeking out more hidden celestial gems, these massive spikes in streaming show just how deeply we rely on music to elevate and connect us in the real world during shared human experiences.”

Bonnie Tyler on stage - 2013 AP Photo

Tyler's 'Total Eclipse Of The Heart' was released on 11 February 1983 and featured on her fifth studio album, 'Faster Than The Speed Of Night'. The song topped the UK Singles Chart and became the fifth-best-selling single in 1983.

The iconic love song sold more than 13 million copied worldwide. Its music video has surpassed 1.3 billion views on YouTube and has had over a billion streams on Spotify.

Following Tyler's death, it re-entered the UK Singles Chart, peaking at number 29.

Tyler's funeral service will take place on 17 August at St Mary's Church in Swansea, Wales.

World.title: NATO Baltic Air Policing jets shoot down drone over Latvia
World.content:
Fighter jets operating under NATO's Baltic Air Policing mission shot down a "foreign drone" in Latvian airspace on Friday, according to the country's military.

 

In a statement, the Latvian armed forces said the drone had entered Latvia "as a result of Russian electromagnetic warfare" and that it was intercepted over the Balvi region in the east of the country.

The military has deployed additional air defence units to Latvia's eastern borders and will continue to monitor its airspace, it said.

"As long as Russia's aggression in Ukraine continues, a recurrence of cases where foreign drones enter or approach Latvian airspace is possible," the military added in its statement.

Further airspace threats were identified in the municipalities of Augšdaugava, Preiļi, Rēzekne, Balvi, and Alūksne, but these have since ended.

The latest interception follows mounting drone incursions into NATO airspace along the alliance's eastern flank, which remains particularly vulnerable to security challenges arising from Russia's war in Ukraine, which began after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of the country in February 2022.

In July, Romanian fighter jets shot down three drones over just three days amid a surge in drone-related incidents in the country. The Romanian Prosecutor General's Office determined that at least one of the intercepted drones was of the Shahed-type used by Russian forces in its war against Ukraine, officials have said.

Romanian military divers also destroyed two Gerbera-type drones in the Black Sea on Tuesday, close to the Neptun Deep gas project.

"To ensure the safety of the shipping lane and the work being carried out around the platform, the decision was taken to carry out a controlled destruction by detonation," Romanian Defence Minister Radu Miruță said at the time.

In June, a Ukrainian sea drone exploded in the Romanian port of Constanta after the Ukrainian military said it had veered off course as a result of Russian electronic warfare interference.

Another drone exploded close to a compressor station of the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline in Bulgaria last week.

NATO allies gathered on Wednesday to discuss the recent drone incursions and incidents, signalling their "full solidarity with and support for the affected Allies."

"Allies reiterated that Russia bears full responsibility for the airspace violations, which are dangerous and unacceptable, and demonstrate Russia’s increasing tolerance for risk," NATO said in a statement, adding that it "stands ready to deter and defend against any aggression."

A Romanian F-16 fighter jet flies during an air policing exercise at Borcea Air Base 86, amid heightened security concerns over cross-border drone incursions linked to Russia. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

NATO's Baltic Air Policing mission sees allies deploy in four-month rotations to air bases at Šiauliai in Lithuania and Ämari in Estonia, where they can be called into action by the NATO Combined Air Operations Centre in Uedem, Germany.

Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia, as host nations, provide air command and control infrastructure and personnel for the mission, which was initially launched in 2004 and was expanded in 2014 following Russia's illegal annexation of the Crimean Peninsula.

World.title: 30,000 trees on 200 hectares: Europe's new mega-park is being built here
World.content:
With more than 30,000 trees and around three million shrubs covering 70 per cent of its area in greenery, The Ellinikon Park in Elliniko, Greece, will transform a former airport into one of the largest urban green spaces in Europe.

 

The 200-hectare park in the southern suburb of Athens is expected to open to the public in early 2027, with further infrastructure to be added through 2030.

This includes facilities for sustainable water management, such as a wastewater treatment unit with a capacity of 7,000 cubic metres of treated water per day, a storage tank holding 10,000 cubic metres, as well as a 'smart' irrigation system that can save up to 90 per cent of water.

At the same time, a network of "cool routes" is planned, where the temperature can be up to four degrees Celsius lower than in neighbouring asphalted areas.

Children playing in the fountain at the Ellinikon Experience Park AP Photo/Thanassis Stavrakis

A model for sustainable park design

The park is the subject of a guide to designing and operating sustainable green spaces, authored by landscape architect Dimitra Theochari and UNEP Global Chief Heat Officer Lenio Myrivili, who also acts as a Special Advisor for Climate Resilience.

The study records international practices for the design and operation of modern urban parks, using The Ellinikon Park as an example of how these principles are applied, bringing together the design and management of microclimate, water, vegetation, materials and routes.

This approach treats the park not simply as a leisure space but as an integrated piece of urban infrastructure capable of responding to the environmental challenges of the modern city.

Model of the urban park in Elliniko https://theellinikon.com

A park with cooling comfort woven into its design

Digital simulations were used to weave microclimates into the park's design, using thermal mapping and Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) to plan areas around shading and air flow. The simulations led to the design of the network of "cool routes".

Rest areas are being designed with a shading ratio of more than 60 per cent, while maintaining the potential for natural air circulation. Vegetation is also being used to enhance evapotranspiration and improve thermal comfort conditions.

Water features, including channels, misting systems and low-consumption basins, are integrated into the overall composition of the park. Their presence enhances evaporative cooling and helps lower ambient temperatures.

The park's network of paths will be integrated into the natural terrain to form a unified, accessible system with continuous shading. Individual paths will be embedded in the vegetation, creating pockets of microclimatic protection and a succession of light and shade.

Archive photo - Part of The Ellinikon Experience Park https://theellinikon.com

Smart use of water will help the park survive heatwaves

Continuous collection of data on air temperature, relative humidity, solar radiation, soil moisture and levels of shading will be used to manage the park's microclimate, irrigation and maintenance of green areas more effectively.

The park's smart irrigation system will use data from weather and soil sensors, allowing water volumes to be adjusted more precisely to the actual needs of the vegetation. According to the study, this approach can lead to water savings of up to 90 per cent.

The goal is to include more than 520 species of flora, around three-quarters of which will consist of native or suitably adapted species.

A tertiary wastewater treatment unit capable of producing up to 7,000 cubic metres of treated water per day will suppy all permitted non-potable uses, including irrigation.

Meanwhile, a storage tank with a capacity of 10,000 cubic metres is planned for irrigation water. This infrastructure will strengthen the park's water security and provide greater resilience during periods of increased heat stress.

Rainwater will be managed through green and blue infrastructure, with the aim of handling 100 per cent of it on site. At the same time, the restoration of natural flows is being pursued, such as that of the Trachones stream, which will play an important role as a flood-protection infrastructure.

The park will draw on local Greek materials

The park's surfaces and pavings will use Greek natural materials such as Kavala marble, white Dionysos-Penteli marble, Karystos slate and Mandras sandstone. They have been chosen both for their durability and contribution to thermal comfort, and to ensure the park blends harmoniously into the Attic landscape.

Materials originating from the former airport facilities will not be wasted but reintegrated into the new design. Concrete slabs are being used to build retaining walls, plinths and other structural elements, while crushed aggregates will be used in gabions and backfills, thereby reducing the construction's environmental footprint.

Archive photo/ The bioclimatic skyscraper under construction at The Ellinikon AP Photo/Yorgos Karahalis

How the park on the Athenian Riviera compares with others abroad

The Ellinikon Park will cover a total area of 2,000,000 square metres (200 hectares). At this scale, it will be the largest coastal urban park in Europe and one of the most ambitious urban regeneration projects worldwide.

To grasp its size, Ellinikon far surpasses some of the continent's most iconic historic parks. It is 40 per cent larger than London's Hyde Park (142 hectares), and is almost on a par with Berlin's vast Tiergarten (210 hectares). Ellinikon will be almost seven times larger than Brussels' Parc du Cinquantenaire (30 hectares).

Even when set against New York's world-famous Central Park (341 hectares), which is about 1.7 times bigger, Ellinikon stands as a project of comparable global scale.

The project's defining difference, however, lies in its coastal character. Most large European parks are enclosed within the urban fabric. By contrast, Ellinikon is directly connected to a two-kilometre seafront.

Among purely seaside European parks, it will be significantly larger and more modern than Barcelona's traditional Parc de la Ciutadella (around 31 hectares) and is four times bigger than the future fully developed Faliro Bay redevelopment (around 54 hectares) in Greece.

Only non-urban protected forests, such as Parco della Sterpaia in Tuscany (296 hectares), or vast national parks like Pembrokeshire Coast in Wales (62,000 hectares), exceed it in area.

World.title: "In our country, abandonment is normalised": animals are still left behind
World.content:
Ziro and Mike spent their whole lives in happy homes. For both of them, water, food and having their owners nearby was all they needed. Each lived alone with their now elderly owner. They were one another's only company. They did not know each other, did not walk the same streets, but at the end of their lives they shared the same home: SOS Animal's. In both cases, the owners left no document indicating what should happen to their friends; most likely they did not realise they could. Their future was therefore decided by a relative who chose to leave them on the street.

 

Ziro wandered the streets of Setúbal, was run over and beaten, and was left with serious injuries to his mouth. Mike was a ticking time bomb: a heart disease dictated his daily life and, despite the best efforts of the neighbours, friends of his owner, they could not help him in the way he needed. He stayed at SOS Animal until he died. Ziro is still at the association, waiting to be adopted.

Abandoning an animal in Portugal is a crime and has been punishable by law since 2014 with a prison sentence of up to six months or a fine of up to 60 days (source in Portuguese), but it is not always possible to see justice done. Sandra Duarte Cardoso, a veterinary surgeon and president of SOS Animal (source in Portuguese), has been fighting numerous battles in the name of animal protection and welfare.

"The microchip [for companion animals] is registered in the name of the person who has died, so the administrative offence is issued in the name of the deceased," she explains. "To date, of all the complaints we have filed – because whoever inherits the estate should also inherit the animals – none has ever resulted in a conviction, so no one has suffered any consequences for dumping their mother's or father's dog or cat on the street," she tells Euronews in an interview.

From left to right: Mike and Ziro SOS Animal

This Saturday, 15 August, is International Abandoned Animals Day, a harsh reality in Portugal that unfortunately worsens in the summer. "Nobody thinks about moving country, or house, and leaving their children behind or dropping them off at an organisation, but with animals they do," laments Sandra Duarte Cardoso, who deals with the situation every day.

In Portugal, microchipping dogs became compulsory in 2008 and cats in 2022, a measure introduced to combat animal abandonment. However, the rule is often ignored and, on its own, does not appear to have led to a fall in the number of abandoned pets.

Related European Parliament backs mandatory microchipping of all cats and dogs in the EU

The president of SOS Animal distinguishes between two types of situation: "There are surrenders, when people hand over their animals and look for a solution for an animal they no longer want or are able to keep; and there is abandonment, when they simply open the car door and leave the animal, or put it in a bag and dump it at the door of an association," she explains.

The National Republican Guard (GNR) warned in a statement at the end of July that, between 2024 and the first half of 2026, more than 2,400 crimes had been recorded and, in this context, 28 people had been arrested across the country.

According to the force, July and August see the highest number of incidents, with 142 cases (38.1% of the annual total), linked to people travelling on holiday.

SOS Animal, a non-governmental environmental organisation formally established in 2007, has a mission to protect and defend animals and their habitat. In addition to its veterinary clinic, it runs a sanctuary whose address is currently not made public. For a time, animals were being dumped there on a daily basis. "At the beginning, people would throw animals over the fence. I remember a case of a four-week-old puppy that was thrown in with other dogs running loose here, a goat that broke its legs, and cats were 'our daily bread'," she recalls in horror.

For Sandra Duarte Cardoso, there is a serious problem of "civic education" when it comes to our relationship with animals, and she struggles to understand how people capable of creating life can "discard another life".

"In our country, abandonment has been normalised," she begins, describing the daily stream of emails the association receives from people threatening the NGO that they will abandon their animals if it does not take them in. "They are so completely comfortable with this option that it becomes a form of blackmail. When no one in their right mind says: 'If you don't help me with my child, who has a problem, I'm going to abandon them, I'm going to leave them by the side of the road'," she says.

Sandra Duarte Cardoso traces these attitudes and behaviours back to the way people see animals. "Animals are still seen as a possession, as something a person owns, that is useful up to a point and, when it no longer is, they think they have the right to get rid of this 'thing' and that caring for it is not a non-negotiable responsibility," she says.

Why do people abandon animals?

In an article for the scientific journal "Journal of Applied Animal Welfare Science (source in Portuguese)" (JAAWS), published in 2022, the veterinary surgeon set out to identify the factors associated with the abandonment of dogs and cats by their owners in Portugal. The reasons most often cited were "lack of time to care for the animal", "illness of the animal", "lack of space" at home or aggressive behaviour towards other animals. The fact that animals destroyed things at home also came up frequently.

The post-pandemic period revealed just how many people lacked real commitment. "During Covid there was a boom in adoptions because many people suddenly had more time at home and adopted without knowing what their lives would look like later," she recalls. However, many had to return to their workplaces and, once they resumed their former routines, many of the animals adopted during the pandemic were returned to shelters.

According to Eurostat data from 2025, the cost of veterinary care and related services has risen by more than 30% in the eurozone and by almost 37% across the EU over the last decade, which has also been a factor that may be driving up the number of abandoned pets. "In fact, people often let animals reach an indescribable breaking point, and it is not because they want to, or because they are unaware of the animal's pain, but because they have no money," says the veterinary surgeon.

Putting animals down also ends up being a decision that is often taken not because the animal has no other chance, but because people cannot afford the treatment. "This is a dreadful situation," she says.

For Sandra Duarte Cardoso, the state's responsibility for this issue is glaring. The veterinary surgeon is highly critical of successive governments. "We are facing this structural, nationwide, agonising problem, and there needs to be an effective national strategy that also includes the islands," she argues. According to the president of SOS Animal, methodologies and cooperation proposals from international organisations have already been submitted, but "governments do not treat this as a priority".

One of the measures put forward by Sandra Duarte Cardoso is the compulsory sterilisation of dogs and cats. The proposal envisages large dogs being neutered by nine months of age and small dogs by six months. As for cats, she argues that "all should be neutered by five months of age".

In proven cases of financial hardship, people would receive a voucher for the sterilisation, which could cover the full cost or part of it.

In Greece, the sterilisation of dogs and cats may be compulsory, unless owners send in a sample of their animals' genetic material as a precaution. This allows the authorities to identify the animal in the event of abandonment or if litters from these animals are found.

Countries such as Belgium, Spain, Austria and Germany all have mandatory cat sterilisation laws, albeit with different nuances.

SOS Animal promotes responsible animal adoption and has its own protocol that requires supporting documents. It also urges people to reflect seriously on their routines and living conditions before adopting an animal. "We do not make things easy; we are quite demanding, because we care much more about quality than quantity," she explains.

Animals living at SOS Animal available for adoption SOS animal

"We would rather have 80 or 100 adoptions a year, knowing that the return rate is zero, than 300 adoptions followed by a huge number of animals being brought back. That is extremely traumatic for the animals," she concludes.

World.title: Farage wins UK by-election to return to parliament
World.content:
British politician Nigel Farage has comfortably won a local by-election on Friday after all the main political parties boycotted the vote in protest.

 

The former MEP had declared a "resounding victory" early Friday but said he would not attend the official result announcement that pitted him against Count Binface and a list of independent candidates.

Farage picked up over 22,000 votes in an election that saw a 44% turnout.

"The verdict is in and it is a convincing and overwhelming win," he said as supporters chanted his name at an event in Essex, which was broadcast on X.

Farage triggered the vote by resigning his parliamentary seat, which he had held since 2024, over an investigation into his finances in the constituency of Clacton in the county of Essex.

The vote had been shunned by Britain's main political parties, including the ruling Labour Party, as a stunt by the Reform UK leader - once touted as a potential prime minister - to dodge scrutiny of his dealings.

That has left candidates such as Binface - the alter ego of comedian Jon Harvey - to seize the spotlight.

"What an upside-down world it is, where Count Binface is now the candidate of the establishment," Farage said in his speech.

He said he would not attend the count, where candidates traditionally gather for the declaration of results, saying Essex Police had warned him that an "organised campaign to disrupt and degrade the result" was planned.

The BBC reported that this was not true, quoting Essex Police in a statement that read: "We have a proportionate and robust policing operation to ensure the safety and security of all participants in the count."

Acting Returning Officer Ian Davidson said election officials had worked with police to ensure the process was "completed safely and securely", adding there was "no reason not to proceed with the count process at this time".

Analysts expected a win for Farage, but forecast that the self-styled "intergalactic space warrior", who campaigns wearing a rubbish bin on his head, could secure an uncomfortably large share of the vote, possibly approaching 20 percent.

Count Binface (centre) has run against prime ministers in previous British by-elections including Andy Burnham and Boris Johnson. 14 August, 2026. AP Photo

Binface took to social media after the result to declare himself the winner "of the candidates that 'bothered to turn up for the results'" and, in a video, suggested Farage had been "humiliated" as one in four people in Clacton would prefer him to the Reform UK leader.

Turnout reached about 44.7 percent, down from 59 percent in the 2024 general election.

In the coastal community, many voters appeared unenthusiastic about the poll, with even some Reform party volunteers describing the contest as a joke.

"It's a bit ridiculous," party campaigner Jane Embelton told AFP.

"It's all to make Nigel Farage look like an idiot, basically. But he doesn't look like an idiot to me or his supporters."

A record 33 fringe candidates, including Binface, stood in the vote, with some of the longest ballot papers in the country's history seen being unfolded at Clacton Leisure Centre, where the count was held.

- 'We can't decide' -

Farage, whose party had topped national polls for 18 months before falling behind recently, surprised voters with his July 7 resignation amid the probe into his finances.

The investigation by the parliamentary sleaze watchdog is examining allegations he and Reform's deputy leader, Richard Tice, failed to declare financial gifts. They deny any wrongdoing.

Farage has framed Thursday's vote as "the people of Clacton versus the Establishment", aimed at thwarting the "stitch-up" over his finances.

"The people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions," he said in a video released before casting his vote.

Clacton voter Phil predicted the vote was "not going to change anything", noting if Farage won as expected, the parliamentary probe would restart.

Political pundits have downplayed the vote's wider significance in a constituency that overwhelmingly backed Brexit a decade ago.

"It will be astonishing if Farage were not to win," political scientist John Curtice told AFP.

But some assessed Farage's election gambit had backfired as his Reform party slips down national polls.

"Farage's plan to turn this by-election into a serious political battle failed," Queen Mary University of London politics professor Stijn van Kessel told AFP, noting the resulting spectacle "makes Farage look rather silly".

Farage netted 46 percent of the vote in the 2024 general election to become an MP on his eighth attempt.

- Police probe -

The probe into Farage, which paused when he resigned, relates to a £5 million ($6.7m) donation from cryptocurrency billionaire Christopher Harborne.

Meanwhile, London police have confirmed starting a investigation last year into donations to Reform before the 2024 election.

UK media have reported that the police probe concerns undeclared financial support from longtime Farage ally and convicted fraudster George Cottrell and his mother.

The decision to trigger a by-election has seen a drop in support for Reform, which recently won a vast number of council elections across the UK in May.

World.title: Child's play: French artist Saype's giant ephemeral frescoes takeover Swiss alpine resort
World.content:
Much of Saype's art works revolve around child's play but that doesn't mean to say there's anything simple about it. Childhood observations lie at the heart of what the French artist describes as a child's ongoing adventure to become the 'author of his own destiny,' but they're also meant to remind us that possibilties are endless.

 

That's precisely why Saype has picked the peaks of a Swiss ski resort, Villars-Gryon-Diablerets, to show off his latest pieces; enormous ephemeral frescoes, composed with environmentally-friendly paints and materials.

Saype, who's real name is Guillaume Legros, said: "This is the kind of artwork I create all over the world, and it’s part of a series that began four years ago in Villars, where I’ve been crafting a story that spans several years—and it’s usually the children who, year after year, develop or create the story themselves."

'À portée de ciel': An eco-responsible painting on grass by French land artist Saype adorns a hill on Swiss alpine resort Villars-sur-Ollon, July 2026 Courtesy of Saype/All rights reserved

Largely made by using chalk and charcoal, Saype's creations are both compelling and immense. Nature also plays an intrinsic part in the works, highlighting the fragility of the environment and the art's temporary status.

"The challenge is twofold. It's physical because there's a bit of a slope...and there's the weather, I had to deal with thunderstorms, wind, rain, so that’s always what makes it complicated for me," explains Saype.

French artist Saype prepares the ground for his latest work at Swiss alpine resort Villars-sur-Ollon, July 2026 Courtesy of Saype

From New York to Nairobi, Saype's stunning creations have been exhibited around the world on various canvases including grass, earth, sand and snow.

Each piece is intended to slowly but deliberately disappear, to emphasise the challenges facing societies and humanity.

Saype's second fresco, created at the Bretaye pass, depicts a child drawing the sun and clouds; this drawing is part of a diptych, the other fresco being located a little further down in the resort.

"This is the first time I’ve used colour in my drawings. Kids have been inspired by the cosmos, by adventures, and by their observations—and for the first time, they’re putting that into drawings, and the drawings come to life. That’s why I added colour—it feels as though the sky is reflected in the drawings, and my idea is to convey that the cosmos acts as a kind of window onto the world," says Saype.

'À portée de ciel': An eco-responsible painting on grass by French artist Saype as part of his Villars project in the Swiss mountains, July 2026 Courtesy of Saype

Work in progress: French land artist Saype in action on the Villars project Courtesy of Saype/All rights reserved

Time is running out however if you want to catch sight of Saype's latest ephemeral creations. The extremely dry conditions in Switzerland have meant the grass has hardly grown but predicted wet weather and storms will fast alter the outlook.

For Saype, the end is always bittersweet but something still worth celebrating.

"I love that moment because, ultimately, it’s when nature reclaims what I’ve created. But basically, I think it’ll be visible until the end of August without too many problems."

World.title: ‘The real challenge starts after sundown’: Europe’s heatwave boosted solar by up to 17% on hot days
World.content:
Solar has been doing the “heavy lifting” to help Europe meet its energy needs amid a string of blistering heatwaves.

 

A new analysis from energy think-tank Ember found that solar output in European countries rose by up to 17 per cent on heatwave days in June and July.

Researchers say that this helped power the grid as electricity demand increased by as much as a quarter on hot days. Heatwaves often trigger a spike in electricity consumption due to the sudden need for cooling, mainly from energy-intensive air conditioning (A/C) units.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimates that space cooling, which is mostly A/C units and fans, consumed around seven per cent of the world’s electricity in 2022. Even in countries where A/C ownership is low, countries experience energy demand spikes when scorching temperatures hit.

During the early summer heatwaves of 2025, France, for example, recorded an evening electricity peak that was 25 per cent above the off-season average due to air conditioning.

Solar performing ‘better than usual’ amid heatwave

Ember’s analysis found that during the late-June heatwave this summer, daily electricity demand rose byup to 28 per cent in Italy, 23 per cent in Hungary, 14 per cent in France and 13 per cent in Spain compared with pre-heatwave days.

It says as heatwave-driven demand increased, solar was the only major power source to perform “better than usual”. Compared with other days in June and July, average daily solar generation during the heatwaves was 17 per cent higher in France and Hungary, five per cent higher in Spain and the same in Italy.

“Solar is already doing heavy lifting during heatwaves, but the real challenge starts after sundown,” says senior energy analyst Chris Rosslowe.

“In the evening, when cooling demand is still high, the grid is most exposed to expensive gas-fired power.”

How Europe’s blistering summer impacts energy

Europe’s back-to-back heatwaves, which scientists say would have been “virtually impossible” if it weren’t for climate change, have triggered mass droughts across the continent.

Low water levels along the Danube River forced nuclear output to be curtailed in Hungary, while experts warn that hydropower neared an “all-time low” in the Alpine region.

Fossil-fuelled energy has suffered from the drought too, with Poland forced to reduce output at a coal-fired power plant due to critically low water levels in the Vistula River.

The late-June and early-July heatwaves also saw average daily electricity prices surge 119 per cent higher in Hungary, 44 per cent in France, 13 per cent in Italy and seven per cent in Spain than on comparable days in the preceding weeks.

Experts say the price surge reiterates the need for battery storage systems, which can prevent excess solar energy from being wasted.

“While solar saves the day, battery storage can save the evening,” Rosslowe says.

“Together, they are one of the clearest ways to make Europe’s power system more resilient in the hotter summers. As solar output rises during heatwaves and other power sources struggle, storage can carry that cheap electricity into the evening.”

World.title: India news: 7 dead, 3 trapped in Uttarakhand tunnel collapse
World.content:
Skip next section Seven killed in Uttarakhand tunnel mishap, three missing

08/14/2026 August 14, 2026 Seven killed in Uttarakhand tunnel mishap, three missing

At least seven workers have died in a tunnel collapse in the northern Indian hill state of Uttarakhand, officials said on Friday, adding that a search was underway for three missing people.

The incident occurred overnight when a landslide sent water and debris streaming into an under-construction tunnel belonging to Tehri Hydro Development Corporation Limited (THDC) in Pipalkoti, in Chamoli district.

According to officials, 22 workers were inside the tunnel at the time of the disaster.

The injured are undergoing treatment.

A multi-agency effort is underway to reach the three workers still trapped inside the tunnel, with teams from the National and State Disaster Response Forces, the Indo-Tibetan Border Police and fire services at the site.

Rescue workers seen with machinery near the tunnel Image: ANI

Rescuers are battling rising water and debris during the search, as the state has seen heavy rainfall in recent days.

Visuals circulated by local authorities show rescue teams wearing head-mounted torches and using makeshift rafts to reach the flooded section of the tunnel.

Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami visited the collapse site on Friday morning and reviewed the rescue operations.

"Evacuating every worker safely is our topmost priority," Dhami said in a statement.

In 2023, a tunnel collapse in Uttarakhand left 41 workers trapped for 17 days before they were rescued.

World.title: Can childhood trauma be prevented with a drug?
World.content:
Researchers in Munich and Stockholm blocked the lifelong social cost of early adversity in mice with a single compound. The catch: it only worked when given during the trauma, not after.

Trauma is usually treated as something you carry managed, worked through, sometimes eased. Rarely as something that could be stopped before it takes hold. That is what a group of researchers in Munich and Stockholm set out to test .

They began by making the first days of life hard. Mother mice were given far less nesting and bedding material than normal. That was enough to make mothers erratic, and the first days of life unpredictable. The mice raised in that hardship grew up looking perfectly healthy – with no obvious illness or anything visibly wrong.

Then researchers put them in groups and watched what happened. Repeatedly, these mice ended up at the bottom. Pushed into the lowest ranks of their social hierarchies, first as adolescents, then again as adults. A difficult infancy had left no visible mark — but it had set the position they would occupy for the rest of their lives.

When the researchers gave some of them a drug, the pattern disappeared.

The study, published in June, was led jointly by Mathias Schmidt at the Max Planck Institute of Psychiatry in Munich and Juan Pablo Lopez at the Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm .

How does childhood trauma affect the brain and body?

Start with cortisol, the body's main stress hormone. When something stressful happens, cortisol floods the system. This is a standard, protective response.

What matters just as much is the off switch. The body needs to register that the danger has passed and wind the response back down. It does this through cortisol receptors — the parts of cells that detect the hormone and signal the system to stand down.

A protein called FKBP51 controls how sensitive those receptors are. Early hardship, the research suggests, causes the body to produce too much of it. That makes the receptors harder to trigger, so the signal to stand down never fully lands, and the stress response stays switched on far longer than it should.

Schmidt's point is that none of this is something a person can feel. "Your cortisol response is something you don't feel," he said. "You may think you're very stress resilient, but your body is pumping out cortisol, and you don't know."

Can a drug block the effects of a difficult childhood?

The researchers used a compound called SAFit2, which blocks FKBP51. Given to the mothers during the stressful period, it reached the offspring through breast milk.

The treated mice went on to perform identically, within their social groups, to mice that had experienced no adversity at all — the social cost of a hard start erased.

The effect showed up in the brain as well as in behavior. The team screened gene activity across six stress-related regions and found that early adversity had left a broad imprint across them. The drug largely reversed it, most clearly in two: the medial prefrontal cortex and the nucleus accumbens, regions involved in emotional control and reward.

Can childhood trauma be reversed?

Not on this evidence.

In the Munich study, the compound was given during the stressful period itself, not after. What the study demonstrates is prevention, not repair.

Other studies have shown behavioral effects when the drug is used in adult animals, but full reversal of trauma already in place remains unproven. And prevention only works if you can identify who's at risk before the harm is done — a problem this research doesn't address.

Would this drug actually work on humans?

It's too early to say.

The study tested male mice only, so it is not yet known whether the same holds in females. And SAFit2 remains a research compound 3 effective in animals but not yet developed or safety-tested for human use. Still, Schmidt sees a realistic path toward clinical application within the next decade, noting that stress mechanisms are "very, very similar in animals and humans."

War scars and genes: Can the impacts of trauma be inherited? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How is trauma treated now, and why doesn't it always work?

Existing treatments for stress-related disorders, including PTSD and trauma-linked depression, rely heavily on selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. These drugs target serotonin pathways. They work for many patients, but the mechanism is not fully understood, and a significant portion of patients don't respond at all.

By contrast, targeting FKBP51 would mean treating the pathology at its source. "We would actually not only be treating the symptoms, but also the cause of the disorder by acting directly [on] a stress mechanism," said Schmidt. "These types of drugs are currently not on the market."

Longer term, Schmidt envisions a more targeted approach: identifying individuals who are genetically vulnerable to stress, whose FKBP51 expression is already elevated, and treating that group specifically after acute traumatic events.

On the other end of the spectrum are people who, through genetics or prior experience, prove remarkably resilient even under extreme conditions, and may not need medication at all. Understanding who does need it, Schmidt said, and reaching them in time, is where the research is heading next.

What are the signs of unresolved trauma?

Schmidt is careful that trauma is highly individual, psychologically, and physiologically. The rough guide he offers is duration, not intensity.

A strong stress reaction immediately after a car crash or a violent event is considered normal — the body doing its job. What concerns clinicians is when the response persists well beyond that: still unable to cross a street a month later, still unable to sleep six weeks on. Those are his illustrative examples rather than diagnostic thresholds, but the principle holds. If a stress response isn't fading, it's advisable to speak to a doctor.

That remains practical guidance for now. The drug, if it ever exists, is at least a decade away — and on current evidence, it would need to come before the damage, not after.

Editor: Kaukab Shairani

This article is an excerpt from our podcast Science Unscripted. You can subscribe to the podcast here .

World.title: Four dead, thousands stranded as record rain lashes Japan
World.content:
Unprecedented rainfall in Japan's Chiba prefecture has stranded thousands of passengers at Tokyo's Narita airport and prompted authorities to issue the highest-level rain warning for the first time.

At least four people have died in eastern Japan as heavy rain flooded roads, cut power and left thousands of travelers stranded overnight at Tokyo's Narita airport, authorities said Friday.

More than 36 centimeters (14 inches) of rain fell in 24 hours in parts of Chiba prefecture, which borders Tokyo, triggering landslide warnings and power outages for nearly 25,000 households.

Japan facing 'unprecedented' rain during busy holiday week

The downpour struck during one of Japan's busiest holiday weeks, prompting the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) to issue its highest-level heavy rain warning for the region for the first time.

A JMA official on Thursday said this was "shaping up to be an unprecedented level of heavy rain."

"This case was an extremely unusual situation, even ​by Japan's historical weather standards," Chiba Governor Toshihito Kumagai told reporters early Friday. "I have responded to many disasters in the past, but ⁠I ​have never experienced a case like this."

Several roads in the Chiba Prefecture were inundated Image: Kyodo/REUTERS

The Chiba Prefecture Disaster Management Office said those confirmed deaths included a man in his 60s or 70s found on a flooded road and a 66-year-old woman found in her submerged car.

A third victim was a man of unknown age found collapsed in the street, and a fourth was a person whose age and gender have not been determined, AFP reported. A fifth person is feared dead and a sixth remains unaccounted for. Soldiers have been deployed to help with relief efforts.

Thousands stranded at Narita airport

More than 6,000 people were stranded overnight at Narita, one of Tokyo's two major international airports. Many train services to and from the airport were also canceled into Friday afternoon.

"I never thought I'd spend the night at the airport but it is what it is and we are learning," a traveler told Japanese public broadcaster NHK. "We're never going to forget this trip."

Hundreds more were stranded at Chiba station after train services were suspended. Several people spent the night in shelters. NHK footage also showed cars submerged up to their headlights in Kashiwa city.

Hundreds were stranded at the Chiba Metro Station as weather authorities issued their highest-level heavy rain warning for the region Image: Philip Fong/AFP

Major highways in Chiba, including routes connecting Narita to central Tokyo, remained closed Friday, according to highway operator NEXCO East, forcing drivers onto alternate routes. Some train services connecting Narita to Tokyo had resumed early Friday.

An airport spokesperson said all flights were scheduled to operate normally, and Japan Airlines said some delays were possible, but no cancellations were expected.

The level-5 heavy rain warnings issued Thursday were downgraded to level 4 by Friday morning.

Scientists warn that human-driven climate change is making extreme weather events more frequent and intense.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

World.title: Romania shuts nuclear plant, Hungary dams dry Danube River
World.content:
Romania has shut down its only nuclear plant in a rare move prompted by the lack of cooling water from the Danube River. Hungary, meanwhile, is racing to dam the Danube, trying to keep its Paks plant online.

Romania shut down its lone nuclear power plant on Thursday, a rare move amid the drought that has caused record lows on the Danube River and other major waterways in Europe.

The Danube is the sole source of cooling water for the Cernavoda plant, which usually generates around one-fifth of Romania's electricity.

The power station has only been shut down once before, in 2023, again as a result of drought and a hot summer.

Meanwhile, Hungary was scrambling to dam the Danube, as it tries to keep its Paks nuclear power plant at least running at the minimal levels that it has maintained in recent days, which are far below capacity.

Attempts to divert more water to Cernavoda earlier this month didn't prevent a shutdown Image: Alex Nicodim/Anadolu/picture alliance

What did the operator and authorities in Romania say about the shutdown?

Romania's Nuclearelectrica company had already shut one of the two reactors at Cernavoda last month.

On Thursday, it said it needed to shut the second "because of the significant and ongoing drop in the water level of the Danube River."

The company tried earlier this month, with help from the Navy, to improve the plant's chances of staying operational.

Most memorably, it blew up a rocky outcrop exposed by the low water levels and strategically deposited the rocks on the riverbed in a bid to direct more water to Cernavoda.

But ultimately, continued dry weather and sinking water levels prompted the total shutdown.

"We do not foresee a restart within the next 10 days," the plant director, Romeo Urjan, told the AFP news agency.

Romania's Energy Ministry said it was procuring alternative power sources, including from wind power but also from energy imports, to try to ensure adequate supplies. Still it appealed to the public to consume responsibly.

It warned that as a last resort, large industrial users would have to face restrictions in the evening hours to save electricity. Carmakers Ford and Dacia had already committed to pausing production until August 19 to save power.

Earlier in August, the Romanian Navy detonated submerged rocks as part of a bid to funnel more water to the power plant Image: Andreea Alexandru/AP Photo/picture alliance

What is Hungary doing to try to prevent a similar shutdown of the Paks plant?

Prime Minister Peter Magyar on Thursday visited Hungary's only nuclear power plant, the Paks facility that is also cooled by the Danube.

"We have begun construction of the low weir that will permanently contribute to raising the Danube's water level," Magyar told reporters at the site, roughly 100 kilometers (about 60 miles) south of Budapest.

Only one of Paks' four reactors is currently operational amid the drought.

Nine days ago, the plant was at risk of a complete shutdown, but the government was able to abort those plans at the last moment as the Danube's levels ended up being a few millimeters higher than forecast.

The unusually low river levels near the Paks plant are hard to miss at present Image: Robert Nemeti/Anadolu/picture alliance

Under normal circumstances, the plant is responsible for around half of Hungary's electricity generation, and about one-third of its consumption.

Before the completion of the weir, authorities plan to deliberately sink two 80-meter-long barges — placed end-to-end and perpendicular to the river's flow — to create an initial damming effect and raise the water level somewhat.

Magyar said that Hungarian soldiers were working round the clock on the construction, and that it should be completed in the next four weeks. He said the project should elevate water levels in front of the Paks plant cooling system by more than a meter.

The project might not be finished long before the summer starts to fade and the rains return, but the low water levels also provide a rare opportunity to undertake such construction projects relatively cheaply and easily.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

World.title: Kennedy Center board approves Trump name on facade, renovation plan
World.content:
The move appears designed to circumvent a judge's ruling that the US president's name should be removed, potentially setting the stage for a new legal fight over the Kennedy Center's name and future.

The board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts voted Thursday to add President Donald Trump's name to the building's facade, according to US Congresswoman Joyce Beatty.

The board also voted to proceed with a two-year closure of the performing arts venue in the US capital, Washington, D.C., for major renovations.

The decision comes after a federal judge in May ordered Trump's name to be removed from the building, ruling that only Congress can change the institution's name or authorize major alterations.

"This latest development is a transparent effort to circumvent the Court's ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed," Beatty, a Democrat who is also an ex-officio board member, said in a statement. "I will continue to fight for this treasured national monument."

The latest vote revives a dispute that has been unfolding since Trump reshaped the center's leadership after returning to office.

Why was Trump's name on the building in the first place?

Trump became interested in the Kennedy Center's operations after winning the 2024 election. He installed a mostly handpicked board that named him chairman, and his name was added to the building's facade in December.

The move was part of a broader effort to overhaul the institution. At the time, the president also announced a two-year closure of the performing arts venue for renovations that were scheduled to begin in July.

That decision soon faced a legal challenge. In May, Judge Christopher Cooper said, "the Kennedy Center's organic statute makes crystal clear that the Center is to be named for President Kennedy, and it cannot bear any other formal name or public memorial based on the Board's unilateral say-so."

The Kennedy Center dispute became one of several obstacles to Trump's broader efforts to remake prominent Washington landmarks. An appeals court last week halted his planned White House ballroom after he demolished the East Wing.

His Reflecting Pool renovation also faced major problems, though he still plans to build a massive Memorial Arch.

How has the Kennedy Center board justified the move?

"In its meeting today, the board voted to change the front of the building's facade to read 'The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump,' and renamed the physical site 'the President Donald J. Trump Plaza,'" Congresswoman Beatty said.

According to The New York Times, an inscription underneath the institution's name would read: "Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump."

The newspaper said the wording appears intended to avoid a provision in the federal law governing the Kennedy Center that states "no additional memorials or plaques in the nature of memorials shall be designated or installed in the public areas."

Edited by: Karl Sexton

World.title: US disputes reports of trying conditions on carrier in Gulf
World.content:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called reports of poor conditions and mental health strain aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier in the Middle East "completely misrepresented." Senators want an investigation.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has defended conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier, which has spent a record-breaking number of days at sea during a period of more than eight months with only brief stops at ports.

Hegseth called recent reporting in two military-focused outlets in the US, the Navy Times and the Stars and Stripes, "completely misrepresented."

The reports had quoted relatives of sailors recounting stories of poor conditions on board and even a thwarted attempt by a crewmember to throw themselves overboard.

The aircraft carrier's crew of around 5,000 provide crucial aerial and naval support to US operations in the Gulf Image: U.S. Navy/Planet Pix/ZUMA/picture alliance

What did Hegseth say about conditions?

The 5,000-person aircraft carrier left San Diego in November for what was scheduled to be a Pacific deployment.

It was subsequently rerouted to the Middle East ready for what the Trump White House called Operation Epic Fury, and has been in the Persian Gulf or the wider region since January amid the war with Iran.

"We make sure every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment," Hegseth told reporters during a visit to Panama on Thursday. "Some deployments are longer than others, and I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody. What they do in those high seas in those austere conditions with less port calls — it's incredible."

Longer deployments at sea, particularly in wartime with higher stress and danger levels and fewer chances for rest and recreation, have always been a challenge for the US Navy.

During the longest period at sea without docking in US military history, the ship had to be restocked on the move, with several non-essential supplies falling by the wayside Image: U.S. Navy/SIPA/picture alliance

Senate calls for inspection visit

A day earlier, Arizona Senator Ruben Gallego said he was calling for an official oversight visit to the USS Abraham Lincoln by a bipartisal Senate Delegation to "investigate the alarming conditions."

"Unlike Donald Trump, I've seen active duty," Gallego said. "They way he's treating our service members as he carries out this illegal war is not just disgusting; it's dangerous. These sailors are owed a sense of when they will go home."

Gallego repeated the call on Thursday, saying Congress "needs to do its job and hold this administration accountable."

Senator Richard Blumenthal also called for the Navy to account for conditions aboard the aircraft carrier, noting "widespread reports of shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns" and other problems aboard the Lincoln.

What if Iran and Oman split control of the Strait of Hormuz? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did the military media outlets report?

The Navy Times and Stars and Stripes have had their eye on the USS Abraham Lincoln's record-setting deployment for months but both revisited the issue in depth this week. This followed a direct appeal late last week by family members to Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao and other senior officials in town hall meetings.

The deployment has included 40 days of continuous combat operations in the US Fifth Fleet area of operations and 250 consecutive days at sea, including a record-breaking number of days without even a port stop, restocking supplies at sea and by air as best as the crew could.

"We already had an instance where watchstanders had to stop someone from jumping," Stars and Stripes quoted one sailor as saying .

It also noted various supply and service issues affecting morale, like food rationing, water shortages, and a stretch of more than a week when crew could not do laundry.

It said that many of these issues had since improved, as had mail delivery services — but nevertheless reported a situation of deteriorating morale where, as one sailor put it, "All we want is a date home."

The Lincoln made a brief port call in Oman in early July. Stars and Stripes reported, that allowed it to stock up on valuable produce like fresh fruit and vegetables, but sailors were only permitted to disembark into a secure compound within the port. The ship had also briefly docked in Guam in December, but again with limited shore leave. In the interim it spent the longest period at sea without ever docking in US military history.

The Reuters news agency on Thursday cited a US official, who it said was speaking on condition of anonymity, as saying that another aircraft carrier — the USS George Washington — was headed to the region to relieve the Lincoln. The Wall Street Journal in the US carried similar reports on Thursday. The ship departed Vietnam earlier this week.

Both combat aircraft and tactical early-warning aircraft like the E-2D Hawkeye operate from the Lincoln Image: NAVCENT Public Affairs/SIPA/picture alliance

Hegseth, Trump both indicate much longer deployment conceivable

When asked about what the US calls its "blockade" of Iran's ports — with the Lincoln a crucial command and air-superiority component in the operation — Hegseth said that the US could continue to enforce it for as long as it wished.

"Indefinitely the United States Navy can maintain a blockade like that because we'll rotate ships in and out, as we have, and we'll continue to," he said.

President Donald Trump had claimed on Wednesday that the navy had "total control" of the Strait of Hormuz and speculated that he might try to permanently police it.

"The USA has total control over the Strait of Hormuz. I THINK WE WILL KEEP IT!" Trump wrote online. "Our Naval Blockade is being called, by everyone, 'A WALL OF STEEL,' and there is nothing Iran can do about it."

The head of Iran's Basij paramilitary unit, Hossein Taeb, on Thursday disputed Trump's assesment saying the Strait is "under Iran's control and management."

Commercial shipping — whether bound for Iranian ports or for Gulf states, or trying to sail out of the Gulf — has been drastically reduced in volume throughout the conflict, with risks to commercial crews of all stripes from both sides complicating and often halting journeys.

Can Trump end the Iran war and sell it as a victory? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: When the earth moves: 6 major earthquakes of 2026
World.content:
Colombia, Venezuela, Mindanao: Thousands have died in powerful earthquakes this year. Six such events show that the magnitude of the quake isn't the only factor determining the scale of the disaster.

Is 2026 a particularly bad year for earthquakes? The number of extremely strong quakes so far this year is not, in fact, unusual. Over the long term, around the world, there are an average of about 15 earthquakes per year registering above magnitude 7 on the Richter scale. By mid-August this year, there had been 10. The devastation some of the quakes have wreaked has, however, been striking.

Venezuela: two quakes in just 39 seconds

On June 24, Venezuela was hit by an earthquake that proved to be by far the deadliest this year. A magnitude 7.2 quake was followed just 39 seconds later by an even stronger one of magnitude 7.5. The north of the country and the capital, Caracas, were the areas worst affected.

Two earthquakes wreaked destruction in Catia La Mar, Venezuela Image: Maxwell Briceno/AFP

According to official figures, more than 6,300 people were killed in the double earthquake. The effects on the impoverished country's infrastructure have also been dramatic. Shortly afterward, a satellite-based assessment by researchers at Oregon State University provisionally concluded that more than 58,000 buildings may have been damaged or destroyed.

Venezuela quakes death toll rises to almost 4,000 To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Philippines: the strongest quake of the year

With a magnitude of 7.8, the earthquake on June 8 off the southern coast of the Philippine island of Mindanao was the strongest of 2026 so far. It occurred at a depth of about 57 kilometers (35 miles), and was felt across large parts of the island.

This university building in General Santos City on Mindanao in the Philippines collapsed during the earthquake in June Image: Daniel Ceng/Anadolu/picture alliance

At least 107 people were killed. But the fact that, despite the very high magnitude of the quake, far fewer people died in the Philippines than in Venezuela demonstrates that the strength of the quake does not necessarily determine the severity of the consequences.

Colombia: hundreds dead, despite the depth

On August 10, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake shook western Colombia. The epicenter was in the Choco region, near San Jose del Palmar. Although the quake occurred at a depth of 100 kilometers (62 miles), the damage it caused was immense.

Pereira, in the foothills of the Andes, was one of the cities worst hit by the earthquake in Colombia Image: Jaime Saldarriaga/AFP

More than 250 people are currently estimated to have died. Landslides and damaged roads are hampering the search for victims buried beneath the rubble, as well as the provision of supplies to remote areas. After Venezuela, this quake is the most consequential so far this year for Latin America.

Tonga: powerful earthquake with little damage

On March 24, the earth shook near the island group of Vava'u in the Pacific kingdom of Tonga. With a magnitude of 7.5, it was one of the strongest globally this year. But because there was no severe damage and no deaths, it received almost no attention from the media.

Tonga is located on the Pacific Ring of Fire and suffers frequent natural disasters, as here, after a volcanic eruption in 2022 Image: New Zealand Defence Force/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

The quake occurred unusually far below the Earth's crust, at a depth of around 230 kilometers (143 miles), meaning that the tremors were significantly weakened by the time they reached the surface. To date, there have been no reports of deaths, or damage to infrastructure.

Japan: strong undersea quake off the Sanriku Coast

On April 20, there was an undersea quake off the northeastern coast of Japan. The US Geological Survey recorded a magnitude of 7.4.

This region, the Sanriku Coast area in Iwate prefecture, achieved terrible notoriety after the catastrophic earthquake and tsunami there in 2011, which also resulted in the Fukushima nuclear disaster. A tsunami warning was issued after this year's earthquake, too, but fortunately the region was spared the devastation of that magnitude 9 quake 15 years ago.

After the earthquake off Japan's Sanriku Coast, people were evacuated as a precaution Image: Haruki Kobayashi/AP Photo/picture alliance

There was no major tsunami this time, but the quake illustrated once again how much Japan is affected by its location on the Pacific Ring of Fire. This 40,000-kilometer (25,000-mile) volcanic belt runs around the edge of the Pacific Ocean where several tectonic plates collide.

Afghanistan: weak, but deadly

The earthquake in the northeastern Afghan province of Badakhsham on April 3 only reached a magnitude of 5.8, which puts it right at the bottom of the list of the strongest earthquakes this year. Despite this, at least 12 people were killed, which is why it counts as one of the most significant quakes of 2026.

Poor building construction contributed to the deaths of several people in a magnitude 5.8 earthquake in Afghanistan in April Image: Saifurahman Safi/Xinhua/IMAGO

In poorer countries, even slight tremors can have deadly consequences. The risks are heightened by inadequate building construction, the difficulty of accessing remote areas and underdeveloped disaster response protocols.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Israeli military moves as settlers besiege 3 West Bank homes
World.content:
Israel's military has moved to try to stop a group of settlers from besieging three homes in the occupied West Bank. One was owned by a Palestinian American, prompting an unusually sharp rebuke from the US ambassador.

Israel has sent soldiers to try to protect three homes in the occupied West Bank village of Qusra that have been surrounded by a small group of Israeli settlers for several days.

One of the three homes is owned by a Palestinian American, and the incident prompted an unusually critical reponse from the US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, typically considered an ally of Israel's settler movement.

The case comes amid continued Israeli settlement building, which is considered illegal under international law, in parts of the occupied West Bank, and allegations from critics of the Israeli government that it sometimes turns a blind eye to, or does too little to prevent, settler violence against Palestinians.

What is happening and where?

Starting on Sunday, a group of settlers started gathering around three houses in the village of Qusra.

One of the buildings belongs to Palestinian-American homeowner Loui Ridi. Local officials said the settlers sometimes numbered several dozen. They supposedly threw strones, attempted to bring down a stone wall, and prevented occupants from leaving their homes as their supplies dwindled.

Israel's military moved into the area on Wednesday and moved settlers away from the properties Image: Nidal Eshtayeh/AP/dpa/picture alliance

Ridi's brother, Qusai Abu Rida — who had holed up in the house with his son — said on Thursday morning that they had been moved to another home by the Israeli military but still could not leave the area some 16 kilometers (10 miles) from the Palestinian city of Nablus. Loui Ridi resides in Ohio but owns the property.

Israel's IDF military said its troops had dismantled "two illegal outposts" near the homes, and detained one Israeli. It wasn't immediately clear if the individual was subject to arrest or investigation, or just detention.

The local mayor, Abdel Azim Wadi, said that Israeli forces evacuated seven Palestinian households from their homes to make space for soldiers to take up positions in the village. He said that the settlers remained in other parts of the village, despite being removed from their outposts.

Locals said the village was on effective lockdown.

"No one is allowed to enter. Even food and water are prohibited from reaching those besieged," the Associated Press cited Yasser Ahmad, a resident of a neighboring village, as saying as he watched the operation unfold from one hilltop over.

Qusra is in one of the most violent pockets of the northern West Bank, surrounded by settlements. Its mosque was damaged in attacks last month.

Qusra has been a frequent flashpoint of late; its mosque was set on fire in a settler attack in late July Image: Debbie Hill/UPI/newscom/picture alliance

What did US Ambassador Huckabee say about the incident?

US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, typically a supporter of the Israeli settler movement — but also critical of settler violence — spoke out in unusually sharp terms against an incident impacting a US citizen in the West Bank.

"The actions of those doing this to this family's home is criminal," he said. "Actions by those who carried out this horrific act of terror meant to intimidate and harass this family are disgusting. No excuse for such thuggish behavior."

However, Huckabee also repeatedly defended both US and Israeli authorities response to the incident, saying the US Embassy in Jerusalem had been "very involved," and that "the IDF and Israel Police have gone at our request to remove the Israeli terrorists doing this."

He later repeated this message, posting video footage seeming to show Israeli security vehicles driving into the area.

The UN Human Rights Office in the occupied Palestinian territory on Thursday called on the Israeli authorities to "immediately" act against the settlers .

"These criminal actions by the settlers, supported or acquiesced to by Israel, the occupying power, are making life unbearable for these Palestinian families, and are clearly aimed at forcing them to leave their homes and land," it said in a statement.

EU foreign policy spokesperson Anitta Hipper called on Israel to take "concrete action to prevent settler violence."

What's the wider issue with West Bank settlement building and settler violence?

Palestinians and some in the Israeli opposition accuse Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government of turning a blind eye to attacks by settlers against Palestinians, as such cases have increased in recent years since the October 7 attacks and amid the war in Gaza.

Israeli government officials tend to describe the violence as the actions of a few fringe youth acting outside the law. The UN's human rights office (OHCHR) said 18 Palestinians have died in the first seven months of this year in attacks involving settlers.

Most of the international community condemns Israeli settlement building in the West Bank as an impediment to a lasting peace and the so-called two-state solution.

More than 500,000 Israelis live — most with but also some without Israeli government authorization and support — in the West Bank, which is home to roughly 3 million Palestinians.

The Palestinians seek the West Bank, captured by Israel in the 1967 Six-Day War, as part of a future state. Many settlers and some members of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government claim the area should belong to Israel, often citing a mixture historical, religious and security reasons.
