World.title: Marruecos despliega cientos de policías y militares en la frontera ante los llamamientos a una nueva irrupción masiva
World.content:
Este sábado aparece marcado en rojo en el calendario de los responsables del Ministerio del Interior, pero también en el de las autoridades marroquíes. En las redes sociales circulan desde hace días mensajes que alientan a repetir las escenas vividas los pasados 30 y 31 de julio con miles de migrantes entrando de manera irregular en Ceuta a nado, bordeando el espigón de El Tarajal. “La frontera de Ceuta estará abierta el día 15 [de agosto], festivo en España”, rezan algunos mensajes difundidos a través de internet para animar a participar en una nueva irrupción masiva. Ante ello, Rabat ha reforzado el puesto fronterizo de Fnideq (Castillejos en su denominación colonial española) con cientos de miembros de las fuerzas de seguridad apoyados por tropas militares, según se observa en vídeos que circulan desde hace casi una semana en medios digitales del país magrebí. También se han difundido imágenes de la instalación de concertinas y alambradas en las vallas que marcan el límite fronterizo del lado marroquí.

“Se han tomado todas las medidas necesarias para impedir cualquier intento de cruce ilegal e interceptar a cualquier persona que intente participar en él”, aseguró el miércoles Rachid el Jalfi, portavoz del Ministerio del Interior, quien definió el actual despliegue como parte de un “sistema de vigilancia continua” en los pasos de Ceuta y Melilla. El Jalfi instó a los ciudadanos a desoír llamamientos considerados “sospechosos y engañosos”, que suponen “graves riesgos para la seguridad de las personas”. Desde el otro lado de la frontera, el ministro del Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, incidía este jueves en el mismo mensaje en una comparecencia ante la prensa durante su segunda visita a la ciudad autónoma: “Se lo digo a ellos para que no atiendan a las mafias que juegan con su vida. Ninguno de ellos se va a quedar [en Ceuta], ninguno de ellos va a ir a la península, ninguno de ellos va a ser regularizado”.

En el lado español de la frontera, el refuerzo de efectivos también ha sido significativo, según se desprende de los datos facilitados este jueves por el ministro. Desde el inicio de la crisis, el número de policías y guardias civiles desplegados ha pasado de algo más de los 1.100 que componían las plantillas de ambos cuerpos a cerca de 1.600 que hay en la actualidad. Además, 2.000 militares han pasado a realizar funciones de apoyo. Sin embargo, estos esfuerzos no se centran solo en la frontera, sino que con ella también se busca hacer más visible la presencia de agentes en las calles —el ministro ha admitido que devolver la “normalidad” a Ceuta del 29 de julio “evidentemente” llevará tiempo ante las quejas de los vecinos que hablan de inseguridad―, como en agilizar la expulsión de los 5.000 migrantes irregulares que permanecen aún en la ciudad. Marlaska muestra así, una vez más desde que estalló la crisis, su confianza en que Marruecos asumirá buena parte de la responsabilidad de frenar cualquier intento de repetir una entrada masiva este sábado. “Siempre ha sido, es y será extraordinaria y excepcional”, ha afirmado el ministro al ser preguntado por la colaboración entre Madrid y Rabat, incluso cuando se le recordó el anterior incidente grave en la frontera de Ceuta, la entrada de 10.000 migrantes en mayo de 2021.

Como ejemplo de esa disposición a impedir una nueva crisis migratoria, las autoridades marroquíes han asegurado haber detectado numerosos mensajes en las redes sociales para organizar y coordinar un nuevo cruce masivo este sábado hacia las ciudades autónomas españolas. Varias personas han sido detenidas y han sido procesadas tras ser acusadas de lanzar bulos para favorecer a la migración irregular, según informó el portavoz de Interior a la agencia estatal de noticias MAP. No obstante, y en línea con lo anticipado por los Ministerios de Asuntos Exteriores y Justicia de Rabat, Interior reclama a las autoridades españolas que asuman sus responsabilidades y aceleren, por ejemplo, los procedimientos de retorno de los miles de menores marroquíes que irrumpieron en Ceuta ―Marlaska aseguró este jueves que se habían tutelado ya a 1.898― junto con decenas de miles de adultos. El ministerio de Interior marroquí también insiste en la alegación oficial de ese país de que la lucha contra la migración irregular y las redes de trata de personas no puede depender de los esfuerzos de una sola parte y exige una responsabilidad compartida para poder aplicar el mecanismo de “retorno inmediato” o responsabilidad compartida.

Mientras los ministerios de Exteriores e Interior, cuyos titulares son designados directamente por el rey Mohamed VI, mantienen un discurso diplomático institucional en la presente crisis migratoria, el ministro de Justicia, Abdelatif Uahbi, está adoptando un perfil de confrontación política con España. Como uno de los principales líderes del Partido de la Autenticidad y la Modernidad (PAM, centro derecha), el ministro Uahbi está en campaña para las elecciones legislativas que se celebrarán el 23 de septiembre, en las que se perfila como ganador el candidato de esa fuerza política, Fuzi Lekjaa, presidente de la Federación Marroquí de Fútbol y ministro de Presupuestos. El ministro marroquí de Justicia ha criticado a España por haber aceptado a los migrantes irregulares mientras su país, según ha afirmado, se ha esforzado por impedir su salida. En una entrevista con la agencia Efe, Uahbi declaró: “Nosotros impedimos la salida de los inmigrantes, no solo de los marroquíes, sino también de otros, pero cuando llegan a España son aceptados y se regulariza su situación”.

Sin embargo, EL PAÍS y otros medios constataron durante los primeros días de la crisis que en la frontera de Castillejos las fuerzas de seguridad marroquíes se inhibieron ante el paso de decenas de miles de migrantes irregulares hacia Ceuta. Una fuente gubernamental de Rabat justificó esta actuación a Efe tres días más tarde, en que las fuerzas de seguridad no se enfrentaron a la multitud para evitar daños. Pese a todo ello y a las voces discrepantes de la oposición, pero también en su propio Gobierno, Marlaska insiste una y otra vez desde el estallido de la crisis en que “la cooperación y coordinación” con Rabat ha sido “de una complicidad fuera de toda duda”. El mismo jueves que estalló la crisis, el entorno del ministro recuerda que este recibió una llamada telefónica de su homónimo marroquí, Abdelouafi Laftit, para intercambiar información sobre lo que estaba pasando en Ceuta.

Tras el despliegue de la barrera marítima en el espigón de El Tarajal y ahora otra similar en el dique sur de Melilla ―con una altura en superficie de entre 30 y 70 centímetros únicamente, pero que faculta a las fuerzas de seguridad a devolver en caliente a los migrantes en aplicación de la reciente sentencia del Tribunal Supremo―, los esfuerzos de Interior se centran no solo en el límite fronterizo. El mismo día de la entrada masiva, Interior envió cerca de 350 agentes para apoyar a las plantillas de ambos cuerpos en la ciudad, que aquel día se vieron desbordadas. En el caso de la Policía Nacional, se desplegaron cinco equipos (225 agentes) de las Unidades de Intervención Policial (UIP, los conocidos como antidisturbios), cuya misión principal ahora es el control de las playas donde se han asentado muchos migrantes, así como vigilar otros puntos sensibles.

Para hacer visible la presencia policial en las calles ―en los últimos días, los jueces de Ceuta han enviado a prisión a nueve de los migrantes llegados en la entrada masiva y han expulsado a otros dos por la comisión de diversos delitos―, Interior ha doblado los turnos de los policías de seguridad ciudadana. Ahora se les refuerza con 45 miembros de la Unidad de Prevención y Reacción (UPR) procedentes de la península. A ellos se suman seis de la Unidad Central de Expulsiones y Repatriaciones (UCER) que llegaron a la ciudad horas después de estallar la crisis migratoria para apoyar en las labores de filiación de los migrantes, y los 20 de la Brigada Central de Extranjería y Fronteras que se incorporan para agilizar las expulsiones. También hay seis miembros de la Comisaría General de Información, encargados de la lucha antiterrorista, aunque el ministro este jueves ha negado que la situación creada haya supuesto un incremento de la amenaza yihadista. “Estamos vigilando, estamos monitorizando a todas las personas que han entrado”, añadió.

Por su parte, la Guardia Civil envió 60 agentes para reforzar la vigilancia fronteriza y otros 160 para realizar labores de seguridad ciudadana. Para el control de la línea costera, el instituto armado ha enviado buceadores del Grupo Especial de Actividades Subacuáticas (GEAS) y el buque Duque de Ahumada, el más grande del instituto armado, con una dotación de 12 guardias civiles. El Servicio Aéreo se ha reforzado con un helicóptero. Desde la semana pasada, a los agentes del instituto armado destinados en Ceuta, pero también en Melilla, no se les autorizan nuevas “vacaciones, permisos ni licencias” ante “la situación operativa derivada del incremento de la presión migratoria irregular”.

World.title: Las siete vidas de Daniela
World.content:
Daniela llevaba ya varias horas sepultada cuando alguien, desde una montaña de cascotes, le preguntó su nombre. Ella gritó también el de su hijo. Y después el nombre de su padre. Fue así como los rescatistas supieron que la mujer que acabarían sacando de allí con vida era la misma cuyo rostro y cabello rubio llevaban casi dos días circulando en un cartel: “Se busca. Daniela Andrea Largo Sánchez, 32 años. Desaparecida en Pereira durante el temblor”.

El lunes del terremoto, a las 7.34 de la mañana, Daniela se disponía a cumplir una promesa. Volvería a casa de su madre para celebrar el cumpleaños de su hijo, que ese día soplaría 12 velas. Su afán por llegar a su destino, a tres horas por carretera de Pereira, es quizá lo que hizo que el temblor le sorprendiese en las escaleras, ya en marcha y no en el catre de la pensión donde pasaba algunas noches con un amigo. O eso piensa su madre.

El cuerpo delgado de la joven quedó sepultado bajo el edificio. Su rescate congregó decenas de voluntarios, bomberos, policías, topos y vecinos de mala vida. Fueron horas despejando escombros mientras se congregaba una multitud alrededor, expectante por alguna buena noticia en mitad de una catástrofe que ya suma 273 fallecidos. Entre esa multitud, abrazados, esperaban Julio César, el padre de Daniela, y Sandra, su pareja desde hace seis años. No se soltaron. Cada vez que un rescatista salía del hueco con las manos vacías, los dos se apretaban más fuerte. Él apenas se movía; no perdía de vista el agujero del que debía salir la niña de sus ojos.

Daniela Largo hacia es trasladada a una ambulancia. Chelo Camacho

A Daniela la sacaron con el celular en la mano a las 20.27 del martes entre aplausos y oraciones. “¡Daniela, Daniela, Daniela!”, gritaba la muchedumbre. Pero cuando la subieron a la ambulancia sufrió un paro cardiorespiratorio y tuvieron que reanimarla durante cerca de 20 minutos. “Estaba muy deshidratada”, cuenta su madre, Martha Emilce Sánchez. “La reanimaron ahí mismo”, dice en la puerta del hospital en el que su hija permanece en la Unidad de Cuidados Intensivos. No es exactamente la séptima vez que Daniela vuelve de un lugar del que no se suele volver, pero casi.

La madre de Daniela cuenta la historia frente a la Clínica San Jorge, poco antes de poder verla por primera vez desde que supo que estaba viva. Su hija nunca paró, desde pequeñita, pero hace cinco años la vida se le complicó. Se dio cuenta tras una caída que la llevó al hospital. En una radiografía apareció un tumor óseo ya grande, en la pierna, un cáncer de huesos. La mantuvieron hospitalizada tres meses. La junta médica recomendó amputar, pero uno de los médicos se negó: dijo que se arriesgaría a colocarle una prótesis en la pierna y la rodilla. Y Daniela conservó la pierna. Y siguió su vida. Hasta hace dos años, el tumor reapareció.

Daniela se sometió a ocho sesiones de quimioterapia que, según su madre, no sirvieron de mucho. “No le había mermado nada”, dice. Al revés, habían encontrado metástasis en los pulmones y los médicos volvieron a hablar de amputación. Fue entonces cuando Daniela tomó una decisión que su familia todavía cuenta en susurros: no más tratamientos. “Ella quería que cuando ya Dios la llamara, estuviera toda completica”, cuenta Martha. Daniela dejó de ir a controles. Dejó la quimioterapia. Y, aunque nadie se lo explica, el tumor de la pierna dejó de crecer. Y el de los pulmones, que también se había extendido, se hizo cada vez más pequeño. “El cáncer no se curó”, aclara Martha, “pero remitió”.

Martha E. Sánchez, madre de Daniela Largo, a las afueras del hospital donde está internada su hija. Chelo Camacho

Daniela retomó lo que era su vida normal, aunque no fuese la que su madre y su padre querrían para ella. Una normalidad marcada por el dolor en la que desaparecía varios días hasta que volvían a saber de ella.

Tras el terremoto, Martha comenzó a llamar a su hija, pero no había señal. Respiró profundo, rezó y quiso pensar que todo estaba bien, pero cuando la red volvió y todos los vecinos, menos ella, empezaron a poder comunicarse con los suyos, se preocupó de verdad. “Ella no iba a faltar al cumpleaños de mi niño”, pensó. “Algo pasa”. Fue cuando el padre y su esposa pusieron rumbo a Pereira para patearse el centro con los carteles.

Estuvieron a punto de perder la esperanza porque nadie la había visto, hasta que sonó el teléfono y se oyó la voz de una amiga al otro lado. La estaban buscando en los escombros de un edificio; sabían que era ella porque dijo el nombre de su hijo y su papá.

Daniela se salvó, entre otras cosas, porque alguien se empeñó en sacarla de allí. Entre los primeros rescatistas que llegaron al lugar donde había caído el edificio estaba Yeivinson Fontalvo, un colombiano de la Chaplains International, una organización estadounidense de capellanes cristianos que entrenan y despliegan equipos internacionales para responder desastres y emergencias. Fue él quien se introdujo como un topo ya en la mañana del martes en busca de supervivientes y el que, según cuenta, escuchó una voz débil que respondía cuando la llamaban. “No hay un manual único, pero no hay improvisación. Hay años de terremotos anteriores”, contaba Yeivinson minutos antes del rescate, que acabaron asumiendo profesionales. El hombre, al ver a Daniela saliendo en una camilla, rompió a llorar. Y, a continuación, se puso a rezar en voz alta, como en trance.

Un bombero coordina a su equipo para apuntalar unos escombros tras establecer contacto con Daniela Largo. Chelo Camacho

Los médicos dicen que Daniela está fuera de peligro, pero todavía no ha despertado. Empieza a ser consciente de que sobrevivió esta vez a un terremoto. Y su madre ya le ha contado que el aplastamiento ha obligado a los médicos a amputarle el brazo derecho. Después de resistirse tanto tiempo a perder una pierna, de decidir que prefería morir, Daniela se despertó obligada a luchar contra su peor pesadilla. Su madre reza y confía en que Dios “sacude a uno” con un propósito y que el de su hija deberá ser el de construir una vida distinta a las anteriores. “Si Dios le da otra oportunidad”, dice, “debe cambiar”.

Alrededor de Daniela, mientras los médicos la mantienen sedada y entubada en la UCI, se ha reunido una familia rota. Su madre, Martha, el padre de Daniela, del que se separó hace seis años tras 35 años de matrimonio, y la madrastra Sandra, que se volcó en la búsqueda de Daniela como si fuese su propia hija. Ambas mujeres nunca habían hablado hasta que se encontraron en la puerta del hospital y se cerraron algunas heridas. “Que Dios le pague”, le agradeció Martha. Y en el centro de todos, un niño de 12 años, monaguillo en su iglesia, que muestra orgulloso el reloj, la pulsera y los 60.000 pesos que le regalaron el día de ese cumpleaños que, aunque él aún no lo sabe, marcará la historia de su casa y de Colombia.

World.title: 16 pueblos españoles que piden manga larga cuando cae la tarde
World.content:
Vielha (Lleida). La gran baza de los pueblos seleccionados radica, sobre todo, en la posibilidad de tener que taparse para descansar, algo que se ha convertido en todo un lujo durante la canícula. Es un requisito que cumple Vielha, a la vera de los ríos Garona y Nere, con su casco histórico construido a la manera aranesa, a golpe de piedra, pizarra y madera. Sus mínimas descenderán hasta los 12ºC la noche del domingo; las máximas alcanzarán picos de 33ºC en las horas centrales del jueves y viernes, pero bajarán a los 24ºC (y con probabilidad de lluvias) el lunes, según la Aemet. La capital del Valle de Arán se presenta como un buen campamento base para conocer este territorio del Pirineo catalán, con sus 33 núcleos de población, sus algo más de 10.000 habitantes y sus iglesias románicas. Es recomendable acercarse a la cascada Saut deth Pish, probablemente la más bonita de la zona. Más información: visitvaldaran.com/descubre-la-val-daran/pueblos/vielha/.

World.title: Fifth heatwave confirmed as temperatures reach 37°
World.content:
Temperatures will reach 37° on Friday, after forecaster Weeronline confirmed the fifth regional heatwave of the year.

Maximums will range from 33° in the north to 37° in the south and southeast, the national weather service KNMI said.

Five heatwaves in a single year have happened only once before, in 1947. Then it was Maastricht alone – this year several southern stations have reached the tally.

There will be no national heatwave, which is measured at the KNMI station in De Bilt, near Utrecht. Most of the country, including the Randstad and the north, will fall below the threshold.

KNMI has issued a code yellow warning for heat across the country. The national heat plan, run by public health institute RIVM, puts care homes and health services on alert. It covers the whole country on Friday and only the southeast on Saturday.

Friday night will stay warm, with temperatures holding near 20° in towns and cities.

Saturday will be cooler, with a chance of thunderstorms, although the southeast may still reach about 32°. Sunday will peak at 24°, and next week will be cooler and wetter, with maximums of 21 to 25° and rain likely from Tuesday.

The weekend rain will do little for the drought. Weeronline says short showers run off ground that is baked too hard to absorb water.

World.title: Illegal gambling ads on Meta target vulnerable gamblers: BNR
World.content:
Unlicensed gambling sites are running adverts on Facebook and Instagram that target vulnerable people who have signed themselves onto the national register barring them from gambling, an investigation by radio station BNR has found.

More than 100,000 people in the Netherlands have registered with Cruks, the self-exclusion scheme set up when online gambling was legalised, which requires every licensed casino, arcade and betting site to turn them away.

BNR found that searching Facebook for terms such as “Cruks”, geen Cruks or zonder Cruks (without Cruks) – surfaces a stream of adverts from casinos that hold no Dutch licence, promising large bonuses and offering routes around the register.

The adverts follow a consistent pattern, BNR reported: they suggest Cruks is restricting the user, then point them towards unlicensed alternatives. One features an AI-generated woman who tells viewers that international casinos do not consult the Dutch register and invites them to play the same day.

The accounts placing them carry names such as Betrouwbare Spelsites (reliable gaming sites). Users who encounter the adverts on Facebook go on to see them on Instagram and Threads.

Addiction specialists told BNR they were concerned that people registered with Cruks were being singled out, because seeing gambling adverts can trigger strong urges in addicts.

Meta removed adverts

Meta pulled a large number of the adverts from its public ad library after BNR put questions to the company, and the accounts that were identified were taken offline.

In a written response, Meta said it takes enforcement seriously and that advertisers must comply with the law. It declined to tell BNR what it earns from the adverts.

An estimate published in May by two gambling industry bodies KVA and VNLOK put Meta’s annual revenue from illegal gambling adverts aimed at the Netherlands at between €7.3 million and €13.6 million.

The figure is modelled from publicly available advertising data rather than confirmed by Meta, and the report states that it is not suggesting Meta knowingly allows the adverts.

VNLOK took Meta to court in June in an attempt to force it to act faster, and complained to the European Commission that the company is not meeting its obligations under the EU’s Digital Services Act.

The cabinet set out plans in June for a complete ban on online gambling advertising and bonuses. Junior justice minister Claudia van Bruggen has said the rise in gambling addiction, particularly among young people, is deeply worrying.

If you are concerned about your own or someone else’s gambling, OpenOverGokken, the national gambling helpline run by regulator the Kansspelautoriteit, can be reached free on 0800 24 000 22, day or night.

World.title: Man admits bomb attack on D66 office, calls it protest
World.content:
The man who set off a firework bomb at the D66 headquarters in The Hague in May has admitted the attack, telling a court it was a protest against Dutch asylum policy and what he called the dismantling of the country.

The 37-year-old, identified as Berry van D., appeared at a preliminary hearing at The Hague district court on Thursday. He is accused of causing an explosion with terrorist intent.

About 30 people, most of them members of the party’s youth wing, were inside the building when the firework bomb went off shortly after 9pm. No one was hurt.

Van D. said he had not known anyone was there because he had seen no lights on and that he never intended to hurt anyone.

Prosecutors said he acted alone and told the court he had a political message and wanted to silence people who think differently, ANP reported.

Van D. was arrested about an hour after the blast in the Grote Marktstraat, the city’s main shopping street, carrying two knives. NOS reported that he has a previous conviction for setting fire to city buses in Tilburg, where he had worked as a driver.

He told the court he had turned to violence because voting and peaceful demonstration had achieved nothing.

Psychiatric assessment

Thursday’s hearing was procedural and no trial date has been set yet. Van D. will be transferred to a forensic psychiatric clinic to assess whether he can be held responsible for his actions.

NOS reported that Van D. presents himself on social media as a supporter of the anti-immigration PVV, and described D66 leader Rob Jetten being sworn in as prime minister in February as a black day for the country.

The office on the Lange Houtstraat was also attacked in September last year, when rioters from an anti-immigration demonstration smashed its windows.

World.title: Explosion at Rotterdam port site kills one, injures several
World.content:

One person has been killed and several others injured in an explosion at a site in the Port of Rotterdam, police say.

The blast happened shortly after midday on Thursday at a company on the Moezelweg in Europoort, regional broadcaster Rijnmond reported. Police said they had no further information at this stage.

Multiple people were injured and taken to hospital. Six ambulances, a trauma helicopter and fire crews were sent to the scene.

Rijnmond reported that a hired maintenance crew had been working on pipelines at the site and that something may have gone wrong as those pipes were being disconnected.

Traces of an explosion were visible on a storage tank, the broadcaster said.

Earlier on Thursday, a power cut shut down systems at the Esso refinery on the Botlekweg, sending large flames and black smoke over the port as gas lines were emptied. The Rotterdam-Rijnmond safety authority said it had not established whether the incidents were connected.

World.title: Amsterdam researchers find remedy for fatal child brain disease
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Researchers from the Emma Children’s Hospital at Amsterdam UMC have for the first time found a way to treat a rare genetic brain disease found mostly in children – vanishing white matter, or VWM.

According to The Lancet Neurology, which published the findings, VWM is a neurodegenerative disease “with onset mostly in children aged 1–6 years that causes early death and has no effective therapy.” It’s caused by a genetic defect and occurs in 1 in 100,000 people in the Netherlands.

But now the blood pressure drug guanabenz has been found to inhibit the disease.

In a trial at Amsterdam UMC, 33 children from various countries received guanabenz for four years, while the comparison group included 66 children who did not receive it. Children who received the drug stabilised and ended up needing a wheelchair less often and less quickly.

They also lived – as compared to five patients in the comparison group who died.

“We saw that the disappearance of the white matter in the brain slowed down or even stopped,” chief researcher Marjo van der Knaap told broadcaster NOS.

Moving forward, “the disease-modifying effect of guanabenz should be confirmed in a long-term extension study,” wrote the researchers. The drug also needs the approval of the European Medicines Agency to be used as a treatment for VWM.

World.title: Once-in-a-lifetime solar eclipse has Netherlanders over the moon
World.content:
Eclipse mania took over the Netherlands Wednesday night as people flocked to the coast, roofs and open spaces to watch the largest solar eclipse of the past few decades.

“It looks like a moon giving off light,” a woman on the beach in Petten, a village about 60 kilometers northwest of Amsterdam on the North Sea, told broadcaster NOS. “This is truly very special.”

Indeed traffic jams were rampant on the roads to the sea. But weather conditions were perfect for viewing the eclipse, which was broadcast live on NOS. Some of its broadcasters were clearly moved by the phenomenon.

“This is making me a bit emotional,” NOS weatherman Peter Kuipers Munneke said.

Underwhelmed

But others were less enthusiastic.

College student Sophie joined the crowds to watch the eclipse from the Marineterrein in Amsterdam Oost. Originally planning to make glasses out of old photo negatives, her friend managed to get hold of the hard to come by eye protectors in Amstelveen. But after all the effort, she said they were underwhelmed.

“It wasn’t that special,” she told Dutch News. “The moon didn’t even cover the sun fully. It was like 88% covered and all the sudden, everyone clapped and the sun came back. It wasn’t a total eclipse like in Spain, and it didn’t really become dark. But we had fun.”

A solar eclipse occurs when the moon passes between the sun and earth, blocking all or some of the sun’s light and casting a shadow over the earth.

World.title: Drought means less honey this summer as nectar dries up
World.content:
The persistent drought in the Netherlands has now affected beekeepers, who have noticed that honey production is down this summer. Flowers are blooming for a shorter period, if at all, making it impossible for honeybees to collect the nectar they need to survive.

Professional beekeeper and secretary of the Professional Beekeepers’ Association John Hoogendoorn chalks it up to climate change. “There are increasingly longer periods of drought and higher temperatures, which changes the habitat of the bees,” he told broadcaster NOS. “Nature and the rich biodiversity have deteriorated over the years.”

He said the damage is particularly acute on the dry sandy soils in the east of the country, where the heather honey season has only just begun. Beekeepers report seeing dry shrubs and very little purple, flowering heather there.

Beekeeper Frauke Wessel from Haarlemmermeer has also seen the change. “The bees bring in food to keep their colony alive. But we notice that the honeycomb is no longer filled. The queen bee also lays fewer eggs because she does not get enough food,” she told NOS.

Honeybees need nectar to give them energy for flight and other daily colony tasks. They also convert any excess nectar into stored honey to get them through flowerless winters.

Because the honeybees can’t build up their winter supplies this rainless summer, beekeepers like Hoogendoorn are making up for the lack of honey with dissolved sugar. He told NOS that he needs about 15 kilos of sugar per colony this year to substitute for the honey shortage. “That’s more than in previous years.”

Bees are usually active in the country from the end of February until mid-September. “But due to the high temperatures, the bee season lasts longer and starts earlier,” said beekeeper Joris Knoops.

Flies, wasps, mosquitoes and dragonflies are also suffering from the lack of water.

World.title: Your takeaway habit is feeding Dutch inflation, says DNB
World.content:

Dutch households are spending so much on takeaway meals that it is impacting national inflation, the Dutch central bank DNB has reported.

Delivery meals have nearly doubled as a share of the average shopping basket, from around 1.6% in 2015 to just over 3% today, DNB said on Thursday.

Prices have climbed fast. With more people spending, delivery firms have also passed on higher wage, energy and ingredient costs, and between 2020 and 2023 the category went from adding less than 0.1 percentage point to inflation to a full 0.35 point.

It has since eased back to 0.13 point – but only because prices stopped rising so fast, not because anyone is ordering less, DNB said.

The bank traces consumer habits back to the Covid pandemic, when locked-down households began using ordering apps much more, especially while working from home.

Dutch inflation has sat above the European Central Bank’s 2% target for years, driven mainly by rents and food prices. The pizza and sushi deliveries are now also hitting the figures.

Poland has detained a Russian national who it says was planning to assassinate a person with joint US and Ukrainian citizenship in Warsaw. The news was first announced by Prime Minister Donald Tusk at a press conference on Thursday afternoon. “Thanks to the truly brilliant action of our security services – the Internal Security Agency (ABW) with the assistance of the police – on 7 August we detained a Russian citizen, recruited by Russian intelligence services, whose task was to execute an American and Ukrainian citizen right here in Warsaw,” he said. “This is the first time someone on Russian orders has decided to attack an American citizen on the territory of another NATO country,” added Tusk. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk w #Warszawa: 7 sierpnia zatrzymaliśmy obywatela Rosji, którego zadaniem było wykonanie egzekucji w Warszawie na obywatelu amerykańskim i ukraińskim równocześnie. Dzięki akcji ABW i Policji udało się temu zapobiec. — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 13, 2026 Though the prime minister said he was not allowed to name either the suspect or the target, he revealed that the latter was someone who is “inconvenient for Putin’s regime”. Tusk also gave no details of how the assassination was supposed to have been carried out, but said that it was foiled “at the last minute”. In a subsequent statement, Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of Poland’s security services, confirmed Tusk’s announcement and noted that the operation to prevent the attack had taken place in cooperation with the US. Police headquarters in Warsaw later revealed that the 29-year-old suspect had been charged with planning a murder and accepting an order to carry out murder in return for material or personal benefit. Both crimes carry jail terms of between two and 15 years. He has also been placed in court-approved pretrial detention. 7 sierpnia br. ABW we współpracy z policją zatrzymała obywatela Rosji, który na zlecenie obcej służby przygotowywał zabójstwo obywatela USA ukraińskiego pochodzenia. Do zabójstwa miało dojść w Warszawie. Operacja była realizowana we współpracy ze służbami USA. — Tomasz Siemoniak (@TomaszSiemoniak) August 13, 2026 Poland has been a major target for hostile operations by agents working on behalf of Russia. In February, a report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism found that Poland is the most frequently targeted country in a campaign of sabotage being orchestrated by Russia across Europe. That included an attempt last year to use explosives to derail a train. In June, a Russian artist whose work criticised Putin was assassinated in Poland. Soon after, the Polish security services detained the suspected killer, who they said was using a Georgian passport. Last month, a Russian missile hit Poland during intensive attacks on Ukraine. That followed an incident last year in which around 20 Russian drones violated Polish airspace. Poland has also been one of Ukraine’s closest allies since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, providing significant military, humanitarian and diplomatic support, as well as welcoming millions of Ukrainian refugees, almost one million of whom remain in Poland. World.title: Polish household assets hit record 4 trillion zloty amid fastest growth in years
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poles are building up wealth at the fastest pace in years, with the combined value of household financial assets surpassing 4 trillion zloty (€930 billion) for the first time, according to new data from the Polish Development Fund (PFR), a state entity. The figure reached 4.1 trillion zloty at the end of the first quarter of this year, up 4.3% from the previous quarter, said PFR. That was the largest quarterly increase in just over six years. On an annual basis, assets rose 15.3%, the fastest pace in five years. After deducting liabilities, household net financial assets stood at 3.2 trillion zloty, also a record. Net assets were up 18.4% from a year earlier and 4.9% from the previous quarter. Ponad 4,1 bln zł – tyle wynoszą już aktywa finansowe polskich gospodarstw domowych. To historyczny rekord. W najnowszej analizie PFR pokazujemy, że w ciągu roku wzrosły o 15,3% – to jedna z najwyższych dynamik w historii. Skala i tempo wzrostu aktywów pokazują też, jak duży jest… pic.twitter.com/fSx1yOZtkn — Mikołaj Raczyński (@MikRaczynski) August 7, 2026 The biggest contribution to the quarterly increase came from what PFR classifies as “other equity holdings”, which include shares in limited liability companies, partnerships, cooperatives and mutual insurance societies. They rose by 61.5 billion zloty. Bank deposits recorded the second-largest increase (44.4 billion zloty). Despite the strong rise in equity holdings, bank deposits and cash remained the largest components of household financial assets, accounting for 26.3% and 11.1% respectively. Pension and disability funds accounted for 10.5% of household financial assets. Meanwhile, shares listed on stock exchanges and regulated over-the-counter markets made up 2.9% of household financial assets. Their value is equivalent to 3% of GDP, one of the lowest shares in the European Union, where the average is 8.2%. Although shares make up only a small share of household assets, the Polish stock market has performed strongly in recent years, with its blue-chip index reaching a record high last week and breaking its previous high set 19 years ago. By contrast, Polish households have a relatively high level of cash holdings. Cash was equivalent to 11.5% of Poland’s GDP in the first quarter, well ahead of the EU average of 4.5% and behind only Slovenia (11.7%) and Germany (11.6%). PFR’s data also show that household liabilities in Poland increased by 5.2% year-on-year to more than 891 billion zloty in the first quarter, well below the rate of asset growth. Long-term loans accounted for 92.2% of liabilities, while short-term loans accounted for 5.1%. Rising household wealth reflects three decades of strong economic growth in Poland, accompanied by a rapid rise in wages and living standards. Earlier this year, state research agency CBOS found that a record 39% of Poles say they are financially comfortable, up from just 3% in the early 1990s. Separate data from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show that only 2% of the population live in severe deprivation, the lowest level on record. Poland last year rose to its highest-ever level in a measure of household prosperity in European Union member states, overtaking four other countries. That growth has also fuelled a rapid increase in the number of ultra-wealthy people in Poland, whose number has almost doubled since 2019. However, the PFR data show only total combined household assets and liabilities, not how they are distributed across society. World.title: Poland hit by theft of 19 million patients’ data from medical platform

The personal data of almost 19 million people, including medical information, has been compromised in a major cyberattack on a company that provides services to thousands of medical facilities in Poland. “We are dealing with one of the largest incidents in Poland’s history,” said digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski on Wednesday. He urged people to use government services to check whether their data is affected and to “lock” their national identity number to prevent potential fraud. (￼🧵 1/2) 💬 Dziś doszło do poważnego wycieku danych w firmie MyDr, który może obejmować blisko 19 milionów osób korzystających z opieki medycznej. W związku z sytuacją krytyczną zostały natychmiast podjęte działania mające zabezpieczyć dane i wyjaśnić okoliczności incydentu –… pic.twitter.com/nIp6EvbKiu — Ministerstwo Cyfryzacji (@CYFRA_GOV_PL) August 12, 2026 The attack targeted MyDr, a company that provides services used by many medical facilities in Poland. Its data includes patients’ personal information, as well as medical details such as diagnoses and prescriptions. It was first reported on Monday by Zaufana Trzecia Strona, an IT security news service, which said that it had been contacted on Saturday by the alleged perpetrators, who claimed to have accessed the data of around 18.8 million people. The hackers, who have not been identified, had also sent a screenshot from the compromised database showing the personal data of “one of the most important politicians in Poland”, added Zaufana Trzecia Strona. Shortly afterwards, MyDr confirmed that it had “become the target of an external, deliberate criminal activity involving some of our data”. In an update on Wednesday, it said that, at the time of writing, there was no evidence that the data had been published anywhere. Największy wyciek danych osobowych w historii Polski i co możemy z nim zrobić – nasza analiza incydentu w MyDr i jego potencjalnych skutków.https://t.co/vXUmVfpPAP Opisujemy aktualny stan wiedzy i możliwe scenariusze rozwoju sytuacji. pic.twitter.com/uqhjz1CjZ1 — ZaufanaTrzeciaStrona @zaufanatrzeciastrona@infosec (@Zaufana3Strona) August 13, 2026 Gawkowski addressed the issue at a press briefing on Wednesday. He noted that “there is no indication we are dealing with an external attack…from Russia or any other country”. Poland has recently regularly been targetted by Russian state-linked hackers. It is “very likely” that cybercriminals are behind the attack on MrDr, said Gawkowski, who pledged that there would be an “uncompromising” response from the Polish security services. The minister advised Poles to check in a secure government database whether their data had been leaked. He also advised citizens to use the state web portal, known as mObywatel, to “lock” their identity number, known as a PESEL, which prevents fraudsters from using it. Around 12,000 medical facilities use MyDr’s services, the digital affairs ministry told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The company claims that it processes three million medical consultations and 2.7 million prescriptions a month, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. World.title: Fugitive Polish opposition politician reportedly in pro-Russian Moldovan breakaway region

A letter sent to a Polish court by Marcin Romanowski, who served as a deputy justice minister in the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government and is now on the run from criminal charges, suggests that he is residing in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links with Russia. The Polish authorities have been trying to locate and extradite Romanowski, whose whereabouts have been unknown since he fled Budapest earlier this year after Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who had granted him asylum, lost power. Były wiceminister sprawiedliwości ma przebywać w Tyraspolu, stolicy zbuntowanej mołdawskiej prowincji znajdującej się pod patronatem Rosji. Spod tego adresu w Naddniestrzu polityk PiS miał wystąpić o wydanie listu żelaznego.https://t.co/m05dtQv3KV — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) August 12, 2026 On Wednesday, following media reports that Romanowski had sent a letter to the Polish authorities from Transnistria, a spokeswoman for Warsaw’s district court, which is responsible for extradition matters, confirmed to news website Gazeta.pl that this was the case. “The letter and envelope indicate that the package was sent to the court from Tiraspol in Transnistria,” said judge Anna Ptaszek. “It bears his handwritten signature.” Przemysław Nowak, the spokesman for Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, also confirmed to broadcaster RMF that Romanowski had sent the letter, in which he indicated that he was residing in Tiraspol, the capital of Transnistria, and requested safe passage to Poland. The fugitive politician said that he would be willing to appear in court or before prosecutors, on the condition that he was not placed in detention, said Nowak, who added that prosecutors had not yet taken a position on Romanowski’s request. Transnistria is a region of eastern Moldova, bordering Ukraine, that sought to become a separate state in the early 1990s, even fighting a war between 1990 and 1992. Today, the territory, which has a population of around 360,000, operates as a de facto state but is not recognised by any other country. Transnistria has close ties with Russia, which maintains a military “peacekeeping” force there. The territory’s flag and national emblem feature the Soviet hammer and sickle. Romanowski’s apparent presence in the Russian-linked territory was condemned by figures from Poland’s government. “I would say that Romanowski is now very likely under the influence of Russian intelligence,” said deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk, quoted by broadcaster TVN. Paweł Wojtunik, the former head of Poland’s Central Anticorruption Bureau (CBA), who previously worked in Moldova, wrote that “it is impossible to enter [Transnistria], let alone to live there, without the consent of the local KGB, which is directly managed by the Russian GRU and FSB [intelligence agences]”. – Dzisiaj powiedziałbym, że Romanowski z dużym prawdopodobieństwem jest pod wpływem rosyjskich służb – ocenił wiceszef MON Cezary Tomczyk. Sprawę skomentował też szef MSZ Radosław Sikorski.https://t.co/LuWw0bkh2j — tvn24 (@tvn24) August 12, 2026 Even a deputy leader of Romanowski’s own party, the national-conservative PiS, was unwilling to defend him. In an interview with Polsat News, Przemysław Czarnek noted that it is still not confirmed that Romanowski is in Transnistria. But he agreed, when asked by the host, that it “would be crossing a line” for Romanowski to be in the territory. Romanowski served as a deputy justice minister in the former PiS government between 2019 and 2023. He remains a member of parliament, despite having fled Poland in December 2024 after prosecutors sought to bring charges against him for 11 alleged crimes, including participating in an organised criminal group. Those alleged offences relate to Romanowski’s time at the justice ministry, which was then led by Zbigniew Ziobro, who is also wanted on multiple charges. Both Romanowski and Ziobro obtained asylum in Hungary when the country was led by PiS-ally Orbán. The Polish government says that Hungary has revoked the refugee status and travel documents granted to fugitive ex-justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro by Viktor Orbán. Poland will now seek Ziobro's deportation from the US, where he fled after leaving Hungary https://t.co/TcVw0AiEMX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2026 However, after Orbán lost power earlier this year, Ziobro fled to the United States, where he remains. Last month, Poland requested his extradition, though that is a process that could take years. Romanowski, meanwhile, disappeared completely, leading to months of speculation as to his whereabouts. Both politicians have denied the allegations against them and have claimed to be victims of “political revenge” by the current government, a more liberal coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk that took power in December 2023. They have argued that they would not be able to receive a fair trial in Poland while Tusk remains in power because of the government’s influence over the judicial system. On Wednesday, Romanowski’s lawyer, Bartosz Lewandowski, confirmed that his client had requested safe passage to Poland and that he was “outside the territory of the European Union”. However, he did not confirm that Romanowski is in Transnistria. Poland has formally asked the US to detain and extradite former justice minister @ZiobroPL, who faces multiple criminal charges. World.title: Poland complains to Starlink over exclusion from European roaming zone

The Polish government has appealed to Starlink, the satellite internet service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, to reverse its decision to exclude Poland from its European roaming area. It says that Polish users, who will now face greater costs when travelling, should not be treated as “second-tier customers”. Starlink, which provides users with portable terminals that act as receivers for internet connections from its network of satellites, offers a “Roam” service that lets customers continue using their connection outside their home country without extra charges as long as they remain within their designated region. One region is Europe, in which Starlink has included 36 countries and territories. However, the firm makes clear that “Poland is not included in the Europe region”, meaning users registered in that country are not included in the Roam system. The company offered no explanation for Poland’s exclusion from the system. Some media reports have suggested that it is because terminals registered in Poland are used in Ukraine. However, Ukraine is itself not included in Starlink’s European “Roam” region. The company’s decision prompted an angry response from Polish government ministers. “I do not agree with a global technology company treating Poles worse than other Europeans,” wrote digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski on X, the social media platform owned by Musk. “If Elon Musk’s SpaceX wants to operate in Poland, benefit from the Polish market, and earn from Polish customers, it must treat them fairly and on equal terms,” he added. “That is why I have appealed to SpaceX for the urgent restoration of equal terms for the company’s Polish customers.” Nie zgadzam się, żeby globalna firma technologiczna traktowała Polki i Polaków gorzej niż innych Europejczyków. Jeżeli @SpaceX @Elon Musk chce działać w Polsce, korzystać z polskiego rynku i zarabiać na polskich klientach, musi ich traktować uczciwie i na równych zasadach. Od… — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) August 12, 2026 Meanwhile, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski revived a dispute he had with Musk last year over the provision of Starlink terminals to Ukraine during its war with Russia. That dispute saw Musk tell Sikorski to “be quiet, small man”. “Hey, Elon Musk, big man,” wrote Sikorski today on X, “stop discriminating [against] Polish users of Starlink or we might re-think paying you $50 million p.a. for your services.” The latter was a reference to the fact that Poland spends around $50 million a year to help provide Starlink services for Ukraine. World.title: Negative views of Polish-Ukrainian relations reach highest level on record in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of Polish-Ukrainian relations has risen to 46%, the highest figure ever recorded by Polish state research agency CBOS. Only 12% think relations are good. By contrast, three years ago, in mid-2023, only 3% had a negative view and 64% a positive one. Meanwhile, CBOS also found that belief among Poles that reconciliation between the two neighbours, who share a difficult history, is possible is at its lowest level on record, 53%, down from 78% three years ago. The findings follow other polls showing worsening attitudes towards Ukraine and Ukrainians in Poland in recent years, and come amid an ongoing diplomatic crisis triggered by President Volodymyr Zelensky naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two. Przekonanie o możliwości pojednania między Polakami 🇵🇱 a Ukraińcami 🇺🇦 spadło do najniższego poziomu w historii naszych pomiarów. 📙 Więcej w komunikacie #CBOS "Stosunki polsko-ukraińskie" ⤵️ https://t.co/kw2o4upY3Q#Ukraina #Ukraińcy pic.twitter.com/LItCFC3f2m — CBOS (@CBOS_Info) August 11, 2026 Relations between Poland and Ukraine improved significantly in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, as Poland welcomed millions of Ukrainian refugees and provided Kyiv with extensive military, humanitarian and diplomatic support. However, since 2023, those relations have been hit by a series of controversies over Ukrainian agricultural exports, border blockades by Polish farmers and truckers, and, above all, over the two nations’ difficult World War Two history. Among Poles who now hold a negative view of relations, CBOS also asked them who was responsible for the situation. A large majority, 65%, primarily blamed Ukraine, while only 4% said it was Poland’s fault and 28% placed responsibility on both sides. In its regular surveys since 1997, the agency has also asked Poles if they believe that reconciliation between Poles and Ukrainians is possible or not. In the early 2000s, that figure rose to a record level of 81%, and in 2023 it still stood at 78%. Now, however, it has dropped to an all-time low of 53%. There have long been tensions between Poland and Ukraine over their difficult, intertwined histories, in particular during the first half of the 20th century. In World War Two, Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, in an ethnic-cleansing operation known as the Volhynia massacres. Poland has officially recognised that episode as a genocide. However, Ukraine rejects that label and also points to the persecution of Ukrainians who lived in the interwar Polish state, as well as to massacres of Ukrainians by Polish groups during World War Two. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 Those tensions recently boiled over after Zelensky, in May this year, approved a request to rename a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”, the group that led the Volhynia massacres but is remembered positively in Ukraine for its role in fighting Moscow-imposed Soviet rule. Zelensky’s decision prompted his Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, to strip the Ukrainian president of Poland’s highest honour. While tensions have since calmed somewhat, the dispute remains unresolved. However, even before that diplomatic crisis broke out, polling showed increasingly negative attitudes in Poland towards both Ukraine and Ukrainians, who are by far the country’s largest immigrant group. In its annual survey of attitudes towards various national and ethnic groups, published in February, CBOS found that the proportion of Poles who said they disliked Ukrainians had increased by five percentage points year-on-year, to 43%. Only 29% said they liked Ukrainians. In January, CBOS reported that opposition to accepting Ukrainian refugees in Poland had risen to its highest ever level. In December 2024, a poll in Ukraine found that positive sentiment towards Poles had fallen by half in the space of two years. The proportion of Poles opposed to accepting Ukrainian refugees has reached its highest ever level of 46%, up from 3% in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion. Other recent surveys have also indicated declining sympathy towards Ukrainians among Poles https://t.co/DLPGY2ToZG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 7, 2026 Meanwhile, the number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland rose by 30% in the first half of 2026, including a number of high-profile incidents. Poland’s government has blamed increasing anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from the right-wing and far-right opposition. Last month, Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, called on “Polish politicians to stop inciting hatred against Ukrainians”. CBOS’s new study shows that attitudes towards relations with Ukraine differ significantly depending on political affiliation. Whereas 35% of supporters of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO), Poland’s main ruling party, hold a negative view of relations, that rises to 52% among voters of the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party and 81% for the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja). Among those with a negative view, 49% of KO voters blamed Poland and Ukraine equally for the situation while 10% blamed mainly Poland. By contrast, 86% of Confederation supporters and 82% of PiS supporters placed responsibility on the Ukrainian side. Demonstrations took place in 25 Polish cities on Sunday against the “growing wave of hate and violence” against Ukrainians, who are Poland’s largest immigrant group. World.title: Poland unveils first warship under major naval modernisation programme
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has unveiled its first frigate to enter service in decades at a ceremony in the Baltic Sea port of Gdynia, where the ship was constructed. The development marks a major milestone in a 15 billion zloty (€3.5 billion) programme to modernise the ageing Polish navy and strengthen NATO’s maritime defences. “Poland is becoming a maritime power in the Baltic Sea,” declared Prime Minister Donald Tusk at a ceremony to name the new ship, which he attended alongside opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki in a rare show of unity. World.title: Negative views of Poland’s justice system have grown under Tusk government, finds state pollster
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The proportion of Poles who negatively assess their country’s justice system has increased under the current government, despite its promises to restore the rule of law and ensure that courts function more effectively and independently. New polling by state research agency CBOS found that, in June this year, 61% of Poles had a negative view of the functioning of the justice system, up from 55% in 2022 and 51% in 2017, when the former Law and Justice (PiS) government was in power. Only 26% now positively assess the system, down from 28% in 2022 and 36% in 2017. The last time positive views were lower was in 2005 (22%). The findings come two and a half years after the current government, a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, came to power in December 2023, replacing the national-conservative PiS administration. One of Tusk’s main promises was to restore the rule of law after eight years in which PiS had implemented a series of contested judicial reforms that experts, European courts and many Polish judges had condemned as undermining the independence and functioning of the judiciary. However, Tusk’s government has struggled to implement its promised changes. In many cases, its efforts have been blocked by PiS-aligned Presidents Andrzej Duda and Karol Nawrocki or other officials appointed under the former government. But in other cases, such as with a pledge to separate the functions of justice minister and prosecutor general, which were fused by PiS in 2016, the current ruling coalition has simply not followed through on its promises. In its latest polling, CBOS found that supporters of the current opposition are most dissatisfied with the functioning of the justice system: 72% of PiS voters have a negative view, as do 71% of those who support the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja). However, even among voters of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, a majority, 53%, have a negative opinion, with only 38% holding a positive one. Interestingly, public attitudes towards judges themselves have hardly changed. Currently, 19% of Poles have a positive view towards them and 23% a negative one. That is similar to findings in 2017 (22% positive, 24% negative) and 2012 (19% positive, 23% negative). More Poles (35%) think that the rule of law has got worse under Tusk's government than believe it has improved (24%). A further 28% think there has been no change, finds a new poll https://t.co/KkiuY2vDSW — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 5, 2025 When asked to identify the greatest problems with the justice system, Poles instead often point to structural issues – that is, those that are under the control of politicians. The most commonly identified problem (chosen by 38% of respondents, who could select up to three main problems) was “prolonged proceedings” in court cases. The second biggest issue was “politicisation of courts” (18%). Only 4% said that “judges’ neglect of duty, incompetence and impunity” were among the biggest problems. However, 23% of respondents were unable to name a single major issue that the justice system faces. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 CBOS’s findings echo a number of other polls. After the first year of Tusk’s government, a survey by SW Research for the Rzeczpospolita daily found that 35% of Poles thought the rule-of-law situation had got worse, compared to only 24% who thought it had improved. Another poll by the same agency for Onet, a news website, in January this year similarly found that 40% of Poles believe the justice system has not improved under the current government, while only 33% think it has got better. In response to the latter poll, justice minister Waldemar Żurek admitted to Onet that there had been problems in addressing the rule of law. But he blamed the “hurdles [put] in our path” by Presidents Duda and Nawrocki. Opposition-aligned President @NawrockiKn has vetoed a government bill intended to reform a judicial body at the heart of Poland’s rule-of-law crisis. He argued that the measures would simply create even greater “legal chaos” https://t.co/I7FHRKIoP1 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 19, 2026 In 2024, Duda refused to sign government bills overhauling the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which still contains judges illegitimately appointed under the former PiS administration. As a result, Tusk’s government refuses to recognise rulings issued by the TK. In February this year, Duda’s successor, Nawrocki, vetoed a government bill intended to restore the legitimacy of the National Council of the Judiciary (KRS), the body responsible for nominating judges to positions on courts. In 2017, the KRS was overhauled under PiS in a manner that rendered it illegitimate, according to multiple Polish and European court rulings. That in turn has led to doubts over the legal status of around 3,000 judges appointed by the KRS since 2017 and all the rulings issued by them. Nawrocki has also refused to swear in four new TK judges nominated by parliament this year, despite an order by the European Court of Human Rights that they be allowed to take up their positions. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in.
