World.title: Weekend weather in Hungary: heatwave returns, temperatures may reach 37°C by Sunday
World.content:
The weekend weather in Hungary will bring the return of intense summer heat, with mostly cloudless skies, virtually no rain and temperatures climbing above 30°C across the country. The hottest conditions are expected on Sunday, when afternoon highs could reach 37°C, according to the latest forecast from HungaroMet, Hungary’s national meteorological service.

After a slight easing of the heat earlier in the week, temperatures will rise steadily from Friday, 14 August, through Sunday, 16 August. The dry spell will also continue, adding further pressure to areas already affected by severe agricultural drought. HungaroMet said earlier this week that most of Hungary was experiencing severe or extreme agricultural drought, with no meaningful rainfall expected in the days ahead.

Friday: sunny and dry across Hungary

Friday will be largely cloudless and sunny throughout the country. Some cumulus clouds may develop in eastern Hungary, but rainfall is not expected.

Winds will generally remain light or moderate and will come mainly from the east, although they could strengthen at times over the Northern Great Plain.

Daytime temperatures will already be high. HungaroMet’s latest national outlook indicates maximum temperatures of roughly 28–33°C, meaning summer heat will be felt almost everywhere.

Despite the rising temperatures, HungaroMet said no weather event meeting its official warning criteria was expected anywhere in Hungary up to midnight on Friday.

As we wrote today, the danger is not over, Budapest water supply under pressure again

Weekend weather in Hungary turns hotter on Saturday

Saturday will mark a more noticeable return of the heatwave. Mostly clear and dry weather is forecast, with only limited cloud development possible in eastern and south-eastern parts of Hungary.

Southerly winds may strengthen locally, while temperatures will show a considerable difference between the cool early morning and the hot afternoon.

Minimum temperatures are expected to range between 7°C and 20°C, with the lowest values likely in sheltered and traditionally cooler locations. By the afternoon, however, temperatures will rise to 30–35°C.

HungaroMet has also indicated first-level warnings for high daily mean temperatures in ten counties, including Pest, Bács-Kiskun, Békés, Csongrád-Csanád, Fejér, Győr-Moson-Sopron, Komárom-Esztergom, Jász-Nagykun-Szolnok, Tolna and Veszprém. In these areas, the daily average temperature may exceed 25°C.

For foreign visitors, this means that even if mornings remain relatively comfortable in some parts of the country, conditions can become significantly hotter by early afternoon. Travellers planning sightseeing, hiking or outdoor activities should therefore be prepared for strong summer heat.

Sunday could bring temperatures of up to 37°C

The hottest part of the weekend is expected on Sunday. Mostly clear and sunny conditions will continue, although some clouds could reach north-western Hungary. Rain remains unlikely, while southerly winds may become brisk in places.

Morning temperatures are expected to range from around 10°C to 22°C, before the air heats up rapidly during the day. According to HungaroMet’s current forecast, afternoon highs are likely to reach 33–37°C.

City forecasts also point to intense heat: around 36°C is currently expected in Budapest and Győr, while Szeged and Debrecen could reach approximately 35°C on Sunday.

Dry weather adds to Hungary’s drought problems

The lack of rain is becoming increasingly significant. HungaroMet’s agricultural assessment published on 10 August said that rainfall over the previous months had fallen well below the long-term average in much of Hungary, while soil moisture levels were critically low across large areas.

The weekend weather in Hungary will therefore be favourable for outdoor programmes in terms of sunshine and the low risk of rain, but the rapidly intensifying heat will become the main concern. By Sunday afternoon, much of the country is likely to experience genuine heatwave conditions, bringing another spell of very hot and exceptionally dry weather to Hungary.

World.title: Romania races to complete 4,500 PNRR projects before August deadline
World.content:
Romania is accelerating work to complete and formally receive around 4,500 projects financed through the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR) before the end of August, acting prime minister Ilie Bolojan said on August 13, cited by Profit.ro. He warned that delays could result in financial penalties.

Bolojan held a teleconference with prefectures and government representatives responsible for receiving investment projects, during which he called for as many outstanding works as possible to be completed and formally received over the following two weeks.

Romania has more than 15,000 projects financed through the PNRR across the country, according to Bolojan. Many are managed through the Ministry of Education to equip schools, while others are implemented through the Ministry of Development and local authorities.

The projects include investments in schools and medical facilities, apartment-block insulation and other local infrastructure. Around 4,500 projects have yet to be formally received.

Formal reception requires not only completion of the physical works but also registration in the land register and the submission of final documents through the electronic platform provided to local authorities, Bolojan said.

"For works that will not be completed by the end of August, Romania will face penalties," Bolojan warned, without specifying the potential financial impact.

The government has also established a reserve portfolio of "mature and compliant" projects to mitigate the risk of Romania failing to meet milestones and targets linked to PNRR payment requests 5 and 6.

The reserve portfolio is intended to provide alternative projects that can contribute to the required indicators if some projects in the active portfolio cannot be completed or otherwise fail to meet the relevant targets, according to the government.

Romania's PNRR implementation is under increasing time pressure as the program's deadline approaches. The country is scheduled to submit its fifth payment request, while the sixth and final request is expected at the end of September.

The government has been seeking to ensure that delayed investments and reforms are completed in time to avoid losing part of the EU funding allocated under the Recovery and Resilience Facility.

World.title: Romania relies on Bulgaria and the wind after shutting down Cernavoda nuclear plant
World.content:
Strong wind, the prosumers shifting their input during peak hours, and the imports from Bulgaria helped Romania’s power system on the first day after Nuclearelectrica shut down its last reactor on August 13, leaving the country without nearly 20% of its electricity production.

The electricity provided by the storage facilities reached a power of 600 MW during the peak hours, close to the 680 MW provided by each of Cernavoda's two reactors before shutdown. Household prosumers with storage capacities are not financially stimulated to deliver electricity to the national power grid, but save it and use it later.

"The worst case scenario is that the wind stops blowing, because today the wind blew, it blew over the [past] weekend as well. There were days when we had very good wind power production. So, if we can no longer rely on wind, this will complicate our lives. If, for example, something happens and we cannot import as much from Bulgaria, that will complicate our lives again," expert Eugenia Gusilov explained, speaking to Digi24.

World.title: Romania cuts diesel excise duty by 20% under new price mechanism
World.content:
Romania's Ministry of Finance will cut the excise duty on standard diesel by 20% from August 16 to August 31, following a rise in international diesel quotations and domestic pump prices, the ministry said.

The temporary reduction amounts to RON 561 per 1,000 litres, bringing the applicable excise duty to RON 2,243 per 1,000 litres, or RON 2,655 per tonne. The measure is being implemented under Law No. 162/2026, which introduced a mechanism allowing excise duties to be adjusted temporarily in response to fuel market developments.

The ministry said Platts diesel quotations increased by 34.13% during the reference period, while the average pump price of standard diesel rose by 23.01%.

"We built this mechanism precisely so that the state can intervene quickly and in a targeted manner when market developments require it, without fixed fiscal measures that would produce budgetary effects regardless of the real conditions," Finance Minister Alexandru Nazare said.

"Under these conditions, the mechanism is activated, and the excise duty decreases by 20%. It is a temporary intervention, calibrated to market developments, through which we reduce the pressure on the population and companies, while maintaining control over the budgetary impact," Nazare said.

The mechanism introduced by Law No. 162/2026 provides for an assessment of fuel market indicators every two weeks, allowing the excise duty to be adjusted temporarily when specified conditions are met.

The ministry said the reduction is intended to limit the impact of higher international fuel prices on consumers and businesses, particularly in transport and logistics, where diesel costs feed into a broad range of goods and services.

The level of the intervention will be reassessed every two weeks in line with the provisions of the law, according to the ministry.

World.title: Romania’s industrial output plunges by 4.6% y/y in Q2
World.content:
Romania’s industrial production index contracted by 4.6% y/y in the second quarter (Q2) of 2026, marking the steepest decline since the lockdown in 2020, according to data published by the statistics office INS. In seasonally-adjusted terms, industrial output decreased by 0.4% q/q.

In the core manufacturing sector, the production index plunged even more steeply, by 5.3% y/y, despite a positive 0.7% q/q advance. The segments of utilities (-0.5% y/y) and mining and quarrying (-1.5% y/y) posted more moderate negative growth rates.

Over the past five years, the industrial output in Romania plunged by 8.8% y/y, with a 7.2% y/y decline in the core manufacturing segment. The activity in the segment of utilities, however, dropped by 19.4% over the five-year period.

The food industry posted a marginal 0.1% y/y advance in Q1, but it boasts a robust 17.1% expansion over the past five years. It was surpassed by only a couple of other industries (manufacturing of electronic and optic devices and manufacturing of other transport means). The beverages sector has not demonstrated similar resilience, losing 6.8% on the year and 5.1% over the past five years.

The steepest annual decline in Q1 was posted by the oil refining industry (-18.1% y/y), except for the composite segment of “other industrial activities” that plunged by nearly 27% y/y. The oil refining industry, also 19.5% down on a five-year term, was impacted by the planned technical outage of its refineries.

The automobile industry posts steep declines both compared to last year and compared to five years ago, namely 16.1% y/y and 15.7% respectively, witnessing the problematic episode faced by Romania’s most relevant sector for its exports.

Romania’s industry is likely to mark the fourth consecutive year of decline, despite the managers’ expectations slightly improving in July.

The BCR Romania Manufacturing PMI crossed into expansion territory for the first time in just over two years, reaching 50.1 in July vs 48.8 in June, according to the research note published by Erste Group.

The stabilisation of the manufacturing output at the level reached in May (latest available data) would, however, imply a 3.3% contraction for the entire year, after 1.1%-1.2% annual contraction rates in 2024-2025 and a steeper 2.5% y/y contraction in 2023.

World.title: Romania’s central bank raises year-end inflation forecast to 6.1%
World.content:
The National Bank of Romania (BNR) in its August 13 quarterly Inflation Report raised its forecast for end-2026 inflation by 0.6 percentage points to 6.1%, as governor Mugur Isărescu said the economy remained below potential amid fiscal consolidation and supply-side shocks.

The new forecast, presented by Isărescu, puts inflation further above BNR's previous projection of 5.5%. BNR now expects inflation to return to its 2.5% +/-1pp target range only in the fourth quarter of 2027.

The central bank's inflation report points to the lingering effects of fiscal consolidation measures introduced in 2025 and early 2026, alongside supply shocks affecting energy prices. The report cites the US-Iran war and the extreme decline in Danube water levels among factors pushing up the prices of oil, gas and electricity.

Fuel prices are expected to account for around 1.1 percentage points of the projected 6.1% inflation rate at the end of 2026, according to the BNR.

Isărescu said monetary easing remained likely as inflation declines, but indicated that the timing of rate cuts could not yet be determined.

"It is obvious that interest rates will decrease and the monetary policy rate will decrease, in the coming period, as inflation decreases," Isărescu said. "But we cannot discuss now when inflation is still significantly above the monetary policy rate, or the monetary policy rate is below the inflation rate."

The governor also said the central bank did not expect a rapid recovery in economic activity. The BNR's assessment shows private consumption weakening amid declining purchasing power and low consumer confidence, while lending to households has slowed.

Corporate lending, by contrast, has continued to expand, with leu-denominated loans to companies rising by around 20%, according to Isărescu.

He said the increase reflected companies' assessment that borrowing costs, while high in nominal terms, were relatively low in real terms because of inflation.

"We do not expect a rapid return to economic growth," Isărescu said.

World.title: Romania's Q2 GDP flat q/q, drops by 0.4% y/y
World.content:
Romania's Q2 GDP recorded a decrease of 0.4% y/y under the previous-year-prices methodology, and by 2% y/y under the chain-linked-volumes methodology, the statistics office INS announced on August 14 under its flash estimate.

The seasonally adjusted GDP (chain-linked-volume methodology) remained constant in Q2, compared to Q1, after two consecutive quarters of negative growth (technical recession).

In the first semester of 2026, the GDP decreased by 0.8% y/y (unadjusted terms, previous year price methodology), INS also announced. Under the chain-linked-volume methodology, the decrease was 1.6% y/y.

World.title: Urban art tours at Un-hidden Bucharest
World.content:
The Bucharest public can discover the city’s urban art through a series of guided tours and events organized as part of the project Un-hidden Bucharest.

Inspired by Constantin Brâncuși’s legacy, the project invites the public to take part in five guided tours, discover a multidisciplinary artistic intervention, an exhibition, two interdisciplinary performances and two discussions, “each offering a different perspective on how we live in and share urban space,” the organizers said.

The project highlights existing urban art interventions in Bucharest and “creates opportunities for them to be (re)discovered, understood and viewed as part of the city’s contemporary cultural heritage.”

“Un-hidden Bucharest is a continuation of the efforts of the Un-hidden multi-year program, which seeks to explore how independent art can humanize public spaces and foster feelings of belonging and cultural identity among residents and visitors to Bucharest,” Cristina Popa, co-founder of Save or Cancel, the initiator of the project, explained.

Participation in all activities included in the project is free. Prior registration is required via an online form available on the project’s website.

World.title: Romanian films selected for Sarajevo Film Festival
World.content:
Several Romanian films have been selected in sections of this year’s Sarajevo Film Festival, while others will be screened at the event outside of competitions.

The feature film This Is Not Your Place Here, directed by Florin Șerban, has been selected for the official competition of the event. The film will have its international premiere in the main competition of the 2026 Locarno Film Festival in Switzerland.

This Is Not Your Place Here follows Marius, a respected surgeon in a provincial town and a single father, who learns that his teenage son is suspected of murder. The cast includes Adrian Văncică as a doctor, debuting actor Teodor Butănescu as Ioan, as well as Alex Conovaru, Cristina Richter, Janir Izdrăilă, and Cosmin Dominte. The film is executive produced by Minodora Șerban. Fantascope is the production company.

Director Florin Șerban, a 2010 Silver Bear winner for his feature film If I Want to Whistle, I Whistle.

The short film You Make Your Own Future, But Why Not Leave It to the Professionals?, directed by Alexandra Schinteie, has been selected for the Sarajevo Film Festival’s Student Short Film competition, where it will have its international premiere. The short film has also been selected this year for the Transilvania IFF and Anonimul film festivals.

It centers on Beatrice, who undergoes multiple cosmetic procedures under her husband’s watchful eye.

The cast includes Ilinca Manolache, Nicodim Ungureanu, Tudor Chirilă, Gabriel Spahiu, Radu Stoian, Lorena Dănciulescu and Emilia Ivașcu. The film was produced by the Faculty of Theatre and Film at Babeș-Bolyai University in Cluj-Napoca. Eduard Angheluș is the producer, Dan Osteniuc the director of photography.

Alexandra Schinteie

At the same time, Tudor Giurgiu’s 3 Days in September will be screened in the In Focus section, dedicated to the recent film productions from the region. The film had its world premiere at the International Film Festival Rotterdam (IFFR).

The movie is a dark comedy built around a 65-minute single-take sequence following the collapse of a relationship on the very day of a wedding. The leading roles are played by Andreea Vasile, Emilian Oprea, Conrad Mericoffer, Mirela Zeța, Emilia Popescu, Adela Popescu and Maria Junghietu. The screenplay was written by Conrad Mericoffer, Radu Grigore and Tudor Giurgiu, while cinematography is by Alexandru Dorobanțu. Point Film is the production company.

Tudor Giurgiu

Other Romanian films or co-productions that will be screened at the Sarajevo festival include Fjord, directed by Cristian Mungiu; Atlas of the Universe, directed by Paul Negoescu; Motherhood, an animated short directed by Anca Damian; Titanic Ocean, directed by Konstantina Kotzamani; Electing Ms Santa (2025), a documentary directed by Raisa Răzmeriță; Cristina Was Very Good, directed by Alin Boeru; Don’t Ask Me If I Killed (2026), a documentary directed by Helena Maksyom; and Go Outside and Hug a Tree, a short film directed by Irina Alexiu.

Now in its 32nd edition, the Sarajevo Film Festival is one of Southeastern Europe's leading platforms for promoting regional cinema.

World.content:
Russia on the radar; Slovakia picks a fight with Brussels over same-sex marriage

Slovakia’s Interior Ministry has been forced into an embarrassing retreat over speed cameras with suspected Russian links, a week after dismissing opposition warnings about their origin. The National Security Authority (NBU) confirmed on Tuesday that the two devices in question contain Russian components. The finding vindicates concerns raised by Progressive Slovakia (PS), the country’s strongest opposition party, which had warned that the cameras could pose a security risk. There were red flags from the start. Journalists found that the cameras closely resembled equipment made by the St Petersburg-based company Simicon. More strikingly, the measurement software listed in the Slovak certification had the same digital fingerprint as software used in a Russian CORDON speed camera. The ministry’s story has shifted ever since. It first insisted the cameras were not Russian, then conceded it could not prove their origin, before ordering IT supplier Soitron to remove the test devices. It now says two ministry employees will lose their jobs and cooperation with Soitron will end. Interior Minister Matus Sutaj Estok, of the governing Hlas party, has resisted calls to take political responsibility. “We were lied to,” he said on Thursday, blaming the Slovak Institute of Metrology, which certified the cameras. The institute says checking cybersecurity risks, supply chains or the origin of components is not its job. Soitron also denies misleading the state. Soitron obtained the devices from a Slovak distributor whose CEO had worked in Russia for many years and had previously imported similar equipment to Slovakia through another company. The ministry will not publish the NBU analysis, and it is unclear why the country’s security services failed to spot the potential problem before opposition politicians and journalists did. The General Prosecutor’s Office has now said it will examine the case.

There was another controversy this week involving the Interior Ministry, and Interior Minister Sutaj Estok in particular. His ministry has refused to register same-sex marriages legally concluded abroad. Several Slovak same-sex couples applied in December to have their foreign marriage certificates entered into Slovakia’s special registry. After waiting eight months, they received an answer not from the registry, but directly from Sutaj Estok. He argued that registering the unions as marriages would conflict with Slovak law and the constitution, which has defined marriage as a union between a man and a woman since 2014. Among those affected are former diplomats Ivan Novotny and his husband Metod Spacek. They argue that the minister intervened in a procedure that should have been handled by the registry and are now preparing an administrative lawsuit. At the heart of the dispute is a 2025 ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union involving a Polish-German same-sex couple. The court ruled that an EU country cannot refuse to recognise a same-sex marriage legally concluded in another member state if doing so interferes with rights guaranteed under EU law, particularly freedom of movement and residence. The ruling does not require member states to introduce same-sex marriage into their domestic law. The European Commission has reminded Slovakia that EU law, as interpreted by the EU’s top court, takes precedence over national law and that member states are required to implement its judgments. It told the SME daily that it would continue to monitor the situation and could use the tools at its disposal if needed. The ministry argues that EU law may require Slovakia to recognise same-sex marriages for specific purposes, but does not oblige the country to enter them in its registry as marriages with the same legal status as marriages recognised under Slovak law. Novotny, Spacek and other couples dispute that interpretation. Their planned legal challenge could now put that question before the Slovak courts.

World.title: Montenegro’s Menstrual Leave Law Won’t Succeed Without More Gynaecologists
World.content:
Imagine a woman called Milica. She is 29, on a fixed-term contract, and every month menstrual pain keeps her from working for several days.

Milica has not seen a gynaecologist in two years. There aren’t enough appointments where she lives and she cannot travel to the capital, Podgorica, because of work.

When she finally gets a diagnosis, she learns a law offering paid leave exists, and she must renew her medical diagnosis certificate every year.

But she wonders whether her employer will extend her contract if he learns why she has been absent.

World.title: BIRN Reality Check: What Has Albania’s AI ‘Minister’ Achieved So Far?
World.content:
According to Rama, Diella was to serve as Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, with a specific task: to eliminate corruption from public procurement tenders – a key issue for Albania as it seeks to push forward its EU accession process.

But a year later, the actual role of the bot ‘minister’ role remains unclear.

At the Public Procurement Agency, where the bot’s skills were expected to be tested, work still appears to be at the preparatory stage.

“There is a project to develop an AI-powered procurement system, but it is still in progress,” said Reida Kashta, the Agency’s director, when asked whether it had begun using AI in public procurement.

According to Kashta, the agency has “just completed the drafting of the terms of reference”. This is a document that sets out the technical criteria for launching the tender that will select the company responsible for building the system.

The public procurement system has for years been considered one of the sectors most exposed to corruption in Albania. Investigations by the Special Prosecution Office for organised crime and corruption, SPAK, have uncovered several cases involving schemes to manipulate tenders, in which winners had been predetermined before the procedures were launched. Contracts for the construction of roads, incinerators and other public investments have been subject to investigations over allegations of favouring economic operators and violating competition rules.

The government’s ambition to integrate AI into the sector has been met with scepticism by both opposition politicians and public policy experts, mainly because of the security risks it entails, its lack of human capacity and various legal uncertainties.

Opposition Democratic Party MP Klevis Balliu told BIRN that the use of AI could serve as an assisting tool for the administration, but could not replace the legal responsibility of institutions, nor guarantee the fight against corruption.

According to Balliu, without a clear constitutional and legal basis, the creation of a virtual minister raises questions about who bears responsibility for decision-making, particularly in a sensitive sector such as public procurement.

“Diella does not solve corruption. On the contrary, she raises a fundamental question: who bears responsibility for decisions influenced by a system that has no legally defined status?” Balliu said.

He argued that a virtual system could help increase efficiency and identify irregularities, but “it cannot replace transparency, oversight and human accountability.”

Public policy experts are also concerned about the use of AI in procurement without a comprehensive legal, institutional and technical framework in place.

Alba Brojka, an independent digital policy expert, said artificial intelligence should not be treated as a “magic wand solution” to complex problems such as corruption, but only as a tool to increase efficiency and automate administrative processes.

“Under [UN culture agency] UNESCO’s principles on the ethical use of AI, decision-making ultimately belongs to the expert or human, not the technology,” Brojka said. She sees this particular use of AI as “an excuse for a problem [corruption] that has existed for years”, and that what needs addressing first is the “legal gap and institutional capacity”.

For Aranita Brahaj, head of the Albanian Institute of Science (AIS) the use of AI in procurement cannot be seen as a solution to tendering problems without first consolidating the legal framework and developing a new methodology to monitor the efficiency of such systems.

“Albania still lacks a complete, secondary legal framework and, above all, this process is taking place at a time when public contracting is showing significant problems,” Brahaj said.

Multiple challenges

World.title: What Our Sons Never Asked: Sarajevo Film Breaks Generational Silence About Siege
World.content:
Some of the film’s most charged moments happen in the space between a father finishing a memory and a son deciding what to do with it.

In one scene, Faruk describes risking his own safety to put out fires caused by shelling. His son’s response, a simple, unrehearsed statement of pride, visibly catches his father off-guard. In another, Ismet, who worked as a hotel driver during the siege, describes coming home one day to find his own father, and his son, Adnan, has to work through memories of his own in real time.

Nur said she was conscious of never pushing anyone past what they wanted to say. “I never want to push people to say something that they really don’t want,” she said.

There was real tension in some of these exchanges, a son signalling he wanted to keep certain memories to himself, sometimes, she suspected, to protect a father from seeing how much a story had affected him. Handing the questions to family members rather than asking them herself was, she said, “very experimental”.

A trained interviewer knows how to sit inside a silence and let it do the work; a son doing it for the first time is more likely to wonder if he’s doing it right, whether he should move on to the next question. But what came out of that unfamiliarity, in Nur’s view, was something more honest than a polished interview would have produced.

Feelings that clearly hadn’t been spoken aloud before, including the moment she calls one of her favourites in the whole film: a son telling his father, plainly, that he’s proud of him. “In a lot of families,” she said, “it’s not so much that you tell your parents you’re proud of them. You show it through actions, but maybe not through words.”

Asked how the film manages to hold the brutality of the siege, the deaths, the deprivation, alongside its lighter, almost tender moments, like an improvised birthday cake, Nur pushed back gently on the idea that these are two separate things requiring balance.

The people she interviewed brought up the lighter memories themselves, unprompted – playing football with the journalists, for one – and she came to see those moments as a form of resistance in their own right, inseparable from the horror around them.

A story that didn’t make the final cut, but stayed with her, involves Ismet smoking a cigarette in Baščaršija with a friend while hearing grenades in the distance nearby, and later describing it as the best cigarette of his life.

“It wouldn’t be the best cigarette of his life if the other things weren’t going on,” Nur said. “It’s so intertwined that, for me, it only felt natural to bring both in.” Still, she said she stayed conscious of the balance throughout editing, wary of leaning too heavily on the good stories, in case the film ended up suggesting the siege “wasn’t that bad”.

The film’s end credits list crowdfunding donors ahead of institutional backers, a reflection, Camo said, of how the project actually got made.

The original funding covered a short film. Once it became clear in the edit that the material demanded something longer, that funding no longer covered the film that existed. Additional Dutch funds proved hard to secure mid-production, and some of the feedback the team received was pointed: a strong story, but “European history”, with funders preferring projects more directly tied to the Netherlands, despite what Camo sees as an obvious, substantial connection between the Netherlands and the Bosnian war.

Crowdfunding became the last resort, and it worked. Donors included people from Bosnia, members of the Bosnian community in the Netherlands, and friends and colleagues of the filmmakers. That money went largely toward archive footage, by far the production’s biggest cost. “Without their help, it was really crucial,” Camo said.

The Balkan Investigative Reporting Network (BIRN) supported the archive research for the film.

‘We don’t know this history’

World.title: North Macedonia Indicts Ex-Deputy PM Grubi Over Lottery Machines Purchase
World.content:
North Macedonia’s former First Deputy Prime Minister, Artan Grubi. Photo: vlada.mk.

Prosecutors in Skopje on Thursday charged Artan Grubi and seven others with abusing their official positions to enable the purchase of video lottery terminals that could not legally be put into operation, costing the State Lottery more than 8.2 million euros.

Grubi is accused of allegedly pushing for the move in 2023 and 2024 while serving as first deputy prime minister, despite knowing that the procedure was illegal and that the State Lottery could never use the gambling machines.

“The defendants, acting jointly during 2023 and 2024, took actions that exceeded the limits of their respective powers and duties, with the intention of causing harm to the legal entity the State Lottery,” the prosecution said in the indictment.

The gambling machines were subsequently purchased but, according to the prosecution, were never used.

Grubi has denied any wrongdoing.

The indictment came days before a house-arrest order for Grubi is due to expire. Prosecutors have asked the court to extend his house arrest, while also seeking 30 days in detention for another of the accused, the former State Lottery director Perparim Bajrami, who remains at large.

Grubi fled North Macedonia in December 2024 as authorities moved to investigate suspected wrongdoing at the State Lottery.

An international call for his arrest was issued, and he remained outside the country for more than a year. Grubi initially denied that he was on the run, saying he had travelled to Kosovo for private reasons and would return after completing his obligations there.

He eventually returned to North Macedonia in February this year and was arrested at the Blace border crossing while entering from Kosovo.

He was released from custody the same day after prosecutors asked for house arrest instead of custody, arguing that most of the evidence had already been secured and citing concerns over his personal safety in detention.

A court approved the measure, prompting widespread criticism over the relatively lenient treatment of a former senior official who had already fled the country once.

Grubi, a senior figure in the now opposition, ethnic Albanian Democratic Union for Integration, DUI party, served as first deputy prime minister and minister of political system and inter-community relations from 2020 to 2024.

In December 2024, the US State Department sanctioned him for alleged involvement in corruption.

World.title: Quarter-Century After Peace Deal, North Macedonia Has Yet to Fully Heal
World.content:
The anniversary comes at a time when Ohrid is again at the centre of political debate.

The Democratic Union for Integration, DUI, the main ethnic Albanian party that was formed by the former leaders of the insurgency, and has been in government for much of the time since the conflict ended – before being relegated to the opposition after the 2024 general elections – has accused the current VMRO DPMNE party-led government of undermining the agreement.

It has pointed to several developments.

These include challenges to the constitutionality of the Law on the Use of Languages, opposition to bar exams being taken in Albanian, the abolition of the so-called “Balancer” mechanism for ensuring equitable ethnic representation in public employment – and a current push to adopt an new Law on Fair and Equitable Representation, designed to replace the “Balancer” system.

Popetrevski, however, doubts a coordinated government plan to dismantle Ohrid. “I see no basis for claiming that there is a coordinated plan to dismantle the Framework Agreement,” he says.

“After 25 years, it is not only legitimate but necessary to reassess how the solutions stemming from the Framework Agreement are functioning,” he adds.

The “Balancer” system illustrates the dilemma. Introduced to help ensure equitable representation of ethnic communities in public institutions, it achieved much of its intended purpose, Popetrevski says – but also produced “absurdities”, such as cases of people changing their declared ethnic identity to obtain employment.

The language law, he adds, also should not be beyond scrutiny, particularly given the concerns raised by the Venice Commission over aspects of its implementation, including the broad use of bilingualism in court proceedings.

At the same time, Popetrevski cautions against ignoring the cumulative effect of several contentious issues being raised within a short period.

“Politics does not happen in a laboratory, in an isolated system,” Popetrevski says. If questions concerning language, equitable representation and the Badinter mechanism are raised simultaneously, this may create an impression among some Albanians “that there is a step backwards from 2001”.

That is why, he argues, any changes to the deal must come with a clear political message.

“If dysfunctional solutions are being corrected, it must be unequivocally clear that the constitutional fundamental values and principles are not being called into question,” he asserts.

At the same time, Popetrevski rejects the DUI’s claim that is the sole “guardian” of Ohrid. “The DUI has no exclusive right to interpret and defend the Framework Agreement,” he insists.

A party that spent almost two decades in government, he argues, also bears responsibility for the agreement’s shortcomings.

“If every criticism of a particular solution is declared an attack on the Framework Agreement, then the agreement is transformed from a mechanism for building cohesion into a tool for day-to-day political mobilization,” he says.

Popetrevski’s assessment is also shaped by his own recollections of 2001.

Aged 25, he was reporting for one of the country’s national television stations when the conflict erupted. Covering a war in his own country while attempting to maintain journalistic distance was one of the most difficult professional challenges of his career.

“In a conflict, nuances are very easily erased. Either you are ‘ours’ or you are ‘theirs’,” he recalls.

In an article several years ago, he wrote that those in his newsroom who managed to be “journalists first and Macedonians and Christians afterwards” were a minority. He stresses that this was not a criticism of his colleagues, but a reflection of the atmosphere of the time.

A quarter of a century later, he believes distance has made those lost nuances easier to see.

“There was genuine dissatisfaction among Albanians with their position in the state. Acknowledging that does not mean justifying the taking up of arms,” he says.

The reverse is equally true, he adds: condemning the use of weapons does not mean denying that serious problems existed before the conflict.

“Perhaps the most important thing we know today is that there was no military solution,” he assesses.

The wider international context was crucial. The United States and European Union opposed any redrawing of borders, even though partition and territorial changes were among the ideas circulating during the conflict.

Beyond simply ‘not shooting each other’

World.title: Romania Shuts Nuclear Reactor on Danube as Power Crisis Deepens
World.content:
Romania shut down its last operating nuclear unit on Thursday as record-low Danube water levels threatened the cooling system at the Cernavoda nuclear power plant, adding to concerns over electricity supplies during a prolonged heatwave.

The shutdown leaves both reactors at the country’s sole nuclear plan offline. Cernavoda normally accounts for about 20 per cent of Romania’s electricity production.

Officials say the closure will not significantly affect Romania’s energy situation.

“Shutting down the last reactor is a controlled process that will only last about 10 days … during this time, Romania will have the resources to cover the energy deficit in the grid,” Romeo Urjan, director of the Cernavoda plant, said.

The Energy Ministry in a statement said higher wind power production is expected, while a coal-fired power unit is also due to restart.

Authorities are also preparing to increase electricity imports, mainly from neighbouring Bulgaria and Ukraine, to maintain supplies and avoid disruption, as demand remains high in the extreme temperatures.

The government has already urged households and businesses to reduce electricity consumption during peak evening hours until the end of the month, to ease the pressure on the power system during the ongoing heatwave.

More than 80 large industrial consumers have either reduced production or scheduled maintenance to cut electricity use, while restrictions have also been imposed on water use for agricultural irrigation.

The exceptionally low Danube levels have affected river transport, tourism and the energy sector. The government declared a nationwide energy alert on July 31, which will remain in force throughout August.

The energy crisis has also fuelled a surge in conspiracy theories and fears that Romania could face a nationwide blackout. Energy experts, however, doubt such a scenario.

“People have no reason to fear; they will not be left without electricity. Romania will resort to imports when necessary … though these will be more expensive because all countries in the region need electricity during the same evening peak hours,” energy analyst Corina Murafa said.

Murafa warned that higher electricity costs for consumers could be a likely consequence of the situation, as Romania relies more heavily on imports while domestic nuclear generation remains suspended.

While the shutdown at Cernavoda is not expected to last long, continued heat and low Danube levels could keep pressure on the country’s energy system for some weeks.

World.title: Should Croatia Send SRUUK Messages to Tourists Before Danger Strikes?
World.content:
August the 14th, 2026 – Should Croatia send out SRUUK messages to tourists before danger strikes? With more and more incidents of mountain, sea and other rescues taking place, some believe the country be doing more to warn visitors of potential risks.

Four Portuguese nationals recently went missing at sea after strong bura winds took control of their 1.5 metre inflatable boat. Index reports that this is one incident in an increasingly long list of issues that take place every single summer. From flip flop-donning “hikers” on Biokovo to people trying to cross the Adriatic to Italy on an inflatable flamingo, there’s never a drama-free tourist season in this regard.

The question for some is whether Croatia could be doing more, such as sending out SRUUK messages to tourists about specific dangers they may face during their stay. The latest case of the Portuguese tourists being swept away has once again raised the question of how well tourists are actually warned about the dangers of a strong and stormy bura. This is especially true in the area of the Velebit Channel, where rescue operations for people blown away from the shore by the wind are commonplace during the season.

sruuk messages specifically for bura winds

A similar case occurred at the end of July, when the bura carried a foreign national on a SUP board from Karlobag across the Velebit Channel all the way to Pag. After a multi-hour night-time operation, the Croatian Mountain Rescue Service (HGSS) found him uninjured on an inaccessible part of the Pag coast.

Because of the frequent occurrence of such cases, an inquiry was sent to the Ministry of the Interior, which is responsible for Civil Protection, asking why warnings about a strong and stormy bura on the Adriatic are not sent to citizens and tourists via the Early Warning and Crisis Management System (SRUUK). The ministry was also asked whether the introduction of such warnings is being considered, when they could start being sent, and whether there are any obstacles that prevent strong and stormy bura from being among the events for which citizens receive SRUUK messages.

From the response of Civil Protection it follows that Civil Protection itself doesn’t actually decide whether an SRUUK message will be sent due to a severe weather issue. They explained that the sending of SRUUK messages is regulated by the Ordinance on the procedure for early warning of the population.

warnings for severe weather events

“The early warning of the population is the provision of timely and useful information on the basis of which the competent institutions mobilise communities and individuals exposed to dangers to take measures to avoid or reduce risks and to carry out timely preparations for an effective response to threats,” they replied.

Information for early warning is collected by institutions responsible for meteorology, hydrology and flood defence, fire protection, seismology, ionising radiation, public health and geology. Operators of facilities with hazardous substances and hydro-accumulations, inspection services and scientific institutions also participate in the system. These institutions use their websites, social media channels, the traditional media and other methods as the basic channels for warnings so that the information can reach citizens as quickly as possible. Data on immediate danger are also forwarded to the Civil Protection Directorate.

who can actually issue a sruuk message urgently?

The Ordinance defines the persons who can decide to initiate the procedure for sending an SRUUK message, depending on the type of danger. In the case of floods, the decision is made by the chief flood defence manager or a person authorised by him, and in the case of large-scale fires by the chief fire commander or an authorised person.

For natural disasters and severe weather warnings, which include dangerous weather phenomena such as a strong and stormy bura, the decision is made by the director of the Croatian Meteorological and Hydrological Service (DHMZ) or a person authorised by him. In the case of a threat from military means, the decision is made in accordance with the Defence Act, while in the case of an immediate terrorist threat or other security reasons of a larger scale the decision is made by the chief police director or a person authorised by him.

There is also the possibility of activating the system due to an extraordinary event in the area of a particular county, city or municipality. In that case, a request with the text of the message can be submitted to the competent county 112 centre by the head of the civil protection headquarters of the local or regional self-government unit affected by the event, or a person authorised by him.

Civil Protection therefore emphasises that SRUUK is not an institution that assesses whether citizens should be warned, but a technical system by which the decision of the competent body is transmitted to people in the threatened area. “From all of the above it is clear that SRUUK is only an information tool by which early warning messages are sent to all mobile devices located in the area that the decision-maker has designated as threatened,” they state.

After receiving the decision, the Civil Protection Directorate enters the message composed by the decision-maker and sends it via mobile operators to users in the designated area.

World.title: Temperature Records Broken in Three Croatian Cities
World.content:
August the 14th, 2026 – Temperature records have been well and truly broken in three Croatian cities as the summer heat causes an array of issues nationwide.

Index reports that on the 12th of August, the City of Split recorded the highest air temperature since official records began. At the Split-Marjan measuring station at 14:00, the temperature reached a staggering 39.7 degrees Celsius.

According to official DHMZ data, this officially breaks the previous record of 39.5 degrees measured on the 30th of June this year. It still hasn’t broken the record measured back in 2017 at the Split-Kaštela meteorological station, which still stands at a horrendous 42.2 degrees Celsius.

HRT meteorologist Zoran Vakula reported that the record was also broken on the same day in Senj. 39.8°C was measured, breaking the 2015 record of 39.7°C. On the same date at 12:00 in Dubrovnik, 39.1°C was measured, breaking the 2025 record of 38.6°C.

World.title: Croatian MP Josip Dabro Pushes Harsh Measures Against Illegal Migrants
World.content:
August the 14th, 2026 – Croatian MP Josip Dabro has pushed harsh measures against illegal migrants, stating that “you can’t talk with evil, you need to shoot at evil”.

Index reports that the former DP minister and MP Josip Dabro reacted clearly and sharply to the case of a Pakistani man who imprisoned and raped a Nepalese citizen in a house near Zagreb, stating that Croatia must act significantly more harshly toward illegal migrants who commit criminal offences.

“there’s no talking with evil, you have to shoot at evil”

In a statement titled “The principle of state prevention toward illegal migrants: There is no talking with evil, you have to shoot at evil!”, he called for stricter border protection, including the use of force, and the possibility of temporarily suspending the right to seek asylum.

Dabro referred to the case of Mohamad Sh., whom he claims has been moving for years throughout Croatia and other European countries, repeatedly committing extremely serious crimes, and after police and court proceedings again seeks asylum in order to avoid deportation. He believes this case demonstrates the powerlessness of European states in dealing with people who abuse the asylum system. “What we are witnessing in this case is a public demonstration of the powerlessness and paralysis of state orders, and at the same time an invitation to everyone in the world to come and calmly, with impunity, fulfil their most perverse urges and desires,” Dabro said.

sharp criticism of lax approach by other countries

Dabro claims that the way European countries handle such cases sends the wrong message to potential perpetrators.

“Come, do whatever you want, no one can do anything to you, and on top of that you will have free accommodation, food, pocket money for condoms, possibly knives or even firearms,” he wrote, describing the message which, in his opinion, the existing system sends.

He also criticised political debates about human rights, the European legal order and the possible deployment of the army on the borders. As a positive example he highlighted the policy of US President Donald Trump, whom he claims shows how a responsible state should behave. Dabro also linked the case to earlier attacks on police officers, beatings, murders and mass brawls in Zagreb and other European cities. He claims that because of this “increasingly serious insecurity is becoming a legal European acquis”.

he advocates the use of force at the border

Dabro then set out a series of measures he considers necessary. He stated that “there is no mercy or concessions toward evil” and that nothing that is illegal must subsequently become legal. The security of the population, he believes, must primarily be defended at the state borders.

“The security of one’s own people is primarily defended at the borders, by all means and by shooting if and when necessary,” Dabro wrote. He also claims that international norms must not limit the state if it assesses that national security is threatened. In his view, in the event of a conflict between international rules and national security, such norms should be suspended. “No international norm can legally suspend the sovereign and exclusive right of the state to protect its national security by all available means,” he stated.

suspending the right to asylum

Dabro believes the state must act immediately and without, as he puts it, “false legal labyrinths”, and publicly promote such a policy in order to deter people who intend to cross the border illegally and commit criminal offences. He also called on those who oppose this approach to personally take care of illegal migrants.

“All those who have a moral objection to such state policies, instead of rhetorical one-upmanship – take in the illegal migrants, take them home, feed and care for them, share your security, prosperity and home with them, stop sharing other people’s,” he wrote. As examples of the messages the state should, in his opinion, send, he cited a case in which security forces would kill an illegal migrant during a violent attempt to cross the border, the expulsion of a perpetrator of sexual violence after a police intervention, and the temporary suspension of the right of illegal migrants to submit asylum applications.

Dabro believes such messages can have a stronger deterrent effect than increasing the number of security force members at the border, but only if the state shows it is prepared to implement them. “Whoever plans to enter Croatia illegally and cause disorder in the country must know that persecution or death awaits him, not protection and super-rights,” he said. “Let us be a nation, not a humanitarian refuge for the world’s evil,” Dabro concluded.

World.title: Croatian Tourism Campaign Starring John Malkovich Still Generating Huge Numbers
World.content:
August the 14th, 2026 – The latest and by far most celebrated Croatian tourism campaign starring the one and only John Malkovich is still generating huge numbers worldwide.

The new promotional video of the Croatian National Tourist Board (HTZ), “Croatia – I Hear It’s Beautiful”, starring world-famous actor John Malkovich, has achieved significant international resonance and attracted the attention of both the public and industry experts across numerous source markets.

Net.hr reports that in less than two months since its release, the main six-minute video published on YouTube and its shorter teaser version published on Instagram, Facebook and TikTok of the Croatian National Tourist Board together recorded a total of 17.3 million views, HTZ reported.

On YouTube, where the main six-minute video was published, more than 81,000 shares, more than 2,100 comments and over six million views were recorded, with the greatest interest shown by viewers from the USA, Poland, Italy, Germany, Hungary and others. The shorter version (teaser) also achieved strong audience engagement: it was shared more than 2,000 times on Facebook, more than 17,000 times on Instagram and 1,500 times on TikTok.

In addition to the reach and engagement on social media, the audience reactions to the content of the video itself are of particular value. It should be noted that a large number of positive reactions, apart from the domestic market, also came from the global audience that views the video outside the Croatian national and emotional context. For example, the response on Reddit is interesting, where the video sparked a spontaneous discussion among foreign users, with a series of positive comments highlighting its originality and humour.

Strong audience interest is also evidenced by the large number of independent reviews and reactions to the promotional video that users themselves published on YouTube. Some of these contents attracted tens of thousands of views. In them, the audience comments on and analyses the creative concept, script, humour, performance and the way Croatia is presented, which shows that the promotional video attracted attention and stimulated interest and conversation beyond the official channels of the Croatian National Tourist Board.

The international visibility of the video is additionally confirmed by more than 260 media publications on 15 source markets. These appeared in leading news media, including Kleine Zeitung, oe24, Kurier, T-Online, RTL, NU.nl, Corriere della Sera, Gazeta, WP.pl, France 24, POP TV, Delo, Dnevnik.si and Pravda, as well as in specialised B2B media such as The Drum, Travel Weekly, Travel Market Report, Media Marketing, About Travel and TTG, and lifestyle media such as Falstaff, Stern, Panorama, HelloMagyar, Roadster and Travel Squire

World.title: Hajduk Seal Conference League Play-Off Spot with Dominant 4-0 Win Against Žalgiris
World.content:
Hajduk took on Žalgiris at Poljud in the return leg of the third qualifying round for the Conference League. The Split side easily defended a 5-2 advantage secured in Lithuania seven days ago, winning 4-0 with a 9-2 aggregate. They will face Raków from Poland in the Conference League play-off round next week.

Lineups

Hajduk: Silić – Acapandie, Marešić, Raci, Melnjak – del Moral, Pajaziti – Šutalo, Dalisson, Šoticek – Livaja

Žalgiris: Sarkauskas – Šešplaukis, Lupano, Bosančić, Franke – Kendysh, Capan – Golubickas, Bilenkyi, Teixeira – Petković



Match report

The match got underway in Split at 9 pm.

The match got underway in Split, and Hajduk should have taken an early lead. In the 4th minute, Šotiček played Livaja through in the Žalgiris penalty area, leaving the Hajduk captain with only the goalkeeper to beat. Livaja struck it hard, but the ball flew over the bar — had it gone in, the goal would likely have been checked for a possible offside.

Just a minute later, Dalisson also went close, shooting from around 10 meters out, only for the Žalgiris goalkeeper to make the save. Melnjak then tested the visitors in the 11th minute, firing an effort that flew just wide of the post.

Hajduk continued to dominate, though by the 15th minute the scoreline remained unchanged from kick-off. In the 21st minute, Šotiček had a go from around twenty meters out, but his effort drifted past the goal.

In the 25th minute, Šutalo whipped in a cross from the right for Melnjak, though Kendysh got there first and headed it behind for a corner. Moments later, Dalisson produced a smart piece of defending to snuff out a Žalgiris counter-attack, carrying the ball forward some 20 meters himself before attempting to slip in a teammate — the pass was poorly executed, however, and the promising move broke down.

The game then went through a quieter spell without any major incident, and Hajduk’s resulting corners in the 28th minute failed to trouble the visitors.

In the 33rd minute, Raci tried his luck from distance, but his low effort was comfortably saved by the away goalkeeper. With 10 minutes left until the break, the half had so far been played out under Hajduk’s dominance: the hosts had squandered two big chances, held a 8-1 advantage in shots, led 4-1 on corners and enjoyed 68% of possession to the visitors’ 32%.

In the 38th minute, Franke sent in an awkward ball from the left flank, but no one managed to divert it goalwards. Marešić then blocked Bilenkyi’s follow-up attempt behind for a corner.

In the 41st minute, Šutalo earned a round of applause from the Poljud crowd. Livaja played a ball into space and the young Croatia international surged forward at the two Žalgiris defenders, who managed to stop him after he attempted to dribble past them twice. Hajduk’s right winger refused to give up, however, and won a foul and a free kick from the resulting phase of play. Nothing came of the set piece itself, though.



Hajduk dominated the first hald, but the score is 0-0 at half-time.

Hajduk finally broke the deadlock in the 53rd minute. Šutalo, excellent again, collected a long ball out on the right, drifted slightly infield, and picked out the run of Melnjak with a superb pass. Melnjak made no mistake from close range, tucking it away to make it 1-0!

In the 60th minute, Huram came on for Šotiček. In the 65th minute, Hajduk almost doubled their lead. Šutalo played it through to Livaja, who squared the ball in from the right into the box, where Melnjak was left completely unmarked to head it, but he sent his effort over the bar.

Dalisson then tried his luck from distance in the 66th minute, though his shot was off target. A minute later, Šutalo had a go himself from 18 meters out, but also failed to hit the target. In the 68th minute, Hajduk made a triple change, with Šego, Brruti and Sigur coming on to replace Livaja, Dalisson and Pajaziti.

Hajduk doubled their advantage in the 69th minute. Acapandie crossed from the right for Šego, whose effort cannoned off an opponent’s head, with the loose ball falling kindly for 17-year-old Huram. The teenager reacted brilliantly, turning smartly to fire home and make it 2-0.



In the 75th minute, Bamba came on for Šutalo and made it 3-0 five minutes later. Three minutes after that, Šego made it 4-0, which was the final result.

With this 9-2 aggregate, Hajduk moves on to the Conference League play-offs. The first leg will be played on August 20th at Poljud, with the return leg scheduled for August 27th.

World.title: Croatian Tourism Minister Says Last Minute Bookings are Saving August
World.content:
August the 13th, 2026 – The Croatian tourism minister has stated that last minute bookings are saving August, with more and more people paying closer attention to value for money before making reservations.

Croatian tourism is once again confirming its strength this year, and the results achieved show that we are on the right track, said Tonči Glavina, Minister of Tourism and Sport. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that the month of July’s tourism results were better than expected, and indications suggest that the second half of the summer could follow the same pattern.

According to data from the eVisitor system, which records tourist traffic in commercial and non-commercial facilities as well as nautical charters (eCrew system), Croatia recorded 12.4 million arrivals and 59.1 million overnight stays from January to the end of July. Compared with the same period last year, this represents growth of 1 percent in both arrivals and overnight stays.

Of that total, 56.1 million overnight stays were recorded on the Adriatic (up 0.5 percent year-on-year), while the continent, including the city of Zagreb, recorded more than 3 million overnight stays (up 1 percent).

july was fantastic for croatia

eVisitor data also shows that in July this year, Croatia recorded 4.7 million arrivals and 29.6 million overnight stays, which is an increase of 2.5 percent in arrivals and 1 percent in overnight stays compared with July last year. In the seventh month the most guests came from the markets of Germany, Slovenia, Croatia, Poland, the Czech Republic, Austria, Hungary and others. By counties, the most tourists were counted in Istria, Split-Dalmatia County and Kvarner, while the most visited destinations were Rovinj, Vir, Poreč, Medulin and Dubrovnik.

“We are satisfied with the tourism results achieved in the first seven months of this year, and especially with the fact that in July we recorded the best result of the last two years. This confirms that Croatian tourism continues to maintain its competitiveness and resilience and that, despite changes in the market, we are succeeding in maintaining positive trends. We are particularly pleased that good results are also being recorded in financial indicators.

In July the value of fiscalised invoices rose by 18 percent, while the number of issued invoices was 8 percent higher than in the same month last year. Growth is also being recorded in road, air and maritime traffic, and all these results confirm that we have responded well to market circumstances – both through quality promotion of Croatia and through timely adaptation of the offer. I thank the entire tourism sector for the effort invested, and especially accommodation providers who responded to our appeals and, with their promotional offers, additionally contributed to the competitiveness of our offer.

Ahead of us is still a good part of August, after which we will make a complete overview of this main part of the tourist year. Croatian tourism is once again confirming its strength this year, and the results achieved show that we are on the right track and that together we are successfully responding to changes and challenges,” said Tonči Glavina, Minister of Tourism and Sport.

When Croatia’s tourism results are broken down by counties, in the first seven months the most overnight stays were recorded in Istria (16.7 million), Split-Dalmatia County (11.1 million) and Kvarner (9.7 million), while by destinations the leaders were Dubrovnik, Rovinj, Poreč, Split and Umag.

last minute to the rescue

“The course and results of the tourist year so far show that Croatia still has a very strong position on the global tourism market, despite all the demanding circumstances. What we particularly read from this year’s tourist movements is a change in the way guests make decisions about their trips. Last-minute bookings play an important role, and when choosing a destination, the best value for money is increasingly sought, along with safety and easy accessibility. In this context Croatia has a series of advantages – from proximity to our most important source markets and good transport connections to the diversity of the offer that enables different types of holidays.

Given the considerable number of promotional last-minute arrangement prices in August, the tourism sector believes that the August figures will also be good.

The results achieved therefore give us additional wind in our sails for the continuation of the tourist year, all the more so because the Ferragosto period is ahead of us, traditionally very important for travel by Italian guests. In addition to the main summer months, we are also recording excellent advance bookings for the shoulder season, for which promotional activities begin in mid-August, especially on the Polish and UK markets,” said Kristjan Staničić, director of the Croatian National Tourist Board.

Looking at markets, during the first seven months the most overnight stays were recorded by guests from Germany (10.3 million), Croatia (7.6 million), Slovenia (6.7 million), Austria (4.3 million), Poland (3.9 million), the Czech Republic (3 million), the UK (2.2 million), Hungary (2.1 million) and others.

Given the considerable number of promotional last-minute arrangement prices in August, the tourism sector believes that the August figures will also be good, at least at last year’s level.

59.1 million overnight stays were recorded over the first seven months of this year

Interesting trends can also be seen on individual markets. Thus eVisitor figures show that Croatian tourism in July and during the first seven months of 2026 recorded significant growth in tourist traffic from the Czech, Hungarian and Italian markets.

The most pronounced positive shift was recorded on the Czech market. Compared with July last year, the number of arrivals of Czech tourists rose by 12 percent, while the number of their overnight stays was higher by seven percent. In the period from January to the end of July growth of five percent was recorded in both arrivals and overnight stays compared with the same period last year. The Hungarian market is also a reason for satisfaction. During July the number of arrivals of Hungarian tourists increased by eight percent, while the number of overnight stays rose by seven percent.

In the first seven months of the year growth of seven percent was recorded in both arrivals and overnight stays compared with last year. Hungarian guests stayed most on Kvarner, in Istria and Zadar County. The Italian market, which had stagnated in recent years, is also recovering. In the period from January to July the number of arrivals and overnight stays of Italian guests increased by two percent compared with the same period last year, while in July a one-percent growth in arrivals was recorded.

World.title: Croats are Travelling Less and Taking Less Annual Leave This Summer
World.content:
August the 13th, 2026 – Croats appear to be travelling less and taking less annual leave this summer, with the latest research into these habits showing a marked change.

Almost every third person in Croatia is staying at their usual place of residence this summer, primarily due to a lack of financial resources, according to a survey conducted by Alma Career Croatia. Poslovni reports that the results of the latest survey on annual leave, carried out by Alma Career Croatia, an international company best known for the MojPosao/MyJob portal, show that Croatian employees are planning their holidays a little more cautiously this summer.

According to this latest survey, Croatian workers enjoy an average of 25 days of annual leave, and summer is the period when most employees use the largest part of their free days. However, this year’s results show that habits are slowly changing.

shorter summer breaks

Compared with 2025, the number of workers who plan to use fewer days of annual leave during the summer is rising, as is the number of those who aren’t planning on taking any trips at all this year.

The share of employees who plan to use a maximum of seven days of annual leave has increased from 15% in 2025 to 21% in 2026. On the other hand, the share of those planning to rest for 21 days or longer has almost halved (7% last year, 3% this year). The most common choice remains a holiday lasting 8 to 10 days, planned by 37% of respondents. This is followed by those who will rest between 11 and 15 days (29%), while 10% of employees plan annual leave lasting between 15 and 20 days.

The issue with summer that is becoming increasingly problematic is the fact that the weather is becoming so insufferably hot that sitting under the air conditioner is the only choice for a growing number of people. Most can do that at work or at home.

the croatian coast still dominates for most croats, as opposed to heading somewhere abroad

When it comes to destination, Croatia remains the first choice.

More than half of the survey participants (56%) plan to spend their summer holiday within the country, which is only slightly less than last year, when the figure was 58%. There are also somewhat fewer people planning a trip abroad this summer. Their share has fallen from 21% in 2025 to 17% this year.

However, the biggest change is visible among those who do not plan to travel at all. Their share has risen in one year from 27% to 32%, meaning that almost every third respondent will not go on a summer holiday this year. Finances are most often behind such a decision. Among respondents who will not travel, as many as 60% cite lack of financial resources as the main reason, compared with 56% last year.

One to two weeks on the Adriatic; shorter or longer holidays abroad

There are also differences in the length of holidays depending on whether respondents holiday in Croatia or travel abroad. Those who holiday somewhere else within Croatia most often choose a classic break of one to two weeks. As many as 78% of them plan to rest between 8 and 15 days.

People who travel abroad more often choose either very short or significantly longer trips. Thus, 21% of respondents travelling outside Croatia plan a holiday of seven days or less, while among those staying in Croatia the figure is 10%. At the other end of the spectrum, 7% of travellers abroad plan a holiday longer than three weeks, while among those holidaying in Croatia only 2% plan such a break.

World.title: Adidas Strengthens Presence in Croatian Sport as Cibona Signs Partnership
World.content:
August the 13th, 2026 – Adidas is strengthening its present in Croatian sport as the famous Cibona signs a partnership deal with the global sport brand.

As Poslovni reports, one of the most successful Croatian basketball clubs of all and one of the most recognisable global sports brands are joining forces, and Cibona’s players will compete in adidas kit from the new season.

The global sports brand Adidas and Basketball Club Cibona, one of the symbols of Zagreb and Croatian sport, have officially begun a new collaboration. From the 2026/2027 season, Cibona’s senior and junior teams will compete in Adidas sports equipment.

The new partnership connects two brands deeply rooted in sporting history, yet simultaneously oriented towards the future, the development of new generations of athletes and the creation of top conditions for their work and progress. adidas will provide Cibona with modern sports equipment designed to give players maximum comfort, freedom of movement and the best possible performance on the court.

Founded in 1946, Cibona has over eight decades grown into one of the most important institutions of Croatian basketball. The club reached the peak of European glory in the mid-1980s when, led by Dražen Petrović, it won two consecutive European champion titles – in 1985 and 1986. After Croatia’s independence, Cibona won a record 20 national championship titles, and in 2014 it also won the regional ABA League.

“Collaboration with Adidas represents an important step in the development of the club for Cibona and a confirmation of the values that our club has carried for eight decades. We’re connecting with a global brand that understands sport, excellence and the importance of creating new generations of players. We believe this partnership will further strengthen our sporting identity, as well as the bond with the fans who have always been an inseparable part of Cibona. We look forward to everything we’ll achieve together on and off the court,” said Tomislav Šerić, director of Basketball Club Cibona.

The collaboration between Cibona and Adidas is part of the brand’s broader commitment to basketball, sport and athletes at all levels. Basketball is one of Adidas’s global sports categories, alongside football, running and training, while the brand is also active in tennis, golf, motorsport, winter sports, rugby, cricket and numerous other disciplines. For more than 75 years Adidas has been developing products intended for athletes, combining innovation, design and experience gained in professional sport.

“We are extremely pleased that Cibona is becoming part of the adidas sports family. This is a club of exceptional tradition, whose name holds a special place in the history of European basketball and which for generations has been home to top players. We share a belief in the power of sport, the importance of working with young people and a constant drive for progress. We’re extremely proud to support Cibona’s players with equipment that combines sporting innovations, functionality and the recognisable Adidas design, and we look forward to jointly creating a new chapter in the club’s history,” said Petra Franić from Adidas.

The partnership between adidas and Cibona opens a new chapter in the life of a club that placed Zagreb at the centre of the European basketball map. The recognisable three stripes will thus accompany the Wolves from the new season on the path towards new sporting successes.

Players of KK Cibona have for the first time completed a training session in the new training kit from the collection, while the official match kits will be presented later. The kits and selected items from the collection will be available to fans exclusively in the Basketball Club Cibona fan shop.
