World.title: Bangladesh PM likely to visit India as Dhaka presses for Sheikh Hasina's extradition
World.content:
Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahmanâs proposed visit to India has not yet been finalised, with the timing dependent on his âscheduleâ and the âprogressâ of ongoing bilateral discussions.

"The government is positive about visits to all countries. But it will depend on the PM's schedule and on how far discussions between the two countries progress," state minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed Islam said.

"The government is busy, and so is the prime minister. If everything fits together, of course there will be a visit to India, a visit to Japan; all the visits will happen," she said, referring to ongoing domestic programmes and upcoming constitutional activities.

In April, Bangladesh foreign minister Khalilur Rahman visited India as part of efforts to mend strained bilateral ties following more than 18 months of heightened diplomatic tensions.

Bangladesh has also sought the extradition of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina.

External affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said on Tuesday that India has extended two separate invitations to Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman â one for a bilateral visit and another to attend the outreach session of the Brics Summit in New Delhi in September.





"Brics is still a long way off. A lot can happen in a month,â Shama said.

Asked whether Rahmanâs visit to India could help ease tensions, Shama said direct communication between the leaders of the two governments could provide an opportunity to discuss and resolve outstanding issues.

"Whenever the heads of two countries talk, there is a chance of resolving many problems. That opportunity is there; it remains," she said.

Relations between India and Bangladesh deteriorated sharply after the interim government led by Muhammad Yunus came to power following the fall of Sheikh Hasinaâs government in August 2024.

Efforts to stabilise ties gained momentum after Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla, accompanied by foreign secretary Vikram Misri, represented India at Tarique Rahmanâs swearing-in ceremony in Dhaka on February 17.

Rahman assumed office as prime minister after his party secured a landslide victory in the parliamentary elections.

Bangladeshâs current government, led by Rahmanâs Bangladesh Nationalist Party, has maintained that Sheikh Hasina must surrender and face the law if she returns to the country.

Hasina recently addressed an audio-only virtual press conference from New Delhi, her first public media interaction since fleeing to India on August 5, 2024, amid mass protests.

During the virtual press conference, Hasina said she was determined to return to Bangladesh in December to put the country on the "right track" by restoring democracy, despite facing the possibility of imprisonment or a death sentence.

India distanced itself from Hasinaâs media interaction, clarifying that it had neither played a role in organising the event nor endorsed her remarks concerning the Bangladesh government.

World.title: Siddapur village says no to Hyderabad’s waste, rises in protest
World.content:
Siddapur, a village in Kothur mandal of Ranga Reddy district, is on war path against the solid waste processing facility approved in its 86 acres, designated as the treatment destination for the waste generated in the limits of Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation (GHMC).

Protests had begun long before the government issued orders for the ‘Eco Town’ project — a euphemistic representation of the facility — early in July.

The news of Eco Town project, a solid waste mangement and waste-to-energy plant aimed at promoting circular economy, was broken by The Hindu on May 26, 2026. Objecting to the project, the villagers organised ‘Chalo Collectorate’ protests twice and submitted representations to the district collector, presented the issue before the Mahabubnagar MP D.K. Aruna, held ‘rasta roko’ on National Highway-44, and on August 11, staged a sit-in at the Tehsildar’s office together with opposition party leaders.

Promise of Industrial Park turns out to be waste-treatment plant

“Our lands were acquired in the name of an industrial park in 2021 by the then BRS government. Some allotments too were made to industries. But now we have reason to believe that the solid waste treatment facility will be extended to include all the land acquired. Already, we are hearing that the industries would be shifted elsewhere,” Sri Charan Chari, a B.Tech graduate from Siddapur said.

The proposal for an Industrial Park here was mooted way back in 2008, in 377 acres of land. However, it didn’t take off due to confusion related to the status of lands. After Telangana emerged as a separate State, the government revived the Industrial Park proposal, and decided to acquire a total 330.34 acre land from Siddapur, including government land. The villagers said 248 acre of land was acquired.

“Though the government is setting up the facility in 86 acres now, we are in no doubt that it would be extended to the remaining land too,” says Sri Charan.

No public hearing

There was no public hearing held before the Eco Tourism project since it is a ‘Blue Category’ industry. The Central Pollution Control Board, last year, introduced the ‘Blue Category’ for industries to define Essential Environmental Services such as solid waste management, sewage treatment, and also the Waste to Energy plants. Several concerns have already been raised about the WTE plants, as they are proven cause of severe air pollution at several locations.

“They are assuring that no pollution will be caused, and speaking of a solution for every issue. But we are not sure how effectively all those solutions would be implemented once the site is taken over. There is already one stone crushing unit nearby which rendered a large extent of our croplands useless,” said Yellaram Rajender Reddy, another villager.

The villagers are also concerned about the possibility of a drop in real estate values of the lands around the facility.

The current waste processing facility at Jawahar Nagar, which is causing severe air and water pollution in a radius of 10-15 kilometres around the dump is only aggravating the fears. A survey conducted by the local people revealed that a total 22 villages exist in 5 kilometre radius and 74 villages in 10 kilometre radius, prompting these villagers too join the protests.

“Not only that, the Himayat Sagar drinking water reservoir exists just 25 kilometres away, and water from our lake reaches the reservoir through the chain linked network,” says Mr. Reddy.

While the GHMC authorities claimed that no waste will be dumped at Siddapur, and instead it will be brought from Jawahar Nagar to be treated and land filled, the villagers who visited the GHMC office were told that the Jawahar Nagar facility would be shut down after the Eco Town takes off.

World.title: DMK moving from ‘covert to direct alliance’ with BJP, alleges Minister Nirmalkumar
World.content:
Minister for Energy Resources and Law R. Nirmalkumar on Friday (August 14, 2026) claimed that the DMK and the BJP had been in a “covert” alliance earlier and had now decided to enter into a “direct” alliance.

The Minister was responding to a question during a press conference at the Secretariat in Chennai on DMK parliamentary party leader Kanimozhi meeting Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla in New Delhi on Thursday (August 13).

“The DMK, which had earlier been in an indirect alliance with the BJP, has now decided to enter into a direct alliance. That was why former Minister Anitha R. Radhakrishnan said DMK MP Tiruchi Siva would soon become a Union Minister. Former DMK MP Kanimozhi N.V.N. Somu and BJP leader Vanathi Srinivasam also hinted that there were no permanent enemies or friends in politics,” he said.

When asked about Ms. Kanimozhi’s clarification that she had met Mr. Birla only to discuss the seating arrangements for the DMK MPs, Mr. Nirmalkumar questioned the rationale behind the meeting when the Lok Sabha Speaker had hosted a tea party.

Mr. Nirmalkumar accused the DMK of “surrendering” to the Union government to “protect its ill-gotten wealth.” He said the DMK had decided to do now what it had done in 2001 by forming an alliance with the BJP and giving the BJP “a recognition” in Tamil Nadu.

He said although the DMK had voted in favour of the resolution against delimitation in the Assembly, the party had not so far explicitly said that it would vote against the proposed Delimitation Bill when it was introduced in Parliament.

‘Investments high due to transparency’

Responding to a question on investments worth ₹1 lakh crore coming to Tamil Nadu in the 100 days of the TVK-led government, Mr. Nirmalkumar said all these companies had already been waiting to invest in Tamil Nadu.

During the previous DMK regime, though Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) were publicly signed, a “behind-the-screen MoU had to be entered with the family,” he alleged. Because of this, many companies were reluctant to invest in the State. Now, they are coming forward to invest because of transparency in governance, he said.

Mr. Nirmalkumar said the Southern Zonal Council meeting was expected to be held in Mamallapuram next week. The official schedule had not yet been released and arrangements for the meeting were under way, he said.

World.title: Human factors worsened deadly Assam floods, says global collaborative study
World.content:
GUWAHATI Human factors, and not necessarily climate change, worsened the floods in a part of eastern Assam that killed at least 103 people, a global collaborative study has said.

According to the World Weather Attribution (WWA), an international scientific collaboration, heavy monsoonal rainfall in northeastern India has remained within historical norms, but land-use changes have increased the impacts and risks to the people and their livelihoods.

Between late June and early August, eastern Assam—particularly Sivasagar, Charaideo, and Jorhat districts—alongside hill catchments in Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh, experienced intense monsoonal downpours.

The resulting deluge breached critical infrastructure, washed away agricultural land, and forced hundreds of thousands into relief camps. Thousands of livestock and other domesticated animals were also affected.

Scientists from India, Sweden, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, and the United States analysed historical weather records and climate models, finding that the rainfall totals were not exceptional and are expected at least every two years.

“Although limited datasets for the region mean there is some uncertainty, the analysis showed no clear evidence that climate change was altering the trend in the intensity or likelihood of the rainfall. Instead, they found that the scale of the disaster stems largely from other human factors including colonial-era land regulations, displacement, land degradation, and a lack of sufficient flood mitigation,” the WWA study said on Friday (August 14, 2026).

The study found that unplanned urbanisation, rapid deforestation, wetland destruction, and riverbank erosion degraded Assam’s natural drainage capacity, increasing flood height and downstream impacts.

The scientists said reliance on concrete engineering and hard embankments trapped silt, artificially raising riverbeds and blocking natural runoff. “Embankments frequently exacerbate flooding and increase the risk of catastrophic breaches,” they noted, observing that combining infrastructure with social and nature-based approaches could be more effective in mitigating floods.

Future warming

The study also flagged historical vulnerability. “Historical land reallocation contributed to some indigenous communities living on marginal, flood-prone riverbanks, and sandbars (chars). These historical patterns continue to trap low-income agricultural populations in cycles of repeated displacement,” it said.

“Adaptation efforts must broaden to include floodplain restoration, wetland conservation, and expanded anticipatory disaster risk management using localised early warnings,” the study suggested.

“To understand whether climate change played a role in the rainfall in the Upper (eastern) Assam region and the surrounding hill catchments that led to the landslides and flooding, we analysed short, high-intensity downpours, and longer rainfall accumulations,” Mariam Zachariah, a research associate in extreme weather and climate change at the Centre for Environmental Policy, Imperial College London, said.

Read | Coexisting with the water: learning to live with the floods

“Low station coverage and climate models struggling to capture processes in hilly regions create high uncertainties in the results. Therefore, overall findings suggest no discernible role of climate change. However, a lack of a clear trend today does not make the region immune to future warming. As global temperatures continue to climb, monsoon dynamics across South Asia will keep shifting, making proactive land and river management even more urgent,” she said.

“Hundreds of thousands of people have been affected, with low-income agricultural families and displaced communities paying the highest price. Marginalised populations living on flood-prone sandbars and reliance on rigid concrete embankments can be a recipe for disaster,” Emmanuel Raju, director of Copenhagen Centre for Disaster Research, said.

“True adaptation requires moving towards living with rivers through wetland restoration and proactive early action before floodwaters strike,” he added.

“While climate change is making life harder for most Indians, not every disaster is a climate change disaster. The devastating flooding in Assam was instead driven by extreme human exposure, environmental degradation, and infrastructure limitations,” Friederike Otto, professor of climate science at the Centre for Environmental Policy, said.

“This report is a crucial reminder that building climate resilience is not only about cutting emissions. It is also about sustainable land management, protecting ecosystems, and managing the exposure to disaster risk on the ground,” he said.

World.title: Supreme Court quashes criminal defamation complaint, summon against Rahul Gandhi for Savarkar remarks
World.content:
The Supreme Court on Friday (August 14, 2026) quashed the criminal defamation complaint and summon issued by a trial court against Leader of Opposition (LoP) in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi for his remarks against Hindutva ideologue Vinayak Damodar Savarkar.

A Bench headed by Justice Dipankar Datta noted that an affidavit filed by the Uttar Pradesh government reveals that no sanction has yet been given for the case against the Opposition leader.

“Sanction is required. But there is no sanction. If there is no sanction, there is no case,. You have to follow the law” Justice Datta addressed the State government and the complainant.

The court quashed both the complaint filed by Nripendra Pandey, a Lucknow resident, against Mr. Gandhi, and the summons issued by a Lucknow Magistrate.

The defamation case stems from Mr. Gandhi’s comments on Savarkar made on November 17, 2022 during his Bharat Jodo Yatra at a rally in Maharashtra’s Akola district.

The Lucknow bench of the high court on April 4, 2025 said Mr. Gandhi can file a revision petition before the sessions court, making the high court’s intervention unnecessary at this stage.

The Congress leader had challenged a subordinate court’s decision to summon him in the case, while contesting the ongoing proceedings against him.

Advocate Nripendra Pandey filed a complaint, accusing Mr. Gandhi of intentionally insulting Savarkar during the rally. The complainant alleged Mr. Gandhi’s remarks were part of a well-planned conspiracy to defame Savarkar.

With PTI inputs

World.title: New aircraft carrier heads toward West Asia after reports of issues on long-deployed USS Lincoln
World.content:
The Pacific-based aircraft carrier USS George Washington has begun heading towards West Asia as reports have emerged of mental health and supply issues aboard the long-deployed USS Abraham Lincoln.

The Lincoln has been supporting the U.S. war against Iran, and its deployment has included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 240 days. Several Democratic lawmakers are pressing for accountability from the Pentagon over conditions aboard the carrier, which Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday (August 13, 2026) said were “completely misrepresented.”

Also read:West Asia war LIVE - August 14

Extended deployments of carriers during the Iran conflict have raised concerns about the impact on service members who are away from home for long periods as well as the increasing strain on the ship and its equipment. While renewed hostilities between the U.S. and Iran have calmed in recent weeks, the Navy has reimposed a blockade on Iranian ports in the crucial Strait of Hormuz, and the Trump administration has offered no clarity on how it intends to wind down the war.

A new aircraft carrier is heading west from the Asia-Pacific. The USS George Washington left port in Da Nang, Vietnam, last week, a Navy statement said. The carrier, along with a cruiser and a destroyer, have since been spotted crossing the Singapore Strait.

A Navy official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to detail sensitive ship details, confirmed that the Washington was in the Strait of Malacca, which links the Pacific and Indian oceans and puts the carrier on a course to head into the Indian Ocean. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier that the Washington would replace the Lincoln as one of the two aircraft carriers now stationed in West Asia.

Also read: Infographic of the American aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln

The Lincoln originally deployed November 21 from San Diego, and it arrived in the region in January, ahead of the launch of the Iran war on February 28. The Navy conceded that the conflict created a “highly contested environment where traditional supply hubs in the Middle East were disrupted by combat actions." That, in turn, led to shortages and loss of mail aboard the aircraft carrier, the Navy said in a statement.

“Leadership prioritised mission-critical supplies: first food, then hygiene items, then mail,” the statement said, before assuring that sailors aboard the ship now have access to clean water and “healthy meal options.”

Democrats demand scrutiny

Democrats call for scrutiny, while the Pentagon defends conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.

Democratic lawmakers are calling for investigations, more information and greater visibility into conditions aboard the ship, which was originally set to return home in May.

“The Lincoln's prolonged deployment is especially significant because it is occurring in the context of continuing military operations against Iran and the possibility that substantial U.S. naval forces will be required in the region for an extended period,” Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, wrote in a letter to Navy leadership asking for a response to several questions.

Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, a Marine Corps veteran, said on social media that he is looking to take a bipartisan delegation on an official oversight visit to the ship and that the way sailors are being treated is “not just disgusting; it's dangerous.” Hegseth told reporters during a visit to Panama that he wants the Lincoln's sailors’ home and crews rotated as quickly as possible but pushed back against reports of problems aboard.

“We make sure that every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment. Some deployments are longer than others, and I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody. What they do in those high seas in those austere conditions with less port calls — it's incredible.”

Navy leaders, including acting Secretary Hung Cao, last week held a tense town hall for families of troops aboard the USS Lincoln, at which the commanders of the Navy's air and surface forces promised to do everything they could to relieve the aircraft carrier. MS NOW reported earlier on the meeting.

Issues on USS Lincoln

When reports of food shortages aboard the ship first surfaced in April, the Navy pushed back, calling those reports “false.”

Reports have since emerged that sailors on the Lincoln are struggling with mental health concerns. The Navy said in its statement that it has “not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship,” but officials declined to provide data, citing operational security and patient privacy concerns.

The Navy official said that a sailor aboard the Lincoln went overboard in early August but that the person was quickly recovered, treated by the ship's medical department and transferred off ship for follow-on care. The official would not say if it was being considered a suicide attempt.

Other carriers also have had long runs that have raised concerns about morale. The USS Gerald R. Ford returned home in mid-May after an 11-month deployment, the longest since the Vietnam War, that had it support the U.S. war with Iran and the capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.

During its deployment, the Ford experienced a fire in a laundry space that forced the carrier to turn around and return to the Mediterranean Sea for repairs and left hundreds of sailors without places to sleep.

Concerns about the demands of battle and the dangers of overextending ships and their crew predate the Iran war, with a number of mishaps on ships battling Houthi rebels in Yemen in 2024 and 2025, including the aircraft carrier USS Harry S. Truman on a longer-than-expected deployment.

World.title: Cheers, Professor! Remembering Sumit Sarkar
World.content:
In the History Department’s first-floor lecture room in North Campus, sometime in 1998, Sumit Sarkar walked in to introduce a course titled ‘Social History of Modern India’. I still have vivid memories of that class, which was an overview of what to expect over the coming weeks.

Of the many things he spoke about that day, I remember a few ideas and names that I was hearing for the first time.

Having come to the M.A. programme as a Physics graduate, I had never heard of Bernard S. Cohn, E.P. Thompson or C.A. Bayly. The second was the defining reading of the course: Prof. Sarkar’s own then newly published book, Writing Social History. Within the first week of his classes, I bought a copy. By the end of the year, everything that I saw around me, and experiences that one routinely encountered, seemed to acquire new meanings. Why is the sweeper the sweeper? Why do we think the way we think? How do we come to learn the languages we learn, and in the manner that we do? It was an exhilarating journey of learning.

He is described as a Marxist historian. But that, I think, was too comfortable a chair for Sumit. He was a historian who embraced intellectual discomfort, with the resulting habit of questioning and revising positions he had once endorsed.

I still have that same copy of Writing Social History on my table as a ready reference. Whether I am writing on census, caste, communalism, regionalism, nationalism, globalisation, education or identity, there is invariably something that sends me back to that book. I got it signed in later years and, later still, added a copy of his last book, Modern Times, signed by both Sumit Sarkar and Tanika Sarkar, to my shelf of frequently consulted books.

There is no other scholar, no other historian, who can match the breadth, sweep and intensity of Sarkar. He achieved all this while keeping his own presence barely noticeable in either his books or his lectures. Real scholarship requires humility. In an era of the digital marketing of scholarship, scholars are often expected to compete with rock stars. Sumit Sarkar belonged to a different era, a different ethos.

His last book, Modern Times, was conceived as a two-volume project, but only the first volume could be published. Covering India from the 1880s to the 1950s, it is in itself a monumental achievement. The second volume would undoubtedly have become the supreme epic on the modern republic. I firmly believe that, taken together, the two volumes would have surpassed even the majesty of Eric Hobsbawm’s volumes on modern Europe. An unfortunate accident intervened, and Sarkar could not complete the project. “There will not be a second volume.” I remember hearing Tanika say this, with disappointment, sometime around 2014. I still hope that Tanika Sarkar may one day add her own volume on the modern republic. Even so, Sumit Sarkar’s first volume remains a masterclass on modern India.

Term papers were not mandatory for the M.A. at Delhi University in those days. But Sumit encouraged writing. He would painstakingly write notes in the margins, ask further questions, suggest alternative framings here and there, and then return those handwritten pages. I had preserved them like treasures for several years, but somewhere along the way I misplaced them.

Among his most enduring interpretations was his understanding of the evolution of Hindu identity as a continuum across centuries, expressed through three remarkable phases: Hindu, Hinduism and Hindutva. He explored the limits of drawing a rigid distinction between mainstream Indian nationalism and Hindu nationalism. He also examined the formation of caste identities, particularly their links with colonial administration, educational policies and nationalist mobilisation strategies.

“Ethnocentric arrogance is fairly cross-cultural, but what has been qualitatively new in the modern era is the power developed by dominant groups in one section of the world to impose their values and assumptions on others, and even get them internalised on a global scale,” he wrote in Modern Times. The weight of those words has only grown exponentially in an age of hyper-technologies.

A few months after completing my M.A., I visited him and Tanika at their home on the St Stephen’s College campus. Tanika, too, had taught an optional course that I had taken, on women in the Indian national movement. It was evening, and Sumit offered me a drink. I was thrilled at the prospect of sharing one with the Professor.

“I will add some water,” I said as he handed me the glass.

“Water is already added,” he replied.

Even with the water, it could not have exceeded 60 ml. I was too unsure of myself to ask for a second.

Cheers, Prof., as you pass over to become part of history. Those curious about India will continue to find you, for generations to come.

World.title: North Korea slams U.S.-South Korea military drills, threatens to exercise self-defence
World.content:
North Korea on Friday (August 14, 2026) threatened to exercise its right to self-defence in a statement that slammed the upcoming U.S.-South Korean military drills as a war rehearsal that would be more provocative than last year.

The U.S. and South Korean militaries are to start their annual large-scale drills on Monday (August 17, 2026) and have described the scope of this year's training as similar to past years.

The allies have said the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises are meant to strengthen their readiness against North Korean threats and reiterated that they are defensive in nature.

The North Korean warning signals that the country could conduct more weapons tests in the coming days after its neighbours detected two ballistic missile launches off North Korea's east coast in the past week.

North Korea hasn't commented on the launches, but outside experts assess they were likely meant to protest the U.S.-South Korean drills or upgrade weapons systems.

In a statement carried by state media on Friday (August 14, 2026), North Korea's Foreign Ministry called the U.S.-South Korean training “a rehearsal for an aggressive war” that is triggering a different level of instability in the region.

“It is our consistent principle of ensuring security to respond to a new level of a threat with a new level of a deterrent,” the statement said. North Korea "will more clearly express its stance on the enemies to cope with any threats and challenges through the responsible and decisive exercise of the right to legitimate self-defence.” North Korea also said the drills would be of a “more serious provocative nature and dangerousness than last year" and involve all the military assets and war-fighting modes of the US and South Korea, a claim that those countries haven't said.

Analysts say North Korea has often used its adversaries' military drills as a pretext to ramp up weapons testing activities to expand its nuclear and missile arsenals and promote public support of leader Kim Jong Un.

Mr. Kim has ignored the U.S. and South Korea's offers to resume diplomacy and has focussed on taking steps to bolster his nuclear arsenal since his summitry with U.S. President Donald Trump broke down in 2019.

Experts say Mr. Kim will likely eventually aim to use his advancing nuclear program to win greater U.S. concessions such as extensive sanctions relief.

Mr. Kim has increased his diplomatic engagement with Russia in recent years. North Korea has been supplying troops and ammunition to Russia to support its war against Ukraine in return for economic and military assistance. Mr. Kim has also recently pushed to deepen ties with China, North Korea's biggest trading partner.

World.title: Royal Madras Yacht Club: Sailing through Chennai’s 115-year-old maritime history
World.content:
“Boat number three!” yells Roshni Anand, executive secretary, Royal Madras Yacht Club (RMYC).

I line up in front of the club with five other people, all slipping on green life jackets. Dark clouds loom in the sky, and a strong downpour has just paused. My first sailing experience, which is almost cancelled because of the weather, finally begins. It feels like a stroke of beginner’s luck.

Nested in Chennai Port Harbour, in the heart of the city, the Royal Madras Yacht Club was established in 1911 and is popularly known as the first sailing club in South India.

A small boat takes us out into the waters, where a J/80 sailboat — sturdy and French-built — awaits, with its mighty sail bearing the letters ‘RMYC’. There, Captain Vivek Shanbag helps us aboard. An airline pilot by profession and a sailor by passion, Vivek, the secretary of RMYC, has been sailing with the club for the past 20 years.

“The front of the boat is called 12 o’clock, the back is 6 o’clock, and the right and left are 3 and 9 o’clock,” Vivek begins, giving us directions and introducing us to the vocabulary of sailing. “The left side is called the port side, while the right is called the starboard side,” he adds.

We are participating in RMYC’s leisure sailing programme, where more than 50 people have gathered to experience sailing. “Children as young as seven to adults up to the age of 93 have sailed with us. People enjoy being out at sea,” says Vivek.

Over the past year, the club launched moonlight sailing, says Ram Kumar, a member of RMYC for more than 40 years. “We start sailing at 5.30pm and wind up by 7.30pm. On a clear night you get to see the moon and stars. That is a very lovely experience,” he adds.

The club also promotes competitive sailing, where children are trained to compete at State, national, and international- level competitions along with offshore sailing. Dheer Singhi, a member who is going to represent India for BRICS International Sailing Championship in Belarus at the end of the month, says he started sailing when he was nine years old. “We don’t have a field like other sports. The ocean is our field and it is unpredictable. Discipline, perseverance and adapting to Nature is very important,” he says, adding that values he learnt from sailing have helped him navigate life beyond the sport.

Vivek slips in snippets of Chennai’s history during the sail. He says the club, which was founded as the Madras Sailing Club, was later accorded a ‘Royal’ status by King George V, becoming the Royal Madras Yacht Club. He throws in a bit of trivia: During First World War, the German cruiser Emden shelled the city near Madras Port. While its main target was the oil tanks at the harbour, several shells landed on buildings here including the Madras Sailing Club.

Our trip ends as our small boat carries us back to the club. Onshore, music plays loudly as members gather over refreshments. For Ram Kumar, a member of the club, evenings like these are what make sailing special. “Especially in Chennai, given the humid conditions, it is very pleasant to sail in the open sea, with the fresh air and a nice breeze in the evenings. We meet other sailors, share little tidbits about sailing and simply enjoy being out on the water,” he says.

For further details, contact Capt. Vivek Shanbhag at captviki@gmail.com or 9841030880.

World.title: Pakistan's leadership stresses need for unity, reforms as nation celebrates Independence Day
World.content:
Pakistan’s civilian and military leadership has stressed the need for unity and reforms as the nation celebrates 79 years of independence today.

According to state-run Radio Pakistan, the day dawned with a 31-gun salute in Islamabad and a 21-gun salute at the provincial headquarters. A change of guards ceremony was also held at the mausoleum of Quaid-i-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah in Karachi.

‘Pakistan’s security linked to peace in our neighbourhood’

In his message, President Asif Ali Zardari paid tribute to Quaid-i-Azam, those behind the Pakistan Movement and those who sacrificed their homes, security and livelihoods in the struggle for a homeland.

“But independence is not only a historic achievement. It is also a responsibility that each generation must carry forward. The Pakistan that was created through the democratic will of its people must continue to grow stronger, more secure and more prosperous. Our task is not only to remember what earlier generations achieved, but to add to it through our own work,” he said.

The president said that the past year had reminded citizens of the strength of the Pakistani nation.

Recalling last year’s brief military conflict with India, he said, “The events surrounding Marka-i-Haq demonstrated that Pakistan seeks peace, but also possesses the resolve and capacity to defend its sovereignty and national interests. The lesson of strength is ultimately a lesson of responsibility. A country that can defend itself must also use its strength to prevent conflict, protect peace and serve the interests of its people.”

He said that the security and stability enjoyed today had come at a great cost, paying tribute to the martyrs of the armed forces, law enforcement agencies and police.

“Their courage and commitment have helped safeguard our nation against external aggression and the threat of terrorism. The people of Pakistan remain deeply grateful for their service,” he said.

He also highlighted Pakistan’s efforts to facilitate dialogue in the region.

“Pakistan has effectively used its channels of communication, its geographical location and diplomatic capital to encourage dialogue and de-escalation at a time when wider conflict could have serious consequences for the region and the world,” he said.

He reiterated that all disputes must be ultimately addressed through dialogue and diplomacy.

“Our security is linked to the peace and stability of our neighbourhood and the world at large. Pakistan will continue to support efforts that reduce tensions, protect regional stability and create conditions for cooperation,” he said.

The president also went on to say that the country must focus on the work that will determine Pakistan’s future.

“We must strengthen our economy, create greater opportunities for our young people, improve education and skills, strengthen institutions through a series of governance, economic and social reforms to ensure that the benefits of development and democracy reach every part and community of the country,” he said.

“Pakistan’s greatest strength is its young people. Across the country and around the world, they are demonstrating their talent in science, technology, business, education and the creative industries. Our responsibility is to give them the education, skills and opportunities they need to realise their potential. By investing in our youth today, we are investing in Pakistan’s future,” he added.

“For ordinary Pakistanis, national progress is measured in practical terms. It means a young person finding the skills and opportunity to build a career. It means a family being able to access quality education and healthcare. It means farmers, workers, traders and businesses being able to plan for the future with greater confidence. The strength of Pakistan will ultimately be judged by whether our national progress improves the lives of its people,” President Zardari said.

He also voiced Pakistan’s support for the people of occupied Kashmir, saying Pakistan will continue to support a peaceful resolution of the dispute in accordance with the aspirations of its people and the relevant United Nations resolutions.

On Afghanistan, the president said that Pakistan had always respected and supported the national sovereignty of our neighbour Afghanistan and expected the same reciprocity.

“It is sad that the current interim regime of Afghanistan is allowing and supporting a cocktail of terror groups to use their soil for launching attacks against neighbouring countries including Pakistan. It is sad the Taliban regime of Afghanistan is collaborating with India in launching terror attacks against Pakistani civilians and security personnel. They are doing this to distract us from the peace building efforts of Pakistan, recognised by the entire world,” he said.

“I warn them to stop these evil actions against the people of Pakistan and assure all and sundry that the armed forces of Pakistan are capable of defeating these evil designs,” he said.

He ended his message by calling on the nation to contribute to the country’s progress in whatever field they serve.

‘Pakistan committed to defending its national interests’

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also began his message by paying tribute to the founding leaders of Pakistan, saying the nation owed the fulfilment of its dream of an independent homeland to their vision, statesmanship and sacrifices.

Highlighting the government’s economic achievements over the past two-and-a-half years, PM Shehbaz said the country had successfully navigated challenging circumstances to achieve economic stability and was now moving towards becoming a developed economy.

He noted that remittances from overseas Pakistanis had increased by $11.3 billion over the past two years, which he termed a reflection of their confidence in government policies.

The prime minister said harnessing modern information technology, promoting innovation-driven industrial and agricultural development, creating employment opportunities and establishing a world-class education and skills system remained among the government’s top priorities.

Paying tribute to the armed forces, the prime minister said the military, under the leadership of Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, had demonstrated exemplary unity and courage during Marka-i-Haq, adding another chapter to the country’s history of defence.

He said Pakistan remained committed to defending its national interests, including its right to water resources, and reiterated that the country would continue to play its role as a responsible nation and a stabilising force for regional and global peace.

He cited the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye as testimony to the country’s growing strategic role in the region.

The prime minister also expressed solidarity with the people of occupied Kashmir and the Palestinian people. He said lasting peace in South Asia was contingent upon a diplomatic resolution of the Kashmir dispute in line with United Nations resolutions, international law and the aspirations of the Kashmiri people.

The prime minister also paid tribute to the martyrs of the armed forces and law enforcement agencies who sacrificed their lives for the country, and called upon all segments of society, particularly political parties, to work together for national unity, integrity and the advancement of national interests.

He concluded his message by praying for Pakistan’s continued progress and dignity in the comity of nations.

‘Pakistan’s strength lies in the unity of its people’

CDF Munir, Chief of Naval Staff Admiral Naveed Ashraf and Chief of Air Staff Air Chief Marshal Zaheer Ahmed Baber Sidhu also issued a message to mark Independence Day.

According to Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the armed forces paid tribute to the Quaid and those whose sacrifices resulted in a sovereign Pakistan.

“Their vision, courage and resolve remain a guiding force for the nation and continue to inspire us to uphold the principles and ideals of Pakistan,” the statement said.

“The armed forces of Pakistan respectfully acknowledge the supreme sacrifices of our martyrs, the services of our veterans, the dedication of law enforcement personnel and the contributions of every Pakistani who has served the nation. Their courage and selfless service have bolstered Pakistan’s resilience and safeguarded its independence, security and national interests,” it added.

“As guardians of Pakistan’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, the armed forces reaffirm their unwavering resolve to defend the motherland against all threats, uphold the Constitution and discharge the sacred trust reposed in them by the people of Pakistan. United with the nation, the armed forces will remain steadfast in preserving peace and stability while creating an environment conducive to national progress and prosperity,” the statement said.

“Pakistan’s strength lies in the unity and collective resolve of its people. On this Independence Day, let us renew our commitment to the enduring principles of faith, unity and discipline, strengthen national cohesion, promote tolerance and work together towards a secure, stable and prosperous Pakistan,” it concluded.

Dar reaffirms determination to safeguard country’s sovereignty

In his message on the occasion, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar recalled Marka-i-Haq and reaffirmed Pakistan’s determination to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity.

“We commemorated the first anniversary of Marka-i-Haq, recalling Pakistan’s resolute and successful response to Indian aggression in 2025,” he said in a televised address to the nation.

“The occasion reaffirmed our determination to safeguard Pakistan’s sovereignty, security and territorial integrity while remaining firmly committed to international law, responsible state craft and the pursuit of regional peace.”

At the outset of his address, the deputy PM extended greetings to Pakistanis and expatriates on the Independence Day, saying we commemorate the day “to pay tribute to Quaid-i-Azam whose visionary leadership, unwavering resolve and steadfast commitment transformed the aspirations for a separate homeland into reality”.

He also paid honour to the leaders and workers of the Pakistan movement whose “courage, dedication and countless sacrifices laid the foundations of our independent state”.

Dar said that since independence, the country had made “remarkable strides across diverse fields guided by the enduring principles of unity, faith and discipline”.

“Today we are a resilient nation of more than 250 million people bound together by our shared history, collective heritage and common aspirations,” he added.

He also noted that the country’s achievements in education, science and technology, economic development, sports, culture and other fields “reflect the talent, determination and immense potential of our people”.

The deputy PM also mentioned Pakistan’s “strengthened” position on the international stage over the past eight decades.

“Our expanding diplomatic engagement, growing economic connectivity and partnerships, and deepening defence and security cooperation reflect Pakistan’s confidence and its commitment to contributing to a peaceful stable and prosperous region and world.”

He also mentioned the defence accord signed by Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia last week, saying the “historic agreement reflects our shared resolve to deepen strategic cooperation, strengthen collective security and addresses evolving regional and international peace and security challenges”.

He also paid special tribute to armed forces, police and paramilitary forces of the country, saying their “courage, professionalism and unwavering commitment remain a bulwark of our national security”.

Dar noted the country always “stood for peace, dialogue, cooperation and mutual respect among nations”.

He referred to last year’s conflict with India and said the events “underscored the urgent need of peaceful resolution of longstanding disputes, particularly the Jammu and Kashmir dispute which remains a source of instability in our region”.

“Pakistan will continue to extend its principles, moral, political and diplomatic support to the Kashmiri people in their just struggle for the realisation of their right to self-determination in accordance with the relevant UNSC resolutions,” he added.

On the occasion, he urged people to “draw renewed inspirations from the ideals and vision that led to the creation of Pakistan”.

“Let us reaffirm our collective resolve to strengthen our institutions, uphold our national unity, harness the potential of our people and build a stronger more prosperous and peaceful Pakistan for generations to come,” he concluded.

World.title: More than 80 people injured by aerial firing in Karachi on eve of Independence Day
World.content:
KARACHI: At least 86 people have been injured in celebratory firing incidents in Karachi on the eve of Pakistan’s Independence Day, rescue officials said on Friday.

According to Edhi, the injured include 10 women, 17 children and 59 men. In a statement, the rescue service said 24 people, including one woman, four children and 19 men, were brought to Abbasi Shaheed Hospital.

It added that 35 people, including four women, three children and 28 men, were brought to Jinnah Hospital; and 26 people, including 10 children, four women and 12 men, were taken to Civil Hospital.

The statement added that one woman was shifted to a private hospital.

Firing incidents were reported in Lyari, Saddar, Korangi, Malir, Azizabad, North Nazimabad, Nazimabad, Gulbahar, Gulshan-i-Iqbal, Orangi Town, Jamshed Quarters and Defence, it said.

Meanwhile, police in Karachi’s East district launched a crackdown against aerial firing on Independence Day and took 10 suspects into custody from various areas.

In a statement, police said weapons used for aerial firing were also recovered from the arrested suspects. The arrests were made within the jurisdictions of Gulshan-i-Iqbal, Sharea Faisal, Sachal, Gulistan-i-Johar and Site Super Highway police stations, police said.

According to police in Karachi’s West district, three suspects had been arrested for aerial firing on Independence Day.

Incidents of aerial firing are a routine occurrence on occasions such as Independence Day and New Year’s Eve despite bans imposed in the past, often leaving dozens injured .

Last year, three people, including a minor girl, were killed and over 100 others wounded in celebratory gunfire across the metropolis at midnight on Independence Day.

World.title: Petroleum levy collection hits record Rs1.57tr
World.content:
• Cost of running civil govt rises 16pc, crosses Rs1tr for first time

• Fiscal deficit shrinks to 2.6pc on the back of provincial surpluses, lower interest bill

• Defence spending up 18pc; primary surplus reaches record 2.9pc of GDP

ISLAMABAD: With a record Rs1.567 trillion petroleum levy collection amid record consumer-end oil prices following US-Israel attacks on Iran, the cost of running the civil government rose 16 per cent in the fiscal year 2025-26 to cross Rs1tr for the first time despite restructuring and austerity measures, official data showed on Thursday.

At the same time, record cash surpluses from the provinces and a sharp fall in interest payments helped contain the fiscal deficit at 2.6pc of GDP — the lowest since FY03 for which comparable data is available on the Ministry of Finance website — while the primary surplus reached a historic 2.9pc of GDP.

In its annual report on fiscal operations for FY26, the Ministry of Finance reported that petroleum levy collection surged 29pc to Rs1.567tr from Rs1.22tr a year earlier. It also surpassed the original budget target of Rs1.468tr, which had subsequently been revised upward to Rs1.498tr as part of the FY27 budget exercise.

The Rs1.567tr petroleum levy did not include an undisclosed amount of customs duty and Rs26bn collected through the carbon levy. For the current fiscal year, the government is targeting an even higher Rs1.676tr in petroleum levy, besides Rs50bn through the climate levy on petroleum products.

Despite restructuring and austerity policies, expenditure on running the civil government increased by 16pc to Rs1.033tr from Rs892bn in FY25, breaching the Rs1tr mark for the first time and exceeding the Rs971bn budget estimate.

Defence expenditure also increased by 18pc to Rs2.588tr from Rs2.194tr a year earlier. How­ever, it was only Rs38bn higher than the Rs2.55tr budget allocation despite additional requirements following Indian attacks.

Total revenue collection declined marginally to 15.6pc of GDP in FY26 from 15.7pc a year earlier. Federal Board of Revenue collection stood at Rs13.01tr, around 10pc short of target but almost 11pc higher than Rs11.74tr collected in FY25.

Despite the revenue shortfall, historically high provincial cash surpluses and a steep decline in interest payments enabled the government to sharply reduce the overall fiscal deficit.

The primary surplus — the difference between total revenues and expenditure excluding debt servicing — reached 2.9pc of GDP, the highest since the government began reporting the indicator in FY20.

The fiscal deficit had peaked at 8.9pc of GDP in FY19 before falling to 8.1pc and 7.1pc in the following two years. It rose again to 7.9pc in FY22 but has since declined amid successive IMF-backed fiscal tightening.

Meanwhile, the primary account remained in deficit until turning into a surplus of 0.9pc of GDP in FY24. It improved to 2.4pc the following year and further to 2.9pc in FY26.

Three major contributors to the fiscal improvement were record provincial cash surpluses of Rs1.45tr, petroleum levy collection of Rs1.567tr and a Rs1.939tr decline in interest payments.

The finance ministry reported that interest payments fell to Rs6.947tr, or 5.5pc of GDP, from Rs8.887tr, or 7.7pc of GDP, in FY2024-25 — a dec­line equivalent to 2.2pc of GDP in a single year.

Subsidies were also contained at Rs1.01tr, almost 22pc below Rs1.3tr in FY25, while development expenditure fell to Rs727bn from Rs786bn.

Mainly because of savings on interest payments following the easing of the policy rate from 22pc to 10pc, total expenditure declined to Rs23.09tr from Rs24.16tr in FY25.

As a result, total expenditure fell to 18.2pc of GDP from 21.1pc a year earlier. Current expenditure also declined to 16.3pc of GDP (Rs20.69tr) from 18.8pc (Rs21.5tr) in FY25. Defence expenditure, however, edged up to 2pc of GDP from 1.9pc.

The four provinces posted a 57pc increase in their combined cash surplus to the Centre, taking it to a record Rs1.45tr from Rs921bn in FY25 — an increase of Rs529bn in a single year. They had committed a surplus of Rs1.38tr under the national fiscal pact.

Punjab alone provided Rs915bn — almost equivalent to the combined Rs921bn surplus of all four provinces a year earlier and 163pc higher than its Rs348bn contribution in FY25. Sindh followed with a 24pc increase in its surplus to Rs350bn from Rs283bn. PTI-led Khyber Pakhtunkhwa provided Rs165bn, around 6pc lower than Rs176bn in FY25, while Balochistan posted a surplus of just Rs20.74bn.

On the accounting side, the government reported a record statistical discrepancy of Rs853bn.

The discrepancy stood at Rs329bn in FY25 and had drawn concern from the IMF, which had suggested a technical mission that the government declined.

The finance ministry attributed Rs448bn of the discrepancy to under-reporting at the federal level and Rs405bn to provinces.

It said the federal discrepancy stemmed from “variations on account of time lag in reporting and book adjustments amongst SBP, FBR and EAD data”. At the provincial level, Rs266bn of the discrepancy was attributed to increases in commercial bank deposits, while KP and Balochistan accou­nted for Rs95bn and Rs72bn, respectively, also largely due to movements in bank deposits.

World.title: No Adiala visit without confirmation of meeting, says KP CM Afridi
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Mini­ster Sohail Afridi said on Thursday that he would not visit Adiala jail again before Sept 27 unless the government officially confirmed a meeting with PTI founder Imran Khan.

He also called for the closure of important government offices, including the Prime Minister’s Off­ice, alleging that they had become dysfunctional.

Speaking to the media outside Adiala jail, the KP chief minister said the situation at the prison indicated that the authorities had no intention of allowing him to meet Imran Khan.

“I have come to Adiala for the last time before Sept 27. I will return only when the government itself confirms the meeting,” he said.

It is worth mentioning that Afridi’s name was also included in the list of people who intended to meet Imran Khan on Thursday.

Afridi warned that if the meeting was not allowed, PTI workers would block roads across the country from 10pm on Thursday as part of the party’s “D-Chowk” protest. He urged party workers to prepare to take to the streets carrying national and PTI flags, saying the protest would convey a message that the treatment meted out to the country’s most popular leader since April 2022 was unacceptable.

According to PTI media cell, protests were held in different cities. Workers went to the chowks and chanted slogans in favour of Imran Khan.

Afridi alleged that even government ministers were acknowledging that the country and its system had been paralysed, claiming that the government had failed.

He said the people of Pakistan wanted their issues to be resolved and that this could only be ensured by Imran Khan. He said he would march towards Islamabad on Sept 27 along with two million people.

Afridi urged PTI workers and the public to focus on Sept 27, describing the date as a “nightmare” for the authorities. He claimed that people were enthusiastic and that a large number of supporters had gathered in Khyber district at short notice on Wednesday.

He said a similar street movement would be launched in other districts and claimed that more than two million people would participate in the Sept 27 mobilisation. He added that a street movement would be held in Bannu on Sunday.

He said anyone carrying the flags of Pakistan and PTI would be considered a supporter of Imran Khan.

The chief minister’s warning came amid continuing PTI protests and demands for access to its incarcerated founder. The Islamabad High Court has ordered the jail administration to arrange meetings with family members and lawyers on Tuesdays and with party leaders on Thursdays, but the orders have not been implemented for several months.

Later in the night, while talking to the media, Afridi said there were orders from three judges allowing meetings with Imran Khan twice a week, but the court orders were not being implemented.

“We have filed applications in courts for the implementation of the decisions, but the courts are helpless. In that case, we have every right to hold a protest. Even the prime minister said that he would ask about the meeting and then inform me. If such important offices are dysfunctional, they should be closed as they are consuming public funds. Poor people pay taxes and that money is spent on them,” he said.

The KP chief minister said even ministers were saying that the system had collapsed.

“Today, labourers, industrialists and all other segments of society have been saying that the country is not going in the right direction. Shehbaz Sharif used to say that if he got 30pc support from the establishment, he would deliver and change the fate of the masses, but he has failed despite getting full support,” he added.
