World.title: Georgian Constitutional Court judge issues dissenting opinion on cases involving protests on pavements
World.content:
Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

A dissenting opinion by Constitutional Court judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze has been published on the punishment of people for holding protests on pavements.

Kverenchkhiladze believes that imposing administrative detention on people for peaceful protests and assemblies could cause harm that may later prove impossible to remedy.

The Tbilisi City Court began hearing the so-called “pavement cases” in December 2025. Since January 2026, dozens of demonstrators have faced administrative detention for holding protests on the pavement outside parliament.

Several people petitioned the Constitutional Court to challenge the ban on protests on pavements. They also asked the court to suspend the disputed provisions until it issued a final ruling. The Constitutional Court began hearing the cases but refused to suspend the provisions. Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze believes the court should have suspended them.

However, according to lawyer Giorgi Burdjanadze, Kverenchkhiladze was in the minority among the judges of the Constitutional Court’s First Chamber when they considered the issue.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion

“If the threat of administrative detention or imprisonment forces a person to repeatedly refrain from taking part in an assembly or publicly expressing their position, that opportunity can no longer be restored,” the judge wrote.

He said this was why such a restriction could cause “irreparable harm”.

Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion also includes arguments that lawyers raised before the Tbilisi City Court when it considered cases related to protests on pavements. However, the judges did not take those arguments into account.

One such argument concerns the temporary disruption of people’s normal movement in their daily lives.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze

Kverenchkhiladze notes that pedestrian movement on pavements can be disrupted for various reasons, including parking violations, commercial or construction activities, and other circumstances. However, the state has never considered imprisonment a necessary measure to protect freedom of movement in such cases.

“Temporary restrictions on pedestrians’ freedom of movement do not represent an interest for which a democratic state would normally resort to imprisonment as a means of protection,” the judge wrote.

Kverenchkhiladze also drew attention to the severity of the sanction. He said harsh punishment not only demonstrates the state’s attitude towards a particular action, but can also discourage people from taking part in protests altogether.

“The severity of the sanction provided for by the disputed provisions indicates not only the degree to which the act is considered reprehensible, but also the strength of the ‘deterrent effect’ it may have on the exercise of freedom of expression and freedom of assembly,” Kverenchkhiladze stressed.

Context

Georgia has seen continuous protests since 28 November 2024. Thousands of people took to the streets after Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze of the Georgian Dream party announced that the government would not put EU accession talks on the agenda for the next four years.

Since then, Georgian Dream has repeatedly restricted freedom of expression through new laws. These measures have included bans on wearing masks and using pyrotechnics at rallies, as well as criminal liability for repeatedly blocking roads during protests.

The most far-reaching of these repressive legislative initiatives came with amendments banning assemblies on pavements. Under the new rules, organisers of any assembly or demonstration on a pavement must notify the Interior Ministry five days before the event. The ministry can also propose an alternative time and location for the protest.

The new rules also introduce administrative detention as the initial penalty for violations, except in certain special cases.

Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

World.title: ‘We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads’ — Pashinyan
World.content:
Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said there should be no situation in which anyone could say: “Armenia has nowhere to go and nobody needs it.” Four years ago, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko made a similar statement.

According to Pashinyan, Lukashenko’s words actually reflect a “deeply rooted institutional perception” of Armenia, not only in Belarus but also in other countries that belong to the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). The prime minister sees this as a “disrespectful perception”. He believes it developed from the following assumption:

“There is the Karabakh conflict, there is a conflict with Azerbaijan, there is a conflict with Turkey, and this hostility is insurmountable. So they have nowhere to go, and we can treat them however we want.”

However, Pashinyan said Armenia had managed to prove otherwise:

“We have demonstrated in practice that many countries need Armenia as a responsible partner in the international community and as a very important country. We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads — together with the South Caucasus and the wider region.”

At a briefing, the prime minister again answered questions about Armenia’s choice between the EAEU and the European Union. He also discussed possible decisions on the management of Armenia’s railways, which Russia took over under a concession agreement in 2008. The Armenian government has effectively developed new proposals that would limit Russia’s role but would not yet terminate its concession.

“Before alternatives emerge, we need both the EU and the EAEU equally”

Russia continues to pressure Armenia over the need to choose between the EAEU and the EU. Armenian journalists therefore asked the government again about its position. Pashinyan said Russia expected Armenia to choose between “two alternatives”. However, the “second alternative” has not yet taken shape:

“We will certainly make this choice through a referendum in the future. But this will happen only after we first carry out the necessary institutional preparations and then formally apply for EU membership.”

According to Pashinyan, Armenia currently needs both the EU and the EAEU equally because the second alternative does not yet exist. He also said Armenia could eventually face not only a choice between these two options, but also a third approach:

“Perhaps a third initiative will emerge: neither the EAEU nor the EU. In other words, we do not need either structure. Who said that everyone must belong to some structure?”

Moreover, he said the government was considering many possible options, including “a fourth and fifth alternative”.

Returning to the issue of holding a referendum on EAEU or EU membership, he stressed:

“This choice must be a mature one because we do not yet know how realistic this path is or what the roadmap will look like.”

Without naming Russia, the prime minister said Armenia could not treat anyone’s interests with contempt or disregard. But it also could not put another country’s interests above its own national interests.

“That is why we are trying to discuss and resolve all issues patiently, without escalation or nervousness. We will discuss them for as long as necessary, until we find a solution that more or less satisfies both sides,” he said.

“We will not pursue the termination of the concession agreement”

Nikol Pashinyan once again said Yerevan wanted to resolve the issue of Armenia’s railway “in a friendly manner” without escalating the situation. He said both Armenia and Russia should consider each other’s interests and seek compromises.

This time, the prime minister outlined several possible scenarios for how the situation could develop:

“One of them could involve the Russian side selling its concession rights, either fully or partially. In other words, there could be certain shareholder configurations,” he said.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia does not want to terminate the concession agreement. It has always had that option and still does. However, the Armenian side prefers not to take such measures.

He said a possible solution for Yerevan would involve a Russian company selling its concession rights to a third party at market value.

At the same time, he noted that this approach might not be particularly acceptable to Russia’s partners.

He also said the Armenian government was working with experts to find an option that would at least partly address the concerns of both sides:

“[The experts] say that we could introduce a different management model. For example, Russia could retain part of its shares while transferring the rest. But the Russian side would have to retain a smaller stake. Otherwise, the problem would not be resolved.

There is another idea. The licence could be divided into two parts. At present, the railway infrastructure and its operation form a single package.”

Pashinyan explained the problems facing Armenia:

“The current situation prevents Armenia from seizing the historic opportunity to integrate our railway into the international rail network.”

He noted that countries responsible for the “lion’s share” of rail freight and which could become potential beneficiaries are looking for ways to bypass Armenia:

“They not only tell us this, but we can also see that they are showing no investment interest in this sector. As a result, we understand that the reason lies in the fact that our railway is under a Russian concession.”

Nikol Pashinyan added that this was why the government had raised the issue with its Russian partners in a friendly manner and proposed finding solutions.

Since 2008, Armenia’s railways have operated under a concession held by South Caucasus Railway. The company is a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The agreement provides for a 30-year concession. However, since 2008, freight volumes have halved, some routes have stopped operating, and the required investments have remained on paper. Meanwhile, Armenia wants to fully unblock its borders, which requires restoring railway links to the borders with Azerbaijan and Turkey. Since the Russian company that operates Armenia’s railways has not undertaken to restore these sections, Armenia is looking for ways to implement the plans itself.

Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

World.title: Fuel supplies from Tbilisi-controlled territory to Abkhazia: humanitarian aid or move in Russia’s interests?
World.content:
Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

Amid a severe fuel shortage in Abkhazia, the import of fuel from territory controlled by Tbilisi has sparked political controversy. The government says a private company delivered the shipment in full compliance with Georgian law, while the opposition and critics are calling for further clarification and answers to several questions: where did the fuel go, who brought it into Abkhazia, and for what purpose?

At a briefing on 12 August 2026, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed that fuel had reached Abkhazia from territory controlled by Georgia. He said the government had not organised the operation and that private companies had imported the fuel in accordance with the law.

According to ruling-party MP Rati Ionatamishvili, the shipment amounted to 3,000 tonnes of fuel, delivered to Abkhazia by several tankers. He said the shipment reached Abkhazia while fully respecting Georgia’s sovereignty and legislation.

Ionatamishvili criticised the opposition for its focus on the deliveries and dismissed as absurd suggestions that the operation aimed to supply Russia with several thousand tonnes of fuel. He said the 3,000 tonnes delivered to Abkhazia represented a negligible share of Russia’s annual fuel consumption. He added that presenting the issue in this way served a campaign aimed at undermining efforts to restore Georgian-Abkhaz relations.

Above all, the opposition is demanding details that the government has not yet provided.

According to Levan Samushia, one of the leaders of the Strong Georgia – Lelo alliance, the prime minister’s statement that the fuel was imported in compliance with the Law on Occupied Territories is not enough:

“Who supplied the fuel — in other words, where did it come from — and who was the recipient? Were Georgia’s laws and national interests respected?”

He said it was necessary to know which commercial entities were involved and what route the fuel took to reach Abkhazia.

Levan Samushia

Similar questions have also been raised by Berdia Sichinava, one of the leaders of the Gakharia – For Georgia party. However, he stressed that if the fuel shipment was genuinely humanitarian and did not violate the law, there was no problem with providing such assistance in itself.

“Georgia is involved in more than one such humanitarian project. For example, we fund medical treatment for our citizens from Abkhazia, we receive electricity from the Enguri Hydroelectric Power Plant, and people living in the occupied territory also receive it,” Sichinava said.

In his view, the main problem is the lack of transparency surrounding the process. Sichinava is demanding clarification on who imported the fuel, how large the shipment was, what procedures the cargo went through and where it was ultimately delivered.

Sichinava considers the way the fuel was ultimately used a particularly important question: did it go towards the needs of Abkhazia’s population and critical infrastructure, or was it eventually used in Russia-controlled areas to the south, including infrastructure linked to military activities?

“If the fuel entered occupied Abkhazia as a commercial rather than humanitarian shipment, and if it went through so-called customs procedures at the so-called border — which is actually the occupation line — this could raise serious concerns for our country’s territorial integrity and security,” Sichinava said.

Lasha Parulava, a member of the United National Movement, accused the government of serving Russian interests and betraying Georgia’s national interests.

He called Kobakhidze’s statement that the fuel deliveries complied with the Law on Occupied Territories cynical. Parulava also criticised the government’s policy towards Russia and noted that the fuel was supplied to Abkhazia amid a fuel shortage in Russia itself.

“This is not simply aiding the enemy, but a direct betrayal of national interests,” Parulava said.

Lasha Parulava

Nika Gvaramia, leader of the Coalition for Change, believes the government may have authorised the operation in advance, although the public has not been told why, when or on what grounds it approved it.

Gvaramia points out that Russian military bases are deployed in Abkhazia and that the Russian military is facing fuel shortages.

In his view, these circumstances make it necessary to establish whether humanitarian or social considerations genuinely prompted the fuel shipment, or whether Russia ultimately used the cargo for military purposes.

Gvaramia argues that, in that case, the issue would go beyond the legality of economic activity in Georgia’s occupied territory. The situation could also involve the supply of goods of strategic importance to Russia.

Nika Gvaramia

Expert Gia Khukhashvili assesses the volume of fuel and the logistics of its delivery differently from the authorities. In his view, the “several tankers” mentioned by government officials actually represent a much larger shipment.

“Three thousand tonnes is a convoy of at least 100 fuel tankers,” Khukhashvili wrote.

He said fuel deliveries to Abkhazia could theoretically mark the beginning of a reintegration process. Under the current government, however, he described the decision as “an act of collaborationism and sheer greed”.

Tamta Mikeladze, director of the Social Justice Center, wrote:

“Amid Russia’s economic weakening, Abkhazia may need support from Tbilisi, and this crisis could provide an opportunity to transform the conflict.

Any step that could benefit the people of Abkhazia should not automatically be seen as serving Russia’s interests. That is precisely why full transparency is necessary: who makes the decision, what is its purpose, what mechanisms are in place to monitor the process so that it does not strengthen Russia’s military and economic interests, and what political strategy accompanies it?

Meeting humanitarian or civilian needs and strengthening Russia’s interests are not the same thing. However, a lack of transparency can blur the distinction and turn such actions into part of Russia’s game.

The particular problem with the Abkhaz issue is that a crisis can become an opportunity only if there is a political vision. Georgian Dream has no such vision. The party has yet to adopt either a de-occupation plan or strategic documents for rebuilding trust.

Irakli Kobakhidze has not even attempted to answer the questions raised above.

Given the deep mistrust of Georgian Dream and the complete lack of transparency surrounding its policies, concerns that something could happen that fundamentally and permanently contradicts our national interests are entirely understandable. However, accuracy and attention to nuance are crucial when formulating criticism.”Fuel supplies to Abkhazia (civil.ge)

Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

World.title: EU annual report: ‘serious problems’ in Azerbaijan and ‘serious restrictions’ on fundamental freedoms
World.content:
European Union annual report

The EU says that the human rights and democracy situation in Azerbaijan in 2025 continued to be marked by “serious problems”. It highlighted restrictions on civil society and media freedom, concerns about the independence of the judiciary, and limited progress on structural reforms.

The overall situation in governance remained restrictive. This is according to the European Union’s Annual Report on Human Rights and Democracy in the World for 2025.

The report says legislative, administrative and judicial mechanisms “seriously restrict” the exercise of fundamental freedoms.

At the same time, the assessment notes progress in several areas. These include the criminalisation of child marriage, new measures to promote gender equality, and efforts to combat corruption.

The EU’s assessment of Azerbaijan in 2025 is critical but balanced.

Civil society under pressure

In 2025, civil society organisations continued to operate under restrictive conditions.

The EU notes that the 2017 Law on Non-Governmental Organisations remains in force. Registration, reporting and grant approval requirements continue to restrict the activities of independent organisations.

Local organisations reported persistent administrative pressure and increased scrutiny.

The departure of several UN agencies, including the United Nations Development Programme and UNICEF, also affected their operating environment. This reduced opportunities for international monitoring and assistance.

The EU says it continues to support civil society, independent media and human rights defenders, including through human rights monitoring and legal assistance programmes for vulnerable groups.

Concerns over the judiciary and the rule of law

According to the EU, problems related to the rule of law and judicial independence persist.

The assessment says courts lack sufficient independence when handling politically sensitive cases.

The report cites judgments by the European Court of Human Rights as an important indicator of the problems that remain.

In 2025, the ECHR issued 39 judgments in cases concerning Azerbaijan and found violations in 38 of them. Most cases involved the right to a fair trial, deprivation of liberty, freedom of expression and freedom of assembly.

The report also notes that Azerbaijan’s failure to implement ECHR judgments has affected the country’s relations with the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe.

Electoral system remains unchanged

The EU notes that Azerbaijan’s electoral system underwent no changes in 2025.

The country did not carry out major reforms aimed at implementing the long-standing recommendations of the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights and the Council of Europe’s Venice Commission.

The report identifies the lack of progress in this area as one of the persistent challenges to Azerbaijan’s democratic development.

Progress in some areas

The EU report also notes a number of legislative changes.

In July 2025, Azerbaijan criminalised child marriage.

The authorities approved a National Action Plan on Gender Equality for 2026–2028 and amended the Law on Combating Corruption.

The amendments include provisions on whistleblower protection and corruption risk management.

At the same time, the EU notes that the implementation of these measures remains uneven.

Dialogue continues, reforms remain limited

Throughout 2025, the EU maintained regular contacts with the Azerbaijani authorities.

These included meetings with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Office of the Ombudsman and the State Committee for Work with Religious Organisations.

The discussions covered judicial reform, media freedom, the treatment of people in detention, the rights of religious minorities, gender equality and the fight against corruption.

The EU also raised concerns about individuals who had been arrested or barred from leaving the country for exercising their fundamental rights.

Human rights issues also featured in sectoral dialogues on public administration, justice and social policy.

However, despite the continued channels of engagement, the EU says that “progress on structural reforms remains limited”.

Media freedom and fundamental rights

Media freedom and freedom of expression remained among the areas closely monitored by the EU.

The report notes that throughout the year, the EU closely monitored developments concerning digital rights, freedom of expression and media freedom.

EU-funded programmes supported independent media, human rights monitoring, legal assistance, gender equality and children’s rights.

The EU continued to support civil society organisations and human rights defenders working under restrictive conditions.

Azerbaijan on international platforms

The EU continued to raise human rights concerns in Azerbaijan through international organisations.

At the UN, during the 80th session of the General Assembly’s Third Committee, the EU raised issues concerning the space for civil society, judicial independence and media freedom.

Cooperation with the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights also continued, including preparations for Azerbaijan’s next Universal Periodic Review, scheduled for 2026–2027.

Within the Council of Europe, the EU supported mechanisms for implementing ECHR judgments and engaged with the Venice Commission and the Commissioner for Human Rights.

At the OSCE, the EU and its member states took part in discussions on media freedom and electoral standards, including restrictions affecting the work of the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights.

European Union annual report

World.title: ‘Even if nuclear power plant is shut down, Armenia will not face serious problems’: Reaction to Aliyev’s remarks
World.content:
Yerevan reacts to Aliyev’s AzTV interview

“Every nuclear power plant has an operating lifespan. Neither the Armenian government nor the Azerbaijani government, nor the government of any other country in the world, determines that lifespan,” Armenian ruling-party MP Arman Yeghoyan said in response to the Azerbaijani president’s remarks.

In an interview with AzTV, Ilham Aliyev said the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant was “outdated” and posed a potential threat to the entire region. He said “sooner or later it must be shut down”, after which “Armenia will face a full-scale energy crisis”.

At the same time, the Azerbaijani president said an energy corridor running through Armenia to Nakhchivan, then to Turkey and Europe, would “allow Armenia’s energy system to withstand a crisis”.

MP Arman Yeghoyan responded that “Aliyev has not made any revelation”. The maximum permitted operating period of the nuclear power plant expires in 2036, a fact that has long been known.

“And we have already announced that we are considering building a new nuclear power plant and are negotiating with several international partners,” the MP said.

Political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan believes Azerbaijan is trying to portray itself as a “generous country ready to help Armenia solve its problems”, despite the long-running conflict.

He noted that this was not the first such case. Baku had previously said that Azerbaijan could serve as a reliable partner for supplying energy resources to Armenia. Meliksetyan, however, said Armenia currently has a surplus of electricity. He stressed that even if the nuclear power plant shuts down, the country will not face serious problems.

“The claim that Armenia’s energy system will face a crisis after the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant closes is not true,” the political analyst told JAMnews.

He said Armenia does not currently need additional sources of electricity. He noted that the project for a new nuclear power plant remains under discussion and that Armenia has opportunities to expand solar power.

In addition, the fifth unit of the Hrazdan Thermal Power Plant has roughly the same generating capacity as the nuclear plant. The only problem is that the nuclear power plant produces cheaper electricity.

Aliyev again refers to TRIPP as the “Zangezur Corridor”

During his visit to Nakhchivan, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev gave an interview to state broadcaster AzTV. Alongside the issue of the nuclear power plant’s closure, Aliyev discussed the 2020 Second Karabakh War. He called the trilateral statement of 9 November, which ended the fighting, “an act of Armenia’s capitulation”. He added that “there is no need to look for any humiliating or offensive meaning in this term; it is simply a reality”.

He then turned to the issue of transport links between mainland Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan. He stressed that this route had remained one of Baku’s strategic goals for many years.

“On 9 November, trilateral negotiations took place with the mediation of the Russian president. I insisted categorically that the statement we were about to sign must include a corridor linking mainland Azerbaijan with the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic. The Armenian side did not want to agree to this. But it did not have many alternatives. If the war had continued, we would of course have suffered losses as well, but Armenia’s losses would have been much greater. Its troops were, so to speak, surrounded, and their destruction had effectively become a possibility,” the president said.

Point 9 of the November [statement], which the leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Russia signed, does not refer only to a road linking Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan. It states: “All economic and transport links in the region shall be unblocked.” Moreover, the document does not contain the term “corridor”.

Aliyev went on to say that Armenia had delayed implementation of the relevant provision of the 9 November statement and had taken no practical steps to create the “Zangezur Corridor”.

According to him, Russia, the third signatory to the statement, either could not ensure its implementation or had other reasons for not doing so.

“Until August last year, this issue remained frozen. The situation changed when the United States became involved, around spring 2025. The implementation of the project known as TRIPP then began successfully,” Aliyev said, linking the Trump Route transit project to the idea of the “Zangezur Corridor”.

For several years, Baku had demanded that Armenia provide a “Zangezur Corridor” to connect Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan. The Armenian authorities repeatedly said they were ready to unblock all transport links, but refused to provide a “corridor”. The issue stemmed from the fact that Azerbaijan used the term “corridor” to refer to an extraterritorial route. Armenia, meanwhile, refused to give up sovereign control over its own territory.

On 8 August 2025, the sides reached an agreement in Washington, with the mediation of the US president, under which Armenia would provide a route while retaining its sovereign rights. The transit project therefore received the name “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” (TRIPP).

Aliyev also said that, as part of TRIPP, Azerbaijan had already prepared a project to build power transmission lines from mainland Azerbaijan to Nakhchivan through Armenian territory:

“As a result of our specialists’ survey of Armenian territory, we identified the points where the supporting pylons should be installed.”

The Azerbaijani president expressed hope that “Armenia will not delay this process”, saying it would also benefit the country.

“There is no infrastructure by that name in Armenia” — MP

Arman Yeghoyan, an MP from Armenia’s ruling Civil Contract party, said that documents signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan, including the peace agreement initialled in Washington, do not contain the term “Zangezur Corridor”.

“At the level of political narratives, you can say many things. But we are saying that there is no such concept or infrastructure with such a name or term on Armenian territory.”

The MP urged people to remember that Armenia is implementing the TRIPP project. The leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan and the United States signed the declaration launching the project in Washington on 8 August 2025.

Comment

According to political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan, when the Azerbaijani side explains what it means by the “Zangezur Corridor”, it refers to the railway from Horadiz to Nakhchivan and then on to Turkey. He also noted that Aliyev used the name TRIPP in his interview.

The analyst said the meaning attached to the term “Zangezur Corridor” in 2022–2023 differs from what it means today. In his assessment, the project no longer involves an extraterritorial corridor:

“From a legal standpoint, TRIPP cannot become an extraterritorial corridor. But from a propaganda standpoint, Azerbaijan uses and will continue to use the term ‘Zangezur Corridor’, with some modifications.”

Meliksetyan stressed that the “Trump Route” project would proceed according to principles agreed with US mediation.

Commenting on Aliyev’s statement about building power transmission lines through Armenian territory, the political analyst said the sides were assessing the most suitable routes. He said the involvement of Azerbaijani specialists should not be interpreted as “acting on their own”.

“All the work is being carried out within the TRIPP framework. An electricity link will run through Armenian territory and connect the two parts of Azerbaijan. Azerbaijani specialists can only discuss where the link will enter Armenia from Azerbaijani territory and where it will re-enter Azerbaijan,” the expert explained.

Summing up his impressions of Aliyev’s interview, Meliksetyan said the Azerbaijani president had spoken in his characteristic style, seeking to highlight his “political achievements”.

The analyst said it was no coincidence that Aliyev focused on Nakhchivan’s economic and energy development, as well as its transport prospects. The president said Azerbaijan would finance the railway restoration itself, but also expressed interest in attracting international investors.

“Although Azerbaijan has repeatedly said that it has no financial problems, they certainly exist. Baku is trying to attract new investment to Nakhchivan through TRIPP to restore this section of the railway,” Meliksetyan said.

Yerevan reacts to Aliyev’s AzTV interview

World.title: Severe petrol shortages hit Abkhazia amid Russia fuel crisis following Ukrainian attacks — VIDEO
World.content:
Fuel shortages in Abkhazia

Severe fuel shortages continue in Abkhazia in the middle of the tourist season. All petroleum products are supplied exclusively from Russia, leaving one clear explanation: fuel shortages in Russia caused by Ukrainian drone attacks on oil and gas facilities.

The Abkhaz authorities are holding emergency talks with Moscow and say progress has been made. Reports say Russia has already arranged for 1,600 tonnes of AI-92 petrol to be sent to Abkhazia, with the first shipment expected to arrive in the coming days.

For now, petrol is available only at Rosneft and Podorozhnik filling stations.

Meanwhile, reports say petrol was supplied from territory controlled by Tbilisi

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed this:

“Amid the severe fuel shortage, a shipment was made to Abkhazia, but it was not supplied by the state, it was supplied by private businesses. If we continue to have the opportunity to ease the situation for the people living there, both Georgians and Abkhaz, we will continue to do so,” Kobakhidze said.

The Abkhaz news agency Apsnypress asked the Abkhaz government for comment following Kobakhidze’s statement and received the following response:

“Due to the circumstances caused by external factors, there is not enough motor fuel to meet Abkhazia’s needs. The authorities therefore decided to allow fuel supplies from alternative sources. Fuel market participants managed to arrange a shipment of petrol from Georgian territory. As is well known, Abkhazia also supplied fuel to Georgia from its territory in the post-war 1990s.”

Kobakhidze’s statement drew criticism from the opposition in Tbilisi. Opposition politicians said the fuel supplies to Abkhazia “could in fact mean supplies to Russian military bases”.

Economist and opposition politician Roman Gotsiridze said: “It is possible that the fuel could also have been transported to Russian territory. The company that made these deliveries will not escape sanctions.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Fuel shortages in Abkhazia

World.title: Youth who assaulted woman sleeping rough admits to breaking into businesses
World.content:
A teenage boy who assaulted a woman sleeping rough has pleaded guilty to serious criminal trespass in South Australia's Youth Court.

The now-18-year-old pleaded guilty in June to causing harm with intent against the woman, which was today accepted by the prosecution.

The prosecution had applied for the matter to be dealt with in the District Court, with the defendant to be sentenced as an adult given the "extremely serious" nature and "harrowing nine-minute-long footage" of the offending.

That application is to be fought by his defence lawyers, who are seeking to have the matter remain in the Youth Court.

The lawyer for the defendant said documentation from the centre where he has been remanded in custody reflected "very positive reports from youth justice" and addressed his "complex mental health issues".

The court heard the youth had a long-standing ADHD diagnosis and undiagnosed autism spectrum disorder.

At the time of the attack, police said the 64-year-old victim had been sleeping in the vicinity of Mitcham Memorial Library on Belair Road at Hawthorn.

Police said she had been kicked and punched to the head and body in the early hours of November 13, 2025.

Paramedics treated the woman before taking her to hospital where she was reported to be in a serious but stable condition.

The incident took place near the Mitcham Memorial Library. (ABC News)

The teenager was also accused of breaking into nearby businesses on the same night and subsequently charged with serious criminal trespass.

Magistrate John Wells today urged counsel to consider that the matter involved "highly vulnerable" parties and that it would be "unfortunate" and time-consuming for the case to be referred to the District Court, only to be sent back to the Youth Court.

"I want to say to everyone, I urge you all to do your best to try and resolve it," he said.

"We have a highly vulnerable victim — her interests are important.

"We have a highly vulnerable child in custody, and his interests are also important.

"Please don't let anyone ignore those paramount considerations."

Magistrate Wells told the defendant that he was "very keen to finalise" the matter.

"I'm sure you are, I'm sure your parents are and those who support you are, but we are moving in the right direction," he said.

The 18-year-old remained in custody and would appear in court next month.

World.title: Wind farm workers detail photo with accused farmer after alleged triple murder
World.content:
The trial of a Queensland cattle farmer, charged with murdering three people and attempting to murder a fourth has heard from workers who spent the day of the alleged shooting with the accused.

Darryl Valroy Young, 63, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of murder and one count of attempted murder during the ongoing Supreme Court trial in Townsville.

He is charged with the murder of married couple Mervyn Schwarz and Maree Schwarz, and Mrs Schwarz's son Graham Tighe.

He is also charged with the attempted murder of Graham Tighe's brother Ross Tighe.

Mr Young's lawyer said his client never saw the family at the gate of his Bogie cattle station on the morning he was accused of shooting them.

On Friday, the court heard renewable energy workers Liam Parnell and Matt Garbutt estimated arriving at Mr Young's Bogie property in a ute at about 7:30am on August 4, 2022.

Liam Parnell gave evidence in the triple murder trial on Friday. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

The trial has previously heard that Ross Tighe, who said he and his family were shot by Mr Young, estimated the incident occurred at the farmer's front gate after 8am.

Mr Parnell and Mr Garbutt told the court after meeting Mr Young, they left him at the gate and drove to the property homestead before splitting into separate vehicles.

Mr Parnell said he continued to scout a high-altitude location and saw Mr Young again after 8:30am.

Mr Garbutt was shown a video he had taken at 8:11am that morning.

Matthew Garbutt also gave evidence in the Supreme Court trial on Friday. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

He said he saw Mr Young more than 10 to 20 minutes after he had taken that video.

The colleagues said they learned there had been a shooting after 11am when they were installing equipment on a ridge with Darryl Young, his stepmother and son close-by.

Police asked group for 'selfie'

Mr Parnell said he was initially contacted by his boss, then police who advised the group to stay in place.

"We spent the whole day up there," Mr Parnell said.

" I was asked to take photos and send them across — a selfie of all of us up there. "

Mr Young has taken notes through the trial. ( ABC News: Carole Howlett)

The court was shown photos taken by Mr Parnell.

The group of people, including Darryl Young wearing a dark navy shirt, could be seen giving a thumbs up in one photo.

Earlier the trial heard Ross Tighe describe Darryl Young wore a fluorescent work shirt during the alleged shooting.

Another photo shown to the jury showed all in the group smiling except Darryl Young.

Mr Parnell said during the afternoon he saw Mr Young appearing "relaxed in the ATV" and said he noticed no change in his demeanour.

He and Mr Garbutt said police eventually told the group to travel in one car to the property gate.

Mr Parnell said he drove, and the group was met by a specialist policing unit.

Neighbour missing gun

The court heard from grazier Brett Stagg, a neighbour of both the Schwarz's and Tighe's Sutherland Station and Mr Young's Shannonvale Station.

Mr Stagg told the court he had an "up and down relationship" with Mr Young but would "keep the peace" as they were neighbours.

Crown prosecutor David Nardone asked Mr Stagg about a fire at his house on his property in 2011.

Prosecutor David Nardone (right) is appearing on behalf of the crown. (ABC News: Chloe Chomicki)

"During the time of the fire some guns went missing? A .30-30 and a .223?" Mr Nardone asked.

"Correct," Mr Stagg said.

The grazier confirmed that of the missing firearms the .223 was recovered but the .30-30 rifle never was.

Prosecutors have told the trial that .30-30 ammunition cartridges were found in Mr Young's kitchen and work shed and had the same markings as the spent cartridges found at the scene of the alleged triple murder.

"Those markings were '30.30 WIN RP'," Mr Nardone told the jury in his opening address on Monday.

"Darryl Young was licensed to possess six firearms — none of those were .30-30 rifles."

Mr Nardone said that in a search of Mr Young's dwellings, "no firearm capable of discharging .30-30 cartridges were found".

The trial continues.

World.title: NT politician proposes amendments to own party's VAD bill
World.content:
A Northern Territory government backbencher has announced he will move amendments to his own party's long-awaited bill to introduce voluntary assisted dying (VAD) in the Territory in a bid to make the legislation "consistent with best practice".

Country Liberal Party (CLP) MLA Tanzil Rahman today confirmed he would move three amendments to the party's Rights of the Terminally Ill Bill when it returns to parliament later this month.

The bill is set to pass the NT parliament in a conscience vote after receiving majority support.

With the NT the last jurisdiction where voluntary assisted dying is not legal, after the federal government overturned Australia-first laws in 1997, the bill's passage would legalise the practice in all Australian states and territories.

The bill, proposed by Attorney-General Marie-Clare Boothby, would only allow access to voluntary assisted dying for people with 12 months or less left to live.

Marie-Clare Boothby introduced the laws to the NT Legislative Assembly last month. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Australian states require VAD applicants to have been given less than six to 12 months to live, though in the ACT there is no set timeframe for access.

The NT bill would also bar healthcare professionals from initiating conversations about VAD with patients — a so-called "gag clause" that has recently been overturned in Victoria.

Both of those clauses go against the recommendations of a report by a parliamentary inquiry, led by Dr Rahman, that was tabled in October last year.

Tanzil Rahman says his proposed amendments are consistent with best practice. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Dr Rahman's proposed amendments would dissolve the 12-month prognosis restriction and allow healthcare workers to initiate conversations about VAD if they believed a patient met eligibility requirements.

It would also prevent care facilities from refusing to provide information about VAD in residential settings.

Push to make telehealth available for assisted dying patients Despite voluntary assisted dying being legal in Victoria, many regional patients are not getting the same end-of-life care.

Dr Rahman said he was moving the amendments "in what I believe to be the best interest of Territorians, as a matter of conscience and consistent with best practice and scholarly evidence".

"[The amendments] provide terminally ill people with freer access to information about VAD, and greater freedom to choose VAD when they are clearly dying and suffering," he said.

He said he was pleased to be part of a government that was progressing VAD laws for NT residents and was doing so through a conscience vote.

Attorney-General Marie-Clare Boothby said the CLP believed in "the freedom for MLAs to speak and vote their conscience — to represent their communities".

Seniors advocacy group supports amendments

Council on the Ageing NT chief executive Sue Shearer said she supported the proposed amendments, but had other concerns about the legislation.

"If Dr Rahman can get it through that would be fantastic, but other than that we really don't want it delayed," she said.

"We just want it done and dusted. Territorians have waited since 1997 for this.

" How we control the end of our life is up to us and nobody else. "

Sue Shearer supports the amendments, but says her key concern is that the laws pass without further delays. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Ms Shearer said doctors could have conscientious objections to VAD, but that should not impact their patients.

"When they're dealing with a patient, they should be able to say at the end of this particular disease you have choices … that's just the logical way to do it," she said.

Ms Shearer said if the amendments failed to pass, she hoped the prognosis limit and gag clause would be looked at in a future review of the laws promised by the government.

World.title: Billy Slater to step down as Maroons' head coach
World.content:
Billy Slater will step down as head coach of the Maroons after five years in the role, Queensland Rugby League (QRL) has announced.

He will not return for the 2027 State of Origin series.

Slater began coaching the Queensland side in 2021, ahead of the 2022 series.

While he said the decision was not made lightly, the 43-year-old felt the time was right to step away.

"I want to thank the players, this group gave everything for the jersey, for each other and our State, and I'm proud of what we've built together," Slater said in a statement.

"And to my fellow Queenslanders, thank you for the trust you put in me to be our coach.

" Being a Queenslander has always been a huge part of who I am, and that will never change. "

QRL chair Brian Canavan thanked Slater for his contribution to the Maroons and the game in Queensland.

"His impact on our organisation and on Queenslanders everywhere will be felt long after his tenure as coach concludes," he said.

Queensland Rugby League said it would commence a process to appoint the next Maroons Head Coach in due course.

Slater coached the Maroons to victories in the 2022, 2023 and 2025 State of Origin series, while losing in 2024 and 2026.

The Maroons won eight State of Origin series while Slater was a member of the side between 2004-18. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

As a player, the Nambour-born Slater made his NRL debut for the Melbourne Storm in 2003 and stayed with the club until he retired in 2018.

He scored 190 tries for the Storm,, the third most in Australian first-grade rugby league history.

He also set the club's record for most tries and the NRL record for most tries by a fullback.

Slater represented Queensland in the State of Origin in 31 matches between 2004 and 2018, scoring 12 tries and winning eight Origin series.

He also played 30 times for Australia, making his international debut in 2008.

He was inducted into the National Rugby League Hall of Fame in 2024.

World.title: Colleagues condemn sex predator bishop after 'evil called out'
World.content:
Colleagues of disgraced Catholic Bishop Christopher Saunders, who was found guilty yesterday of sexually abusing young Aboriginal men in WA's remote north, have spoken of their relief at the verdict.

Saunders, 76, was found guilty of 13 counts of sexual abuse committed during his long tenure as Bishop of Broome.

Christopher Saunders leaving court after the fourth day of his trial on sexual assault allegations. (ABC News: David Weber)

Saunders, who worked in some of Australia's most remote Indigenous communities for about 40 years, was acquitted of six other charges.

He will be sentenced next month but remains a bishop, with no action taken by the Catholic Church to defrock him.

'Evil called out'

Former priest Matt Digges reported to Saunders for two decades and said the truth had been a long time coming.

"I was quite overwhelmed when I was driving yesterday afternoon and the news came through," he said.

"I had to pull over and just have a quiet moment, or more than a quiet moment, to just digest the information."

During the trial the court heard Saunders had suppled alcohol to vulnerable young men during "shirts off" parties he hosted.

Mr Digges thanked the victims for their honesty and courage in "allowing themselves to be on show and scrutinised".

"Those people have been targeted by others who didn't want the truth to come out," he said.

"An evil has been called out."

Matt Digges worked alongside Christopher Saunders in Broome. (ABC News: Claudia Jambor)

Reputational damage

Mr Digges condemned Saunders for damaging the Catholic church's reputation.

"Work that has been described as pastoral work is anything but — it was actually destruction of the pastoral basis of the work of the church in the Kimberley," he said.

Chris Bedding thanks the victims for coming forward. (ABC News: Ben Tessler)

The chief executive of the Faith Workers Alliance, which represents and supports religious workers nationwide, shared that sentiment.

"Bishops are supposed to be shepherds and not wolves," Chris Bedding said.

"The perpetrator's actions have brought disgrace upon his church and he's betrayed the people he was sent to serve."

Support for young people and families The Butterfly Foundation: National helpline 1800 ED HOPE (1800 33 4673), 8am-midnight (AEST/AEDT), 7 days a week

ReachOut Australia: Confidential online peer support for young people and online resources for wellbeing

Headspace: Centres in each state and territory or check out eheadspace for online support

The Kids Helpline: 24-hour support on 1800 55 1800

Lifeline: 24-hour support for all Australians on 13 11 14

Mr Bedding believes the verdict represents a moment of reckoning for the church.

"We have to expose disgusting behaviour when it occurs," he said.

"To the young men who exposed this disgraceful behaviour, I just want to say thank you.

"You were mistreated and harmed by someone who should have cared for you."

Father John Purnell, who helped Saunders's offending come to light by accompanying a young Indigenous man to a police station to make a statement, also praised the bravery of the victims.

"I'm so happy justice has been done and welcome the victims being believed," Father Purnell said.

"It's about the bravery of those young Indigenous men."

Bishop of Broome Tim Norton apologised to the victims and encouraged people to raise concerns.

"We are sorry for the shame they have endured," he said.

"We are sorry it has taken so long for their voices to be heard and for their pain to be acknowledged."

Saunders is in custody and is expected to appear in court again next month.

World.title: Ex-One Nation candidate 'sorry' for labelling gay people mentally ill
World.content:
A former One Nation candidate has apologised for describing gay people as having a mental illness, saying he was repeating something he "heard people saying on social media".

Parminder Singh, who ran for an upper house seat in Western Australia's 2025 state election, and was campaigning for the party in the current Secret Harbour by-election, made homophobic comments in a video interview posted by Perth comedian and content creator Jasky Singh, better known as Mr Sikkant.

When asked if he thought people were born gay, he responded "no, no, it's a mental illness".

"No-one born anything … I blame on the parents because parents are too busy," he said.

Loading...

Mr Singh has walked back his comments after One Nation leader Pauline Hanson distanced herself from his comments and said she did not share his views.

"I'm sorry I hurt people," he said in a statement.

"I was repeating something I had heard people saying on social media about homosexuality being a mental illness.

"I should not have presented that as a fact. I respect everyone, and I believe every person in Australia should be free to live their life with dignity, equality and respect."

Failed One Nation candidate makes homophobic comments A failed One Nation candidate in WA describes gay people as having a mental illness in an offensive new video posted on social media.

In the video, when Mr Singh was asked how gay people participating in parades affected him personally, he said it was an "" to young people.

He stood by those comments in his statement.

"I respect everyone, I accept everyone, I just do not like the  and this education in primary school," he said.

"I told [Mr Sikkant] not to publish this, it is a wrong presentation of me."

One Nation Leader Pauline Hanson was quick to distance herslf from Mr Singh's comments. (Facebook: Parminder.Singh.WA)

Jasky Singh told the ABC drafts of the full interview were provided to Parminder Singh prior to being published, and he did not request anything be removed.

However, he said some of the videos had since been taken down from the Mr Sikkant social media channels as he was mindful of how the saga had impacted Mr Singh and his family.

Political backlash

Parminder Singh was number three on One Nation WA's Legislative Council ticket at the 2025 state election but was not elected.

Mr Singh's profile was removed from the party's website following media reporting of his comments.

Rod Caddies responded to Mr Singh's comments outside parliament this week. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

One Nation WA leader Rod Caddies said on Thursday the interview did not reflect the views of the party and said gay people deserved to feel "equal in society".

But WA Labor minister John Carey, who is openly gay, said he was not surprised by Mr Singh's comments because One Nation had a history of preselecting candidates with similar views.

"This is not the exception. This is the norm in One Nation. When you're a party based on extreme issues, extreme views, that peddle hatred, no wonder that you collect candidates that are vile like this," he said.

World.title: Four dead after record-breaking heavy rain inundates Japan
World.content:
At least four people died in eastern Japan after heavy rain that left thousands stranded at one of Tokyo's main airports overnight and inundated roads and railways, authorities said on Friday.

The torrential downpours late on Thursday triggered landslide warnings and power outages, with forecasters issuing the highest-level heavy rain warning for the Chiba region for the first time.

Those killed included a man in his 60s or 70s found floating on a flooded road and a 66-year-old woman stuck in her submerged car, the Chiba Prefecture Disaster Management Office said.

Roads were flooded in Oamishirasato, Chiba Prefecture after torrential rainfall. (AP: Kota Endo/Kyodo News)

The third fatality was a man of unknown age found collapsed on the street and the fourth a person of undetermined gender and age.

A fifth person was feared dead and a sixth unaccounted-for.

More than 360 millimetres of rain fell in 24 hours in parts of Chiba Prefecture, which adjoins the capital Tokyo, inundating roads and railways ‌during one of Japan's busiest holiday weeks.

Heavy rain flooded the city of Sakura in Chiba Prefecture. (Reuters: Kyodo)

Record-breaking rainfall of 115mm fell in just one hour in Chiba city and 97mm fell in one hour in Sakura, also a record for that city.

The Japan Meteorological Agency downgraded its most severe warning for heavy rain in more than a dozen municipalities in Chiba Prefecture as rain subsided on Friday morning but forecast more rain later in the day.

Photos and television footage showed widespread damage after daylight, with homes, cars and parts of railway tracks flooded with muddy water.

"This case was an extremely unusual situation," Chiba Governor Toshihito Kumagai told reporters on Friday morning.

"I have responded to many disasters in the past, but I have never experienced a case like this."

Typhoon Dolphin hits Japan's Okinawa Typhoon Dolphin has lashed Japan's southern islands of Okinawa and turned toward China.

Hundreds of people were left stranded in Chiba station due to suspended train services.

"This happened all of a sudden so it was a complete surprise. The power is out so I'm worried whether I can open my business in the next couple of days," a woman in Chiba's Ichikawa city told NHK on Thursday.

In Chiba city, hundreds of people ⁠spent the night under foil blankets at government ‌buildings serving as temporary evacuation ‌centres.

As of Friday morning, more than 26,000 households across Chiba Prefecture were without power, the disaster management office said.

Japan's Ground Self-Defense Force also said it dispatched buses to pick up about 4,000 stranded people who stayed overnight at the Soga train station, a local route that also serves Tokyo Disney. The theme park did not report any damage.

Passengers stranded at major Tokyo airport

The transport disruption left about 7,000 people stranded at Narita International Airport, one of two main airports serving Tokyo, however all flights were scheduled to operate normally on Friday, an airport spokesperson said.

Japan Airlines said some flights may experience delays but no cancellations were expected.

Many trains to and from the airport were cancelled until Friday afternoon, the Chiba disaster office said.

Passengers at Narita International Airport were stranded due to heavy rain. (Reuters: Kyodo)

Users on social media said that airport staff handed out free water, food and sleeping bags.

"I never thought I'd spend the night at the airport but it is what it is and we are learning," one stranded air traveller told Japanese broadcaster NHK.

"We're never going to forget this trip," he said.

AFP/AP/Reuters

World.title: Teenager charged over $2m fire that destroyed multiple Melbourne shops
World.content:
A 16-year-old boy has been charged over a fire that caused $2 million worth of damage to a retail strip in inner Melbourne last month.

An alleged stolen car was used to ram a convenience store on Victoria Street, on the border of Abbotsford and Richmond, in the early hours of July 6.

The shop was then set alight, with the fire spreading through up to adjoining businesses.

Two women living in one of the businesses were forced to flee the fire.

Police at the time said the offenders fled on foot.

Dozens of firefigther battled the blaze through the early hours of the morning. (ABC News)

It took 80 firefighters an hour and a half to bring the fire under control.

Fire Rescue Victoria said up to 10 businesses were impacted by the fire.

The street was cordoned off for much of the day, with store owners unable to get in to check on their properties.

Detectives today arrested the teenager and charged him with arson, reckless conduct endangering life and car theft.

He has been remanded in custody to appear at a children's court at a later date.

World.title: Expired sample tubes at the centre of trainer’s EPO ban appeal
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Expired sample tubes at the centre of trainer’s EPO ban appeal Craig Kerry August 14, 2026 — 5:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Gosford trainer Greg McFarlane is determined to fight “all the way” to overturn a two-and-a-half-year disqualification for an erythropoietin (EPO) positive, basing his appeal on the fact expired blood collection tubes were used in the test. McFarlane, who has two runners at Rosehill on Saturday, was handed the penalty on August 7 for the out-of-competition test on mare Bremel in February 2025. He lodged an appeal and was granted a stay of proceedings on the same day. He is still waiting for a date to be set for that hearing. Trainer Greg McFarlane (right) plans to fight his looming ban. Getty Images EPO, identified by the presence of peptides fragments VYSNFLR and SLTTLLR in Bremel’s test result, stimulates bone marrow production of red blood cells and is considered a prohibited list A substance. McFarlane pleaded not guilty to the EPO charge and another of having a container not labelled properly at his stables. He was fined $300 for the labelling error and $600 for having inaccurate treatment records. EPO was not found during inspections of McFarlane’s stables.



He said he and his legal team were shocked when they looked into the evidence and found expired collection tubes had been used in the Bremel swab. “The black and white of it is we’ve appealed the decision and the appeal challenges the evidence, including the use of expired blood collection tubes when the out-of-competition test was taken,” McFarlane said. “Using expired tubes is significant, and we maintain therefore that the evidence does not sustain the charge. Expired blood collection tubes are not to be used in anti-doping testing for a number of reasons. There are numerous standards and regulations worldwide to prevent the use of expired blood collection tubes.” A Racing NSW source confirmed to the Herald that the blood collection tubes were past their expiry date, but stewards, after hearing expert evidence, believed that this would not have affected the results. In handing down the disqualification, stewards took McFarlane’s disciplinary record, “which included prior like offences” into account. McFarlane served a two-year ban in 2013-15 after he was caught stomach-tubing a horse at Rosehill.



The former track cyclist, who won the Melbourne Cup on Wheels race in 2003 before moving into thoroughbred training, said the case was “going to be fought all the way”. He has 22 horses in work at Gosford, where he has been for seven years. “It’s very difficult for business because it’s not just yourself,” McFarlane said. “It’s owners and everyone else who don’t know where they stand. We know the facts, and that’s the way we are proceeding.” Meanwhile, McFarlane is focused on getting wins on the track. Bremel raced at Canterbury on Wednesday and finished seventh, and he has Kosuke and Sandbi running at Rosehill on Saturday. Sandbi, a winner on debut at Gosford before a sixth at Canterbury, was $26 for race two, a 1300m benchmark 72 handicap for three-year-olds. Kosuke ($71) is resuming the Midway handicap to start the day. “Sandbi is a nice horse,” said McFarlane, who has 197 career winners.



“It’s a typical race this time of the year. They are generally smaller fields and it will be a bit of a mixed bag with the field, so we’ll have a go at it and then he’ll go for a spell and come back a much improved horse from this. “Kosuke, he’ll be starting off. We were tossing up between Newcastle and Rosehill, but it was much of a muchness, and I thought 1500m with the lesser weight was the way to go. But he will better when he gets up over distance.” Up-and-coming talent has Wong excited Hawkesbury trainer Tommy Wong expects unbeaten colt Hostwin King to be competitive when he tackles stakes grade on Saturday in the listed Rosebud (1100m), and then maybe even better when he steps out a second time. Hostwin King, a $210,000 yearling buy for Hong Kong investor Jason Tam, came from midfield to win a 1000m two-year-old maiden on debut at Kembla before racing on speed in a half-length victory at Canterbury at 1200m.



The son of King’s Legacy steps up again when he takes on the likes of group winners Blue Door ($3.60) and Chilly Girl ($6.50), and promising colts Castillo King and Central Europe ($4.60). Wong is chasing a first black-type career victory with the $34 chance. Ash Morgan has the ride. “He’s running against group horses, so it’s a challenge,” Wong said. “If he’s good, then we go one level up. The next step is the Up And Coming over 1300, which could suit him better. According to the pedigree, he could run a bit further. “But we go step by step, there’s no rush. The horse will tell you.



“He’s still a colt but not colty at all, and eating well, doing well, but obviously we are racing with the more expensive horses and big stables. “But we’ve got a good jockey on, barrier six, and we’re only carrying 54 kilos, so he should be competitive.” He said Hostwin King is already one of the better horses he’s trained. Wong came to Australia from Hong Kong in 1991 and has been training full-time since 2001. “This is one which is a bit exciting for us, a small stable,” he said. “We have 30 on the books, but a lot of them are young ones, breaking in, spelling and just turning over.



“This is the first horse I’ve had with Jason, but I’ve known him for a long time, but in those days, his horses were going to Gary Moore and his son. Last year we met at the sales and we bought this one. “On paper, we had selected, with the help of Inglis, 10. This one passed the vet check, he had good confirmation, but we nearly lost it. Somebody wanted to bid up to $200,000, and Jason wanted to stop there, but Jason’s wife raised her hand. ‘One more time’, she said, and we got it.”

World.title: Trump is steering America towards a financial crisis
World.content:
BusinessThe economyTrump's America Opinion Trump is steering America towards a financial crisis

Ambrose Evans-Pritchard August 14, 2026 — 5:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A dangerous view is creeping into the markets that the US has already gone so far down the path of a debt compound trap that it dare not raise interest rates to control inflation. The US Treasury has become acutely dependent on short-term funding from hedge funds, many tapping the $US8.3 trillion ($11.6 trillion) money market and some operating with up to 100 times leverage. The share of purchases coming from stable lenders, such as foreign central banks and sovereign wealth funds, has been drying up. US federal debt is soaring under Donald Trump. Evan Vucci/Pool Reuters via AP Steven Blitz, the chief US economist at TS Lombard, says the Federal Reserve cannot tighten hard without risking a chain reaction. Financing costs would “explode”. “Raising rates today immediately impacts the cost of nearly 25 per cent of the federal debt, where issuance is growing fastest,” he said.



Related Article Opinion

Federal Reserve Meddler-in-chief: Trump is up to his old tricks again Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The US Treasury has to roll over $US6 trillion of debt every three months in an increasingly sceptical market, as well as issuing $US2 trillion of new debt annually to cover the worst structural deficit in US peacetime history. Annual gross financing needs – the key warning metric watched by rating agencies and bond funds – was 26 per cent of GDP in 2010. The International Monetary Fund says the figure will reach 45 per cent this year and is on track for 60 per cent by the early 2030s on current policies. No great power has long endured at that sort of level. Scott Bessent, the poacher-turned-gamekeeper now in charge of the US Treasury, has been concentrating ever more borrowing on short-term bills. It is a way to keep a lid on the spiralling interest cost of the US national debt, which has quadrupled to $US1 trillion in a decade, now exceeds the US defence budget and is fast heading towards uncharted waters above 4 per cent of GDP. But trying to defer America’s fiscal reckoning by monkeying with debt instruments is the trick used by broken hegemons through the ages. It is a Faustian pact.



We know how worried Bessent is about soaring bond yields – approaching a two-decade high – by the way he intervened alongside Japan earlier this month to halt speculation against the yen. He activated an obscure mechanism known as the FIMA Repo Facility to let Japan pawn a chunk of its $US1.1 trillion of US Treasuries in exchange for dollar loans rather than selling these bonds on the open market. He joined the action by mobilising the Treasury’s holding of euros, without first telling the European Central Bank – a shocking breakdown of central bank etiquette. All this screams desperation. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been trying to keep a lid on the spiralling interest cost of the US national debt by concentrating ever more borrowing on short-term bills. Bloomberg Hedge funds have become the marginal buyers of US debt, doubling their share to 9 per cent of total US Treasury purchases over the past four years. They have been borrowing with extreme leverage on the repo market – a core part of financial plumbing – in order to extract arbitrage gains. Both the IMF and the Bank for International Settlements have warned that this structure is an accident waiting to happen. It amplified a spiral of forced selling and a near meltdown of the US Treasury market in the COVID panic of March 2020. The critical point is that the whole US financial and fiscal system has never been so sensitive to short-term interest rates.



Related Article Opinion

Japan Why fears of a Japanese implosion have the world on edge Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Kevin Warsh, the untested new Fed chairman, faces an invidious choice. The indecent manner of his appointment degraded his credibility before he even started. Markets know that President Donald Trump persecuted his predecessor for refusing to cut rates and refusing to become the infamous Arthur Burns of our age. They also know that Warsh’s billionaire father-in-law is a close Trump confederate and a key author of the Greenland grab. Warsh struggled to articulate a coherent intellectual argument after the most recent policy meeting for why he was not raising rates. He could not explain how he intends to bring stubborn US inflation back towards the 2 per cent target when it is clearly going the other way. “Sternly staring at inflation until it melts before our withering gaze is not an option,” fellow Fed board member Christopher Waller said. Warsh faced the unusual rebuke of three voting dissenters and some have been outspoken to the point of contempt. The market verdict has been lapidary.



Warsh argues that AI is deflationary and therefore overrides the Phillips Curve, making it possible to combine blistering growth with low inflation. I am friendly to this line of thinking, but it is not entirely convincing coming from Warsh, who used to be a chest-beating “inflation nutter”. Many suspect that he has latched on to this idea as a pretext for doing Trump’s bidding. Reports that he talks to Trump “all the time” confirm the fears. Previous Fed chairman Jerome Powell’s working code was always that the proper level of intercourse between the US president and the Fed chairman is “zero”. Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh struggled to articulate a coherent intellectual argument after the most recent policy meeting for why he was not raising rates. Bloomberg The Dornbusch adage in the markets is that fiscal and financial crises take longer to happen than you think possible but then happen faster than you ever imagined. We know that US federal debt is compounding at a rate of 3.5 per cent of GDP each year. The mechanical rise in entitlements – ie, middle-class welfare – has been part of the landscape for a long time. Trump 1.0 tax cuts, COVID and Joe Biden’s Rooseveltian New Deal together pushed the envelope a lot further. Trump 2.0’s One Big, Beautiful Bill tests the limits.



Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war Trump’s great humiliation: Middle East may be entering a post-American era Peter Hartcher Political and international editor The IMF forecasts a US general government deficit of 7.4 per cent of GDP or higher every single year from 2026 to 2031. Now Trump wants to raise the Pentagon budget by 60 per cent and fritter away $275 billion on his “golden fleet” of Trump-class battleships – an idée fixe ever since he watched the 1950s telly series Victory at Sea. It takes a serious trigger to detonate a crisis of financial confidence in a great power with deep economic strengths and a world reserve currency. Military overstretch is usually to blame, the cause of imperial Spain’s default in 1575 and Britain’s convertibility crisis in 1947. The ingredients for some sort of American financial crisis are falling into place, disguised for now – but also compounded – by the AI bubble. The global market no longer has full faith in the management of the US Treasury and the Fed. The Dornbusch adage in the markets is that fiscal and financial crises take longer to happen than you think possible but then happen faster than you ever imagined.



The US has stopped upholding free trade and open navigation, switching sides to become the chief instigator of piracy and world disorder. It has squandered much of its arsenal on an ill-planned war that it cannot end without accepting humiliation and that has shown the US to be a weaker military power than we all thought. It has further wrecked US alliances and largely played into the hands of Xi Jinping’s revanchist China. The disaster is nearly complete. Now we await the US midterm elections. Should the democratic transfer of power in Congress be obstructed by meddling with the results in swing states, we may have our trigger.
