World.title: I’ve flown planes into Sydney more than 1000 times. These near-misses don’t surprise me
World.content:
NationalAviation Opinion I’ve flown planes into Sydney more than 1000 times. These near-misses don’t surprise me David Evans Former Qantas captain August 14, 2026 — 5:08pm

August 14, 2026 — 5:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After almost five decades in the aviation business flying to all corners of the globe, I can assure you that some of the most complicated parts of any journey are not the actual flying but the taxiing to and from a busy runway. I was the captain of an A380 lined up on a runway on the north complex of Los Angles (LAX) waiting for my take-off clearance when another aircraft landing on the parallel runway turned off and crossed the runway I was lined up on. As that “intruder” aircraft entered my runway all the lights on the ground in front of me turned bright red, leaving me in no doubt it was unsafe to take off. In this example, no one was at fault as I had not yet received my take-off clearance and air traffic control (ATC) had cleared the other aircraft to cross in front of me. But I was grateful for the automated back-up system just in case a super-busy human made a mistake. By all reports, it was the pilots of the Virgin 737 who saw the Qantas 737 crossing the runway it had been cleared to take off on last Sunday. Michael Howard I have flown into and out of Sydney Airport 1055 times according to my logbook, and I have to say the system of monitoring ground movement of aircraft, on active runways and taxiways, is not as good as I’ve seen in places like LAX. By all reports, it was the pilots of the Virgin 737 who saw the Qantas 737 crossing the runway it had been cleared to take off on last Sunday – the third incident in recent weeks. But what if they hadn’t, or there was low visibility?



Almost all aspects of modern aviation are standardised, from departure to climb out to cruise, and then descent and approach to land. Doesn’t matter if it’s Sydney, London or New York. All aspects of the flying sequence have become standardised to such an extent that – barring weather or unforseen circumstances – a pilot follows a very prescribed procedure. Those daring young men and women in their non-flying machines at air traffic control co-ordinate this aerial ballet to achieve a safe standard of separation between aircraft. It’s a complex task, so to help human air traffic controllers, modern ATC systems have various electronic alerts to warn if safety standards are compromised or if an error has brought aircraft too close together. Flightradar24 shows the latest near miss to be made public: The Virgin 737 is beginning its take-off as the Qantas 737 crosses runway 34L at Sydney Airport. Flightradar24 What’s not standardised is the airport complex itself. Every airport is different and some are way more complicated than others. On the ground, an airport is usually divided into two distinct parts – runways and taxiways. Any movement on or in the vicinity of an active runway is managed by a controller on an ATC Tower frequency. To add a little more complexity, in Sydney’s case there are two Sydney Tower controllers for each of Sydney’s parallel runways. Conversely, aircraft moving around the taxiways are under the control of another ATC group known as Surface Movement Control. Those in charge of ATC ground movement also have a separate radio frequency and go by the call sign of Sydney Ground. As there are separate parts of the airport and radio congestion increases with an increase in traffic movement, those roles can be divided into more than one ground frequency.



To get from the terminal to your take-off runway or from your landing back to the terminal, a pilot may need to speak to up to four or five different ATC individuals. All these controllers must co-ordinate with one another as your aircraft may have to cross active runways and avoid other aircraft trying to do the same thing. Related Article Aviation Virgin plane aborts take-off as Qantas plane crosses Sydney runway Added to the mix are aircraft under tow, which we saw in the case of the second near-miss at Sydney, with a Qatar 777 almost colliding with a Jetstar A320. Sometimes an aircraft needs to move from a terminal gate to some other place on the airport complex. This could be to a maintenance hangar or to a remote parking space, as the aircraft may have a long layover before its next flight. The tug driver is a highly skilled and trained person who is also in contact with ATC and is required to follow ATC instructions when on the move. If it all sounds ridiculously complex, that’s because it is. When an aircraft is airborne, there is a collision avoidance system that provides an audible warning if a plane is on a collision course with another aircraft. Three near-misses in recent weeks at Sydney Airport are also audible warning that it’s time to take a better look at the collision avoidance systems we have on the ground. Yes, lots of air traffic controllers were laid off during COVID, and experience is hard to replace. But in an industry like aviation, redundancies need to be factored in after redundancies take place, for the safety of everyone involved.



As our Australian airspace continues to expand and congestion at our major airports increases, it’s time for CASA to investigate this type of safety system to help aid those hard-working and understaffed air traffic controllers who do a damn fine job under difficult circumstances, where the cost of a mistake is catastrophe. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge threat letter included sender’s real name
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge threat letter included sender’s real name Lachlan Abbott August 14, 2026 — 5:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A man has admitted to sending Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge a threatening letter demanding $100,000 on a hotel bill with his real name on the back. Brendon Berry, 54, pleaded guilty to sending the menacing letter, which was sent to Beveridge’s home last year. Beveridge says he has never met Berry, nor heard of him until the letter. Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge. AFL Photos via Getty Images Melbourne Magistrates’ Court heard on Friday that Beveridge was “shocked and angry” when he opened the letter, which referenced the Moran crime family, after he returned from an interstate trip on June 28, 2025. Prosecutor Andrew McCowan said the letter did not detail specific threats, but insinuated them, prompting extra security for Beveridge at an AFL match against North Melbourne.



“No one likes a hero or a liar. Now you know you have done a bad thing. Do yourself a favour and for once in your life do the right thing, pay what you owe,” the letter said, according to a summary read out in court. “No tomorrow, and this is it. I’m no f---wit pal and it’s hurt me like the Moran’s [sic] hurt Carl. If you think life is a joke it’s not. No second chance my friend, take stock.” Brendon Berry outside court on Friday. Lachlan Abbott The letter, which Berry’s defence lawyer conceded was “unsophisticated”, then referenced late Collingwood footballer Darren Millane, who died in a car crash in 1991. “P.S. Darren Millane, do you remember a fair dusting-off wasn’t it. How many chances do you want. No more.”



Beveridge’s victim impact statement made it clear he did not feel sufficiently intimidated to comply with the demand to pay $100,000 into Berry’s bank account. “I found it deeply disturbing that a person who did not know me could be so callous as to strike fear into everyone close to me in my life,” Beveridge’s statement said. “The letter triggered a side of me that I now know is there if I’m ever threatened like this again.” Getty Images “What frustrated me most was the disregard shown for the impact such a letter could have … it almost sent me down a vigilante-thinking track.” Beveridge added: “The letter triggered a side of me that I now know is there if I’m ever threatened like this again.”



Beveridge initially tuned into the hearing on Friday morning but was not present on an online link in the afternoon when the matter was eventually called. Defence lawyer Katie Powell said the letter was “unsophisticated” and “inexplicable” as Berry was unable to provide much reason about why he sent it. Magistrate Siobhan Whittle then intervened to add: “That’s why it has such a chilling quality.” Powell said Berry believed he went to school with Beveridge in the 1980s, but this was disputed by the Western Bulldogs coach. “He realises, of course, that he should not have sent that letter,” Powell said, adding: “It had nothing to do with Mr Beveridge’s occupation as a public figure.”



The court heard Berry had a notable criminal history, including being jailed for an aggravated burglary with a firearm, but had stayed out of trouble since his last sentence in 2014. His defence lawyer said he was an Aboriginal man with mental health troubles who had been unemployed for much of his adult life. “At this point, I’m concerned about the factors that have driven this offending which are something unresolved from your client’s perspective,” Whittle said. “At this point, I’m going to have him assessed for a community corrections order [CCO] with a mental health appointment.” Berry remained silent for much of the hearing, apart from letting out a loud sigh and assuring the magistrate he would “absolutely” co-operate when he was assessed for a CCO.



Berry will return to court next Thursday to hear his sentence for one count of using a postal service to menace and one count of failing to answer bail. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: A $60b GST fiasco: State vs state argument erupts between WA and ‘east coast whingers’
World.content:
PoliticsFederalGST A $60b GST fiasco: State vs state argument erupts between WA and ‘east coast whingers’ Shane Wright Updated August 14, 2026 — 5:02pm ,first published 2:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An interstate argument has erupted over revelations that the system that carves-up the GST is so broken that a bushfire in NSW would deliver a multimillion-dollar financial windfall to Western Australia, with accusations “east coasters” are whingers and that WA has become a petrostate. A scathing interim report by the Productivity Commission into the GST allocation system put in place by Scott Morrison in 2018 labels the deal a “mistake” that could end up costing federal taxpayers up to $12 billion a year or more than is spent on the nation’s air force. A bushfire in NSW would lead to extra revenue for Western Australia under the “perverse” GST deal. Getty Images As revealed by this masthead, the commission found the current allocation system is on track to cost federal taxpayers up to $60 billion and is failing all of its key objectives while making the annual GST carve-up less equitable and more complex. The 2018 deal was put in place after a collapse in Western Australia’s share of the GST despite the state being in a domestic recession caused by the end of the decade’s mining boom.



Morrison, the then treasurer, came up with a new system that topped up Western Australia’s share until it received the equivalent of 75¢ for every dollar of GST notionally raised by the state. It would then change to the current system, where no jurisdiction can get a smaller share of each dollar raised than either NSW or Victoria. A “no-worse-off” guarantee was put in place, which has been extended by the Albanese government, to 2030, that ensures the GST of every other state and territory is not reduced. The Productivity Commission report, delivered to the nation’s treasurers on Friday, found the 2018 deal had effectively created a two-tier GST allocation system where only one state – Western Australia – got ahead. Commission deputy chair Alex Robson said the GST system was meant to deliver each state and territory enough cash so they could provide similar levels of services and infrastructure to their residents.



Instead, the 2018 reforms had undermined that principle while also not working as the Morrison government had expected. Related Article Analysis

GST Please sir … don’t give WA any more money “The 2018 changes tried to achieve too much and moved too far away from the system’s core objective,” he said. “The result is a system that is now more complex, less consistent and more costly.” The commission found the 2018 changes created perverse outcomes, almost all of which benefit Western Australia at the expense of the rest of the federation and federal taxpayers.



Commissioner Angela Jackson said under the pre-2018 system, if NSW suffered a substantial bushfire, then it would receive extra GST to deal with the disaster’s impact. That extra money would come from every other state and territory. But that has been upended by a “perverse” system under which NSW’s share of the GST is a floor, below which no other state or territory’s share of the tax can fall. That means Western Australia gains a windfall from a NSW disaster while the government of NSW would receive slightly less. West Australian Premier Roger Cook and Treasurer Rita Saffioti launched a campaign to protect the GST deal. WAtoday “Under the current system, if NSW is hit by a natural disaster and spends money on the recovery, it receives more GST to reflect its increased need,” she said. “But under the standard state benchmark, Western Australia also receives more GST from the other states, for a natural disaster it didn’t have.”



Victoria could end up in the same position as NSW if, as expected, its share of GST declines over the next few years. Not only is Western Australia better off from a NSW bushfire, an increase in the price of iron ore – which would previously be shared among the rest of the federation – means it could keep the windfall from higher mining royalties and enjoy an increase in the GST pool. If iron ore prices, currently around $US95 a tonne, were to climb towards $US200 a tonne, then the annual cost to federal taxpayers of not leaving states and territories worse off would reach $12 billion. The 2018 system has delivered Western Australia so much extra revenue that the federal government would have to find $47 billion this year to share with every other jurisdiction to match WA’s financial position. The Productivity Commission, however, has offered three possible changes. They include returning to the pre-2018 system but with the federal treasurer able to direct the Commonwealth Grants Commission, which calculates the annual GST carve-up, to take into account situations where a single state may have a dominant financial position in a particular part of the economy.



Related Article Opinion

GST The GST is broken, and hurting NSW and Victoria badly Shane Wright Senior economics correspondent Another option is to return to the pre-2018 system with the federal government then making direct grants to WA to offset its small share of the GST. WA Premier Roger Cook lambasted the report’s findings, saying it was an assault on his state receiving its fair of the GST which needed the cash to continue to be the nation’s economic engine room. He labelled all other premiers and chief ministers who want the system to change as “east coast whingers”. But NSW Premier Chris Minns said every other state and territory needed a fair share of the GST, likening WA’s demands to the behaviour of a petrostate.



“We’re now in a situation where WA is so wealthy and so rich they are competing and bidding on NSW rugby league games and putting tens of millions of dollars on the table,” he said. “You’re seeing similar behaviour from Gulf states like Saudi Arabia and the UAE and Dubai, and almost for the same reason because they’re digging up natural resources and they’ve got billions of dollars to spend.” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese reassured West Australians they would continue to get a “fair deal”, while the Liberal Party also vowed to protect the 2018 arrangement. The commission plans to hold hearings into its interim report through September, with a final report due by year’s end. Independent economist Saul Eslake, a long-time critic of the Morrison deal, said the commission’s recommendations were a test for both the government and opposition if they believed in protecting the federal budget. World.title: Expired sample tubes at the centre of trainer’s EPO ban appeal
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Expired sample tubes at the centre of trainer’s EPO ban appeal Craig Kerry August 14, 2026 — 5:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Gosford trainer Greg McFarlane is determined to fight “all the way” to overturn a two-and-a-half-year disqualification for an erythropoietin (EPO) positive, basing his appeal on the fact expired blood collection tubes were used in the test. McFarlane, who has two runners at Rosehill on Saturday, was handed the penalty on August 7 for the out-of-competition test on mare Bremel in February 2025. He lodged an appeal and was granted a stay of proceedings on the same day. He is still waiting for a date to be set for that hearing. Trainer Greg McFarlane (right) plans to fight his looming ban. Getty Images EPO, identified by the presence of peptides fragments VYSNFLR and SLTTLLR in Bremel’s test result, stimulates bone marrow production of red blood cells and is considered a prohibited list A substance. McFarlane pleaded not guilty to the EPO charge and another of having a container not labelled properly at his stables. He was fined $300 for the labelling error and $600 for having inaccurate treatment records. EPO was not found during inspections of McFarlane’s stables.



He said he and his legal team were shocked when they looked into the evidence and found expired collection tubes had been used in the Bremel swab. “The black and white of it is we’ve appealed the decision and the appeal challenges the evidence, including the use of expired blood collection tubes when the out-of-competition test was taken,” McFarlane said. “Using expired tubes is significant, and we maintain therefore that the evidence does not sustain the charge. Expired blood collection tubes are not to be used in anti-doping testing for a number of reasons. There are numerous standards and regulations worldwide to prevent the use of expired blood collection tubes.” A Racing NSW source confirmed to the Herald that the blood collection tubes were past their expiry date, but stewards, after hearing expert evidence, believed that this would not have affected the results. In handing down the disqualification, stewards took McFarlane’s disciplinary record, “which included prior like offences” into account. McFarlane served a two-year ban in 2013-15 after he was caught stomach-tubing a horse at Rosehill.



The former track cyclist, who won the Melbourne Cup on Wheels race in 2003 before moving into thoroughbred training, said the case was “going to be fought all the way”. He has 22 horses in work at Gosford, where he has been for seven years. “It’s very difficult for business because it’s not just yourself,” McFarlane said. “It’s owners and everyone else who don’t know where they stand. We know the facts, and that’s the way we are proceeding.” Meanwhile, McFarlane is focused on getting wins on the track. Bremel raced at Canterbury on Wednesday and finished seventh, and he has Kosuke and Sandbi running at Rosehill on Saturday. Sandbi, a winner on debut at Gosford before a sixth at Canterbury, was $26 for race two, a 1300m benchmark 72 handicap for three-year-olds. Kosuke ($71) is resuming the Midway handicap to start the day. “Sandbi is a nice horse,” said McFarlane, who has 197 career winners.



“It’s a typical race this time of the year. They are generally smaller fields and it will be a bit of a mixed bag with the field, so we’ll have a go at it and then he’ll go for a spell and come back a much improved horse from this. “Kosuke, he’ll be starting off. We were tossing up between Newcastle and Rosehill, but it was much of a muchness, and I thought 1500m with the lesser weight was the way to go. But he will better when he gets up over distance.” Up-and-coming talent has Wong excited Hawkesbury trainer Tommy Wong expects unbeaten colt Hostwin King to be competitive when he tackles stakes grade on Saturday in the listed Rosebud (1100m), and then maybe even better when he steps out a second time. Hostwin King, a $210,000 yearling buy for Hong Kong investor Jason Tam, came from midfield to win a 1000m two-year-old maiden on debut at Kembla before racing on speed in a half-length victory at Canterbury at 1200m.



The son of King’s Legacy steps up again when he takes on the likes of group winners Blue Door ($3.60) and Chilly Girl ($6.50), and promising colts Castillo King and Central Europe ($4.60). Wong is chasing a first black-type career victory with the $34 chance. Ash Morgan has the ride. “He’s running against group horses, so it’s a challenge,” Wong said. “If he’s good, then we go one level up. The next step is the Up And Coming over 1300, which could suit him better. According to the pedigree, he could run a bit further. “But we go step by step, there’s no rush. The horse will tell you.



“He’s still a colt but not colty at all, and eating well, doing well, but obviously we are racing with the more expensive horses and big stables. “But we’ve got a good jockey on, barrier six, and we’re only carrying 54 kilos, so he should be competitive.” He said Hostwin King is already one of the better horses he’s trained. Wong came to Australia from Hong Kong in 1991 and has been training full-time since 2001. “This is one which is a bit exciting for us, a small stable,” he said. “We have 30 on the books, but a lot of them are young ones, breaking in, spelling and just turning over.



“This is the first horse I’ve had with Jason, but I’ve known him for a long time, but in those days, his horses were going to Gary Moore and his son. Last year we met at the sales and we bought this one. “On paper, we had selected, with the help of Inglis, 10. This one passed the vet check, he had good confirmation, but we nearly lost it. Somebody wanted to bid up to $200,000, and Jason wanted to stop there, but Jason’s wife raised her hand. ‘One more time’, she said, and we got it.”

World.title: Trump is steering America towards a financial crisis
World.content:
BusinessThe economyTrump's America Opinion Trump is steering America towards a financial crisis

Ambrose Evans-Pritchard August 14, 2026 — 5:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A dangerous view is creeping into the markets that the US has already gone so far down the path of a debt compound trap that it dare not raise interest rates to control inflation. The US Treasury has become acutely dependent on short-term funding from hedge funds, many tapping the $US8.3 trillion ($11.6 trillion) money market and some operating with up to 100 times leverage. The share of purchases coming from stable lenders, such as foreign central banks and sovereign wealth funds, has been drying up. US federal debt is soaring under Donald Trump. Evan Vucci/Pool Reuters via AP Steven Blitz, the chief US economist at TS Lombard, says the Federal Reserve cannot tighten hard without risking a chain reaction. Financing costs would “explode”. “Raising rates today immediately impacts the cost of nearly 25 per cent of the federal debt, where issuance is growing fastest,” he said.



Related Article Opinion

Federal Reserve Meddler-in-chief: Trump is up to his old tricks again Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The US Treasury has to roll over $US6 trillion of debt every three months in an increasingly sceptical market, as well as issuing $US2 trillion of new debt annually to cover the worst structural deficit in US peacetime history. Annual gross financing needs – the key warning metric watched by rating agencies and bond funds – was 26 per cent of GDP in 2010. The International Monetary Fund says the figure will reach 45 per cent this year and is on track for 60 per cent by the early 2030s on current policies. No great power has long endured at that sort of level. Scott Bessent, the poacher-turned-gamekeeper now in charge of the US Treasury, has been concentrating ever more borrowing on short-term bills. It is a way to keep a lid on the spiralling interest cost of the US national debt, which has quadrupled to $US1 trillion in a decade, now exceeds the US defence budget and is fast heading towards uncharted waters above 4 per cent of GDP. But trying to defer America’s fiscal reckoning by monkeying with debt instruments is the trick used by broken hegemons through the ages. It is a Faustian pact.



We know how worried Bessent is about soaring bond yields – approaching a two-decade high – by the way he intervened alongside Japan earlier this month to halt speculation against the yen. He activated an obscure mechanism known as the FIMA Repo Facility to let Japan pawn a chunk of its $US1.1 trillion of US Treasuries in exchange for dollar loans rather than selling these bonds on the open market. He joined the action by mobilising the Treasury’s holding of euros, without first telling the European Central Bank – a shocking breakdown of central bank etiquette. All this screams desperation. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been trying to keep a lid on the spiralling interest cost of the US national debt by concentrating ever more borrowing on short-term bills. Bloomberg Hedge funds have become the marginal buyers of US debt, doubling their share to 9 per cent of total US Treasury purchases over the past four years. They have been borrowing with extreme leverage on the repo market – a core part of financial plumbing – in order to extract arbitrage gains. Both the IMF and the Bank for International Settlements have warned that this structure is an accident waiting to happen. It amplified a spiral of forced selling and a near meltdown of the US Treasury market in the COVID panic of March 2020. The critical point is that the whole US financial and fiscal system has never been so sensitive to short-term interest rates.



Related Article Opinion

Japan Why fears of a Japanese implosion have the world on edge Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Kevin Warsh, the untested new Fed chairman, faces an invidious choice. The indecent manner of his appointment degraded his credibility before he even started. Markets know that President Donald Trump persecuted his predecessor for refusing to cut rates and refusing to become the infamous Arthur Burns of our age. They also know that Warsh’s billionaire father-in-law is a close Trump confederate and a key author of the Greenland grab. Warsh struggled to articulate a coherent intellectual argument after the most recent policy meeting for why he was not raising rates. He could not explain how he intends to bring stubborn US inflation back towards the 2 per cent target when it is clearly going the other way. “Sternly staring at inflation until it melts before our withering gaze is not an option,” fellow Fed board member Christopher Waller said. Warsh faced the unusual rebuke of three voting dissenters and some have been outspoken to the point of contempt. The market verdict has been lapidary.



Warsh argues that AI is deflationary and therefore overrides the Phillips Curve, making it possible to combine blistering growth with low inflation. I am friendly to this line of thinking, but it is not entirely convincing coming from Warsh, who used to be a chest-beating “inflation nutter”. Many suspect that he has latched on to this idea as a pretext for doing Trump’s bidding. Reports that he talks to Trump “all the time” confirm the fears. Previous Fed chairman Jerome Powell’s working code was always that the proper level of intercourse between the US president and the Fed chairman is “zero”. Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh struggled to articulate a coherent intellectual argument after the most recent policy meeting for why he was not raising rates. Bloomberg The Dornbusch adage in the markets is that fiscal and financial crises take longer to happen than you think possible but then happen faster than you ever imagined. We know that US federal debt is compounding at a rate of 3.5 per cent of GDP each year. The mechanical rise in entitlements – ie, middle-class welfare – has been part of the landscape for a long time. Trump 1.0 tax cuts, COVID and Joe Biden’s Rooseveltian New Deal together pushed the envelope a lot further. Trump 2.0’s One Big, Beautiful Bill tests the limits.



Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war Trump’s great humiliation: Middle East may be entering a post-American era Peter Hartcher Political and international editor The IMF forecasts a US general government deficit of 7.4 per cent of GDP or higher every single year from 2026 to 2031. Now Trump wants to raise the Pentagon budget by 60 per cent and fritter away $275 billion on his “golden fleet” of Trump-class battleships – an idée fixe ever since he watched the 1950s telly series Victory at Sea. It takes a serious trigger to detonate a crisis of financial confidence in a great power with deep economic strengths and a world reserve currency. Military overstretch is usually to blame, the cause of imperial Spain’s default in 1575 and Britain’s convertibility crisis in 1947. The ingredients for some sort of American financial crisis are falling into place, disguised for now – but also compounded – by the AI bubble. The global market no longer has full faith in the management of the US Treasury and the Fed. The Dornbusch adage in the markets is that fiscal and financial crises take longer to happen than you think possible but then happen faster than you ever imagined.



The US has stopped upholding free trade and open navigation, switching sides to become the chief instigator of piracy and world disorder. It has squandered much of its arsenal on an ill-planned war that it cannot end without accepting humiliation and that has shown the US to be a weaker military power than we all thought. It has further wrecked US alliances and largely played into the hands of Xi Jinping’s revanchist China. The disaster is nearly complete. Now we await the US midterm elections. Should the democratic transfer of power in Congress be obstructed by meddling with the results in swing states, we may have our trigger. World.title: I’ve flown planes into Sydney more than 1000 times. These near-misses don’t surprise me
World.content:
NationalAviation Opinion I’ve flown planes into Sydney more than 1000 times. These near-misses don’t surprise me David Evans Former Qantas captain August 14, 2026 — 5:08pm

August 14, 2026 — 5:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After almost five decades in the aviation business flying to all corners of the globe, I can assure you that some of the most complicated parts of any journey are not the actual flying but the taxiing to and from a busy runway. I was the captain of an A380 lined up on a runway on the north complex of Los Angles (LAX) waiting for my take-off clearance when another aircraft landing on the parallel runway turned off and crossed the runway I was lined up on. As that “intruder” aircraft entered my runway all the lights on the ground in front of me turned bright red, leaving me in no doubt it was unsafe to take off. In this example, no one was at fault as I had not yet received my take-off clearance and air traffic control (ATC) had cleared the other aircraft to cross in front of me. But I was grateful for the automated back-up system just in case a super-busy human made a mistake. By all reports, it was the pilots of the Virgin 737 who saw the Qantas 737 crossing the runway it had been cleared to take off on last Sunday. Michael Howard I have flown into and out of Sydney Airport 1055 times according to my logbook, and I have to say the system of monitoring ground movement of aircraft, on active runways and taxiways, is not as good as I’ve seen in places like LAX. By all reports, it was the pilots of the Virgin 737 who saw the Qantas 737 crossing the runway it had been cleared to take off on last Sunday – the third incident in recent weeks. But what if they hadn’t, or there was low visibility?



Almost all aspects of modern aviation are standardised, from departure to climb out to cruise, and then descent and approach to land. Doesn’t matter if it’s Sydney, London or New York. All aspects of the flying sequence have become standardised to such an extent that – barring weather or unforseen circumstances – a pilot follows a very prescribed procedure. Those daring young men and women in their non-flying machines at air traffic control co-ordinate this aerial ballet to achieve a safe standard of separation between aircraft. It’s a complex task, so to help human air traffic controllers, modern ATC systems have various electronic alerts to warn if safety standards are compromised or if an error has brought aircraft too close together. Flightradar24 shows the latest near miss to be made public: The Virgin 737 is beginning its take-off as the Qantas 737 crosses runway 34L at Sydney Airport. Flightradar24 What’s not standardised is the airport complex itself. Every airport is different and some are way more complicated than others. On the ground, an airport is usually divided into two distinct parts – runways and taxiways. Any movement on or in the vicinity of an active runway is managed by a controller on an ATC Tower frequency. To add a little more complexity, in Sydney’s case there are two Sydney Tower controllers for each of Sydney’s parallel runways. Conversely, aircraft moving around the taxiways are under the control of another ATC group known as Surface Movement Control. Those in charge of ATC ground movement also have a separate radio frequency and go by the call sign of Sydney Ground. As there are separate parts of the airport and radio congestion increases with an increase in traffic movement, those roles can be divided into more than one ground frequency.



To get from the terminal to your take-off runway or from your landing back to the terminal, a pilot may need to speak to up to four or five different ATC individuals. All these controllers must co-ordinate with one another as your aircraft may have to cross active runways and avoid other aircraft trying to do the same thing. Related Article Aviation Virgin plane aborts take-off as Qantas plane crosses Sydney runway Added to the mix are aircraft under tow, which we saw in the case of the second near-miss at Sydney, with a Qatar 777 almost colliding with a Jetstar A320. Sometimes an aircraft needs to move from a terminal gate to some other place on the airport complex. This could be to a maintenance hangar or to a remote parking space, as the aircraft may have a long layover before its next flight. The tug driver is a highly skilled and trained person who is also in contact with ATC and is required to follow ATC instructions when on the move. If it all sounds ridiculously complex, that’s because it is. When an aircraft is airborne, there is a collision avoidance system that provides an audible warning if a plane is on a collision course with another aircraft. Three near-misses in recent weeks at Sydney Airport are also audible warning that it’s time to take a better look at the collision avoidance systems we have on the ground. Yes, lots of air traffic controllers were laid off during COVID, and experience is hard to replace. But in an industry like aviation, redundancies need to be factored in after redundancies take place, for the safety of everyone involved.



As our Australian airspace continues to expand and congestion at our major airports increases, it’s time for CASA to investigate this type of safety system to help aid those hard-working and understaffed air traffic controllers who do a damn fine job under difficult circumstances, where the cost of a mistake is catastrophe. World.title: Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge threat letter included sender’s real name
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge threat letter included sender’s real name Lachlan Abbott August 14, 2026 — 5:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A man has admitted to sending Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge a threatening letter demanding $100,000 on a hotel bill with his real name on the back. Brendon Berry, 54, pleaded guilty to sending the menacing letter, which was sent to Beveridge’s home last year. Beveridge says he has never met Berry, nor heard of him until the letter. Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge. AFL Photos via Getty Images Melbourne Magistrates’ Court heard on Friday that Beveridge was “shocked and angry” when he opened the letter, which referenced the Moran crime family, after he returned from an interstate trip on June 28, 2025. Prosecutor Andrew McCowan said the letter did not detail specific threats, but insinuated them, prompting extra security for Beveridge at an AFL match against North Melbourne.



“No one likes a hero or a liar. Now you know you have done a bad thing. Do yourself a favour and for once in your life do the right thing, pay what you owe,” the letter said, according to a summary read out in court. “No tomorrow, and this is it. I’m no f---wit pal and it’s hurt me like the Moran’s [sic] hurt Carl. If you think life is a joke it’s not. No second chance my friend, take stock.” Brendon Berry outside court on Friday. Lachlan Abbott The letter, which Berry’s defence lawyer conceded was “unsophisticated”, then referenced late Collingwood footballer Darren Millane, who died in a car crash in 1991. “P.S. Darren Millane, do you remember a fair dusting-off wasn’t it. How many chances do you want. No more.”



Beveridge’s victim impact statement made it clear he did not feel sufficiently intimidated to comply with the demand to pay $100,000 into Berry’s bank account. “I found it deeply disturbing that a person who did not know me could be so callous as to strike fear into everyone close to me in my life,” Beveridge’s statement said. “The letter triggered a side of me that I now know is there if I’m ever threatened like this again.” Getty Images “What frustrated me most was the disregard shown for the impact such a letter could have … it almost sent me down a vigilante-thinking track.” Beveridge added: “The letter triggered a side of me that I now know is there if I’m ever threatened like this again.”



Beveridge initially tuned into the hearing on Friday morning but was not present on an online link in the afternoon when the matter was eventually called. Defence lawyer Katie Powell said the letter was “unsophisticated” and “inexplicable” as Berry was unable to provide much reason about why he sent it. Magistrate Siobhan Whittle then intervened to add: “That’s why it has such a chilling quality.” Powell said Berry believed he went to school with Beveridge in the 1980s, but this was disputed by the Western Bulldogs coach. “He realises, of course, that he should not have sent that letter,” Powell said, adding: “It had nothing to do with Mr Beveridge’s occupation as a public figure.”



The court heard Berry had a notable criminal history, including being jailed for an aggravated burglary with a firearm, but had stayed out of trouble since his last sentence in 2014. His defence lawyer said he was an Aboriginal man with mental health troubles who had been unemployed for much of his adult life. “At this point, I’m concerned about the factors that have driven this offending which are something unresolved from your client’s perspective,” Whittle said. “At this point, I’m going to have him assessed for a community corrections order [CCO] with a mental health appointment.” Berry remained silent for much of the hearing, apart from letting out a loud sigh and assuring the magistrate he would “absolutely” co-operate when he was assessed for a CCO.



Berry will return to court next Thursday to hear his sentence for one count of using a postal service to menace and one count of failing to answer bail. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: A $60b GST fiasco: State vs state argument erupts between WA and ‘east coast whingers’
World.content:
PoliticsFederalGST A $60b GST fiasco: State vs state argument erupts between WA and ‘east coast whingers’ Shane Wright Updated August 14, 2026 — 5:02pm ,first published 2:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An interstate argument has erupted over revelations that the system that carves-up the GST is so broken that a bushfire in NSW would deliver a multimillion-dollar financial windfall to Western Australia, with accusations “east coasters” are whingers and that WA has become a petrostate. A scathing interim report by the Productivity Commission into the GST allocation system put in place by Scott Morrison in 2018 labels the deal a “mistake” that could end up costing federal taxpayers up to $12 billion a year or more than is spent on the nation’s air force. A bushfire in NSW would lead to extra revenue for Western Australia under the “perverse” GST deal. Getty Images As revealed by this masthead, the commission found the current allocation system is on track to cost federal taxpayers up to $60 billion and is failing all of its key objectives while making the annual GST carve-up less equitable and more complex. The 2018 deal was put in place after a collapse in Western Australia’s share of the GST despite the state being in a domestic recession caused by the end of the decade’s mining boom.



Morrison, the then treasurer, came up with a new system that topped up Western Australia’s share until it received the equivalent of 75¢ for every dollar of GST notionally raised by the state. It would then change to the current system, where no jurisdiction can get a smaller share of each dollar raised than either NSW or Victoria. A “no-worse-off” guarantee was put in place, which has been extended by the Albanese government, to 2030, that ensures the GST of every other state and territory is not reduced. The Productivity Commission report, delivered to the nation’s treasurers on Friday, found the 2018 deal had effectively created a two-tier GST allocation system where only one state – Western Australia – got ahead. Commission deputy chair Alex Robson said the GST system was meant to deliver each state and territory enough cash so they could provide similar levels of services and infrastructure to their residents.



Instead, the 2018 reforms had undermined that principle while also not working as the Morrison government had expected. Related Article Analysis

GST Please sir … don’t give WA any more money “The 2018 changes tried to achieve too much and moved too far away from the system’s core objective,” he said. “The result is a system that is now more complex, less consistent and more costly.” The commission found the 2018 changes created perverse outcomes, almost all of which benefit Western Australia at the expense of the rest of the federation and federal taxpayers.



Commissioner Angela Jackson said under the pre-2018 system, if NSW suffered a substantial bushfire, then it would receive extra GST to deal with the disaster’s impact. That extra money would come from every other state and territory. But that has been upended by a “perverse” system under which NSW’s share of the GST is a floor, below which no other state or territory’s share of the tax can fall. That means Western Australia gains a windfall from a NSW disaster while the government of NSW would receive slightly less. West Australian Premier Roger Cook and Treasurer Rita Saffioti launched a campaign to protect the GST deal. WAtoday “Under the current system, if NSW is hit by a natural disaster and spends money on the recovery, it receives more GST to reflect its increased need,” she said. “But under the standard state benchmark, Western Australia also receives more GST from the other states, for a natural disaster it didn’t have.”



Victoria could end up in the same position as NSW if, as expected, its share of GST declines over the next few years. Not only is Western Australia better off from a NSW bushfire, an increase in the price of iron ore – which would previously be shared among the rest of the federation – means it could keep the windfall from higher mining royalties and enjoy an increase in the GST pool. If iron ore prices, currently around $US95 a tonne, were to climb towards $US200 a tonne, then the annual cost to federal taxpayers of not leaving states and territories worse off would reach $12 billion. The 2018 system has delivered Western Australia so much extra revenue that the federal government would have to find $47 billion this year to share with every other jurisdiction to match WA’s financial position. The Productivity Commission, however, has offered three possible changes. They include returning to the pre-2018 system but with the federal treasurer able to direct the Commonwealth Grants Commission, which calculates the annual GST carve-up, to take into account situations where a single state may have a dominant financial position in a particular part of the economy.



Related Article Opinion

GST The GST is broken, and hurting NSW and Victoria badly Shane Wright Senior economics correspondent Another option is to return to the pre-2018 system with the federal government then making direct grants to WA to offset its small share of the GST. WA Premier Roger Cook lambasted the report’s findings, saying it was an assault on his state receiving its fair of the GST which needed the cash to continue to be the nation’s economic engine room. He labelled all other premiers and chief ministers who want the system to change as “east coast whingers”. But NSW Premier Chris Minns said every other state and territory needed a fair share of the GST, likening WA’s demands to the behaviour of a petrostate.



“We’re now in a situation where WA is so wealthy and so rich they are competing and bidding on NSW rugby league games and putting tens of millions of dollars on the table,” he said. “You’re seeing similar behaviour from Gulf states like Saudi Arabia and the UAE and Dubai, and almost for the same reason because they’re digging up natural resources and they’ve got billions of dollars to spend.” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese reassured West Australians they would continue to get a “fair deal”, while the Liberal Party also vowed to protect the 2018 arrangement. The commission plans to hold hearings into its interim report through September, with a final report due by year’s end. Independent economist Saul Eslake, a long-time critic of the Morrison deal, said the commission’s recommendations were a test for both the government and opposition if they believed in protecting the federal budget. World.title: Households cut health insurance as claim payouts rise
World.content:
New Zealanders are cutting back on their health insurance, just as the amount being paid out in health insurance claims increases.

A report commissioned by the Financial Services Council showed 9 percent of people with health insurance terminated their policies last year, up from 7 percent in 2022.

At the same time, the average health insurance claim paid per member increased from $1097 in 2021 to $1921 in 2025.

"The evidence shows insurance is already providing billions of dollars of funding, expanding access to care and protecting families from the financial consequences of illness and death. The opportunity for government is to recognise and strengthen that contribution as part of a more resilient New Zealand health system," Financial Services Council chief executive Kirk Hope said.

Health insurance premiums have risen sharply recently, up almost 75 percent in the past five years alone.

Hope said it was problematic that, as health insurance usage was increasing and treatment costs were rising, households were struggling with the cost of cover.

"Just as New Zealand needs every part of the health system working better together, people are cutting back the very cover that helps them access care sooner."

People who completely dropped their health insurance would usually need to go back through the underwriting process to take it out again, which could mean pre-existing conditions were not covered.

Kirk Hope RNZ / Richard Tindiller

About 35 percent of adults have private health insurance.

Of those, 43 percent are covered through an employer or group scheme.

Hope said the Government could help by removing fringe benefit tax from employee-funded insurance.

"It's a very effective way, it's community-rated and it's not underwritten so it's a very effective way for people to get access if the employer is providing low-cost or no-cost health insurance for them, but it's very expensive for employers because they have to incur a 50 percent to 70 percent tax on premiums."
